title: The home dressmakers' guide
needIt: Teaches measuring, cutting and sewing a garment at home, a skill that saves money.

chapters.title: Common stitches and seams

passages.old: How often I have heard women say: *'I would give a great deal to be able to sew nicely." And yet the ability to sew neatly, giving a workmanlike appearance to all seams, is not a gift but the result of painstaking effort. Any woman, young or old, may possess this accomplishment if she will faithfully persist in her endeavor to sew evenly and neatly and not be satisfied with stitches taken ill a haphazard manner. The appearance of the finished garment depends much upon the kind of stitches put into it. • AMONG the first and essential things the home dressmaker should become familiar with, upon taking up the actual work of dressmaking are the common stitches and seams; what they are termed and how they serve.
passages.plain: You may have heard women say that they would give a lot to be able to sew well. However, sewing neatly and making seams look professional is not a natural gift. It is the result of hard work. Any woman, whether young or old, can learn this skill. You must work hard to sew evenly and neatly. You should not be satisfied with stitches that are messy. The look of a finished garment depends on the types of stitches you use. One of the first and most important things you must learn is the common stitches and seams. You need to know what they are called and how they work.

passages.old: Some of the most important ones follow : Bastings Bastings are temporary stitches put in to hold the fabric together until the finishing stitches can be made. Often in a vain attempt to save time, the home-sewer will substitute pins for bastings, or run up the seams upon the sewihg machine doing away entirely with any attempt at basting. This always results in loss of time in the end and invariably proves that ''haste makes waste." Even Bastings DIAGRAJM 1 The Home Dressmakers' Guide Even Bastings, are longer than the running stitch, but are taken in the same manner. (See Diagram 1.) Do not take too long a stitch, if you do it is likely to slip and shove before the presser foot of your machine, causing endless difficulty.
passages.plain: Some of the most important steps are listed below. Bastings are temporary stitches. You use them to hold the fabric together until you can make the final stitches. Sometimes a home sewer tries to save time by using pins instead of basting. Other times, they sew the seams on a sewing machine without basting at all. This always wastes time in the end. It proves that haste makes waste. Bastings are longer than a running stitch. You make them in the same way. Look at Diagram 1. Do not make a stitch that is too long. If you do, it will likely slip and move before the presser foot of your machine. This will cause endless difficulty.

passages.old: The even basting is the first stitch used in the construction of all garments and is used in all seams that are to be sewed with the sewing machine. Uneven Bastings DIAGRAM 2 Uneven bastings are made by taking two small stitches and one long one. (See Diagram 2.) The uneven basting is used w^hen basting two pieces of cloth together, to hold them in place while w^orking on the garment. Diagonal Basting DIAGRAM 3 Diagonal basting is always used when basting cloth on to the lining or canvass. The stitches are taken crosswise with the point of the needle toward you.
passages.plain: Even basting is the first stitch used to make all clothes. You use it on all seams that you will later sew with a sewing machine. Uneven basting is shown in Diagram 2. You make uneven bastings by taking two small stitches and one long stitch. You use uneven basting to hold two pieces of cloth together while you work on the garment. Diagonal basting is shown in Diagram 3. You always use diagonal basting when you sew cloth onto lining or canvas. You take these stitches crosswise with the needle point facing toward you.

passages.old: You may w^ork from the right to the left or from the left to the right, which ever is the most convenient. These stitches may be taken any size according to where they are being used. The Home Dressmakers' Guide Running Stitch Running stitches are a succession of small stitches, the stitches and spaces in between being of equal length. (See Overcasting DIAGRAM 5 Overcasting is used to finish the raw edges of a seam if you are not going to bind it. Starting at the right hand end of the cloth, work toward the left, smoothing the threads of the material down with the left thumb and finger.
passages.plain: You can work from right to left or from left to right. Choose whichever way is most convenient for you. You can make these stitches any size depending on where you use them. A running stitch is a series of small stitches. The stitches and the spaces between them must be the same length. See the Overcasting diagram. Overcasting is used to finish the raw edges of a seam if you do not plan to bind it. Start at the right hand end of the cloth. Work toward the left. Use your left thumb and finger to smooth down the threads of the material.

passages.old: Overcast by taking one stitch at a tim.e, being careful not to draw the stitches too tight. (See Diagram 5.) Tailor Tacks or Trace Threads Tailor tacks or trace threads must be used if any garment is to be put together accurately. Having chalked a design upon one side of the folded cloth, tailor tacks, or tVace threads will mark both sides alike'. You may also lay your pattern on the two thicknesses of cloth and follow the design marked upon the pattern taking the tailor tacks The Home Dressmakers' Guide through the paper and double cloth and thus marking both sides of the garment perfectly alike.
passages.plain: Overcast the edges by taking one stitch at a time. Be careful not to pull the stitches too tight. Look at Diagram 5. You must use tailor tacks or trace threads to put a garment together accurately. You should first mark a design on one side of the folded cloth with chalk. Then use tailor tacks or trace threads to mark both sides the same way. You can also lay your pattern on the two layers of cloth. Follow the design on the pattern while pushing the tailor tacks through the paper and the cloth. This will mark both sides of the garment perfectly the same.

passages.old: Where two parts of a garment are to be joined together both should be plainlymarked with tailor tacks. Pockets, yokes, plaits, waist-line, and hip line should be outlined in this way. Where the hem is to be turned and wherever a mark for a guide is needed these tailor tacks should be employed. Using a double basting thread, proceed to baste through both thicknesses of cloth, alternating with one long stitch The long stitches may be an inch long and sufficiently loose to permit of a pencil or finger being slipped under them.
passages.plain: Mark the places where you join two parts of a garment with tailor tacks. You should outline pockets, yokes, plaits, the waistline, and the hip line this way. Use these tailor tacks wherever you need to turn a hem or need a guide mark. Use a double basting thread. Sew through both layers of cloth. Alternate your stitches with one long stitch. These long stitches can be one inch long. Make them loose enough so that you can slide a pencil or your finger under them.

passages.old: Now cut through the middle of the long stitch, and separating the cloth slightly, clip the small stitches between the two pieces of cloth. You may now remove the paper pattern without tearing it and opening the cloth, you will find both sides marked alike. Back Stitch DIAGRAM 7 The back stiteh is used when making garments by hand. Seams sewed with a back stitch will be firmer and stronger and can be made to look like sewing machine stitching. (See The Home Dressmakers' Guide Knot your thread and bring your needle through from the under side of the cloth.
passages.plain: Cut through the middle of the long stitch. Pull the two pieces of cloth slightly apart. Cut the small stitches between the two pieces of cloth. You can now remove the paper pattern. Do not tear the pattern or open the cloth. You will see that both sides are marked the same way. Diagram 7 shows the back stitch. You use the back stitch when you make clothes by hand. Seams made with a back stitch are firm and strong. They can look like sewing machine stitches. Knot your thread. Bring your needle through from the underside of the cloth.

passages.old: Then take the stitch by putting the point of the needle in above the first hole and bringing it out below the first hole, thus bringing the first hole in the Take each succeeding stitch back by putting the needle through the next to the last hole made and bringing it out below the last hole made by 'the needle. Take a small uniform stitch. Slip Stitch or Blind Stitch diagra:vi 8 The slip stitch is used when hemming or sewing on facing or at any other part of the garment where stitches are to be made invisible.
passages.plain: Take the first stitch by putting the needle point in above the first hole. Bring the needle out below that same hole. This brings the first hole into the stitch. For each next stitch, put the needle through the hole before the last one. Bring the needle out below the very last hole you made. Take small and even stitches. This is the slip stitch or blind stitch. You use the slip stitch when hemming. You also use it when sewing on facing. Use it on any part of the garment where you want the stitches to be invisible.

passages.old: Knot the thread and bring the needle out from the crease of the fold of the hem, thus hiding the knot in the fold. Just catch a thread on the body of the cloth with the needle and run the needle back into the fold of the hem again hiding a long stitch in the crease of the fold and again bringing the needle out from the fold of the hem and just catching a thread of the body of the cloth. When the hem is pressed down the stitches are in- When sewing on sheer material the best results are obtained by using a fine needle and, splitting the thread, use one strand only; When this is done the stitches are more easily made invisible.
passages.plain: Tie a knot in the thread. Pull the needle out from the crease of the hem fold. This hides the knot inside the fold. Catch one thread of the cloth with the needle. Run the needle back into the hem fold. Hide a long stitch in the crease of the fold. Bring the needle out from the hem fold again. Catch one thread of the cloth again. The stitches will be hidden when you press down the hem. Use a fine needle when you sew on sheer material. Split the thread and use only one strand. This makes the stitches easier to hide.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide Hemming Stitch DIAGRAM 9 Diagram 9 shows a common hemming stitch. This stitch is used on any hem. Tacking Stitch The tacking stitch is used when putting the lining into the jacket or at any part of a garment where the cloth is just tacked together and not sewed firmly. The tacking stitch is a back stitch and a long stitch or two or three back stitches, one on top of the other, and then a long stitch. Cross Stitch The cross stitch is used in many places in the making and finishing of garments.
passages.plain: Diagram 9 shows a common hemming stitch. You can use this stitch on any hem. You use the tacking stitch when you put the lining into a jacket. You also use it on any part of a garment where the cloth is just tacked together and not sewn firmly. The tacking stitch is a back stitch. It is a long stitch or two or three back stitches on top of each other and then a long stitch. You use the cross stitch in many places when making and finishing garments.

passages.old: It is used to finish seams and. The Home Dressmakers' Guide hems. It is also used in sewing the under collar on to the jacket. Begin at the left hand end of the seam and work :^om left to right. With the needle pointing to the left, seam. Bring the needle down and toward the right and take another short stitch like the one taken at the top. This gives a long slanting, or diagonal stitch, between the two short stitches. Remembering to keep the needle pointing to the left, bring the needle up to the top of the seam and toward the right causing the second long diagonal stitch to cross the first, and take another short stitch.
passages.plain: You use this to finish seams and hems. You also use it to sew the under collar onto the jacket. Start at the left end of the seam. Work from left to right. Point your needle to the left and sew. Bring the needle down and toward the right. Take another short stitch like the first one. This creates a long diagonal stitch between the two short stitches. Keep your needle pointing to the left. Bring the needle up to the top of the seam and toward the right. This makes the second long diagonal stitch cross the first one. Take another short stitch.

passages.old: Working from left to right with the needle pointing toward the left you will have no difficulty with the cross stitch. Chain Stitch The chain stitch can be used to finish hems or seams and is always used when sewing on the right side of the cloth. It is also used in making pretty designs on belts, collars or the yokes of blouses. In making the chain stitch work from right to left. Knot the thread and bring the needle through from the wrong side of the cloth at the right hand end of the seam.
passages.plain: Work from left to right with the needle pointing toward the left. You will not have any trouble with the cross stitch. You can use the chain stitch to finish hems or seams. You always use it when sewing on the right side of the cloth. You also use it to make pretty designs on belts, collars, or the yokes of blouses. When you make the chain stitch, work from right to left. Knot the thread. Bring the needle through from the wrong side of the cloth at the right hand end of the seam.

passages.old: Next form a loop with the thread (See Diagram 12) and take your stitch in the middle of the loop. Forming a second loop with the thread take the second stitch in the middle of the last loop at the same time forming a third loop. Continue to make stitches, each time throwing the thread in a loop and placing the needle back each time in the middle of the last loop stitch. Do not pull the thread tight as it will not make a nice looking chain if you do.
passages.plain: Next, make a loop with the thread. Look at Diagram 12. Take your stitch in the middle of that loop. Make a second loop with the thread. Take the second stitch in the middle of the last loop while you make a third loop at the same time. Keep making stitches. Every time, throw the thread into a loop. Place the needle back into the middle of the last loop stitch. Do not pull the thread tight. If you pull it tight, the chain will not look nice.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide SEAMS Binding Seams It is very necessary to bind seams if you are to have a well finished garment. When seams are not bound they should be overcast. If you are going to use the straight ribbon binding you will find it much easier to sew on if you will fold it in the centre and crease it with a warm flat iron ; it will also be easier to get the centre of the ribbon on the edge of the seam. It is better to sew the straight ribbon binding on by hand using a small running stitch and sewing it on from the right side of the seam.
passages.plain: You must bind seams to make a well finished garment. If you do not bind seams, you should overcast them. You can use straight ribbon binding. It is easier to sew if you fold the ribbon in the center. You should crease it with a warm flat iron. This also makes it easier to line up the center of the ribbon with the edge of the seam. You should sew the straight ribbon binding by hand. Use a small running stitch. Sew it on from the right side of the seam.

passages.old: A bias binding may French Seams French seams are used when making garments out of any sheer material such as crepes or voiles, and at any part of the garment where the seam can be seen through the material. French seams are desirable in blouses, dresses, childrens' clothes and lingerie, such as camisoles, combinations and gowns. First sew the seam on the right side of the garment by hand, using a small running stitch. Do not sew on the exact seam line using the full depth of the seam allowance but sew outside of the seam line.
passages.plain: You use French seams when you make clothes from sheer materials like crepe or voile. You also use them anywhere the seam can be seen through the fabric. French seams are good for blouses, dresses, children's clothes, and lingerie like camisoles, combinations, and gowns. First, sew the seam on the right side of the garment by hand. Use a small running stitch. Do not sew on the exact seam line using the full depth of the seam allowance. Instead, sew outside of the seam line.

passages.old: Next trim the seam off close to the stitching and turn the seam to the wrong side The Home Dressmakers* Guide of the garment. Then baste carefully on the exact seam line hiding the trimmed raw edges in the seam. (See Diagram IJ^.) Now sew the seam on the sewing machine. If the machine tension is tight and you are sewing on net or other thin material lay a piece of paper under the seam and sew through it, afterwards removing the paper. . French Felled Seam Sew the seam on the wrong side of the garment the full depth of the seam allowance using a small running stitch.
passages.plain: Trim the seam close to the stitching. Turn the seam to the wrong side of the garment. Carefully baste the seam on the exact line. This hides the trimmed raw edges inside the seam. Look at Diagram IJ. Now sew the seam on the sewing machine. If the machine tension is tight and you are sewing on net or other thin material, place a piece of paper under the seam. Sew through the paper and then remove it. For a French Felled Seam, sew the seam on the wrong side of the garment. Use a small running stitch to sew the full depth of the seam allowance.

passages.old: Then trim off one side of the seam close to the stitching. If there is a bias and a straight side to the seam trim off the bias side. Next fold the remaining side of the seam over the one that has been trimmed off and sew it on the sewing machine. From one side it will look like a binding and from the other side the stitches only will show. This Flat Felled Seam Sew just a common seam on the wrong side of the garment with the sewing machine, sewing on the exact seam line.
passages.plain: Trim one side of the seam close to the stitching. If the seam has a bias side and a straight side, trim off the bias side. Fold the remaining side of the seam over the side you trimmed. Sew it together using a sewing machine. One side will look like a binding. The other side will only show the stitches. This is a Flat Felled Seam. It is a common seam on the wrong side of a garment. You sew it with a sewing machine directly on the seam line.

passages.old: Then trim off one side of the seam close to the stitching and turn the remaining edge of the seam in as you would for a hem, covering the stitching and trimmed edge. Tress this down flat on the body of the garment and stitch right through with the sewing machine. This may be The Home Dressmakers' Guide Sinirle Welt Seam DIAGRAM i: Sew a common seam on the wrong side of the garment with the sewing machine, sewing on the exact seam line. Press the seam flat on the wrong side of the garment using the entire seam allowance and baste it down carefully.
passages.plain: First, sew a regular seam on the wrong side of the garment. You must sew exactly on the seam line. Next, press the seam flat on the wrong side of the garment. Use the entire seam allowance to do this. Then, baste it down carefully. After that, trim one side of the seam close to the stitching. Turn the other edge of the seam inward. Do this just like you would for a hem. This should cover the stitching and the trimmed edge. Press this down flat against the body of the garment. Finally, sew through it completely with your sewing machine.

passages.old: Then turning the garment right side up put in one row of sewing machine stitching. This seam may be finished any desired width according to the prevailing style. (See Dia- Double Welt Seam Proceed in the same way as for the single welt seam putting two rows of sewing machine stitching on the right The Home Dressmakers' Guide Slot Seam A slot seam is made by laying the two edges of the cloth together with the seams turned under reinforced beneath with another strip of cloth as shown in Dia- Smocking DIAGRAM 20 First decide on the design and determine the amount of fullness to be held in.
passages.plain: Turn the garment so the front side faces up. Sew one row of stitching with your sewing machine. You can choose any width for this seam based on the current style. For a double welt seam, follow the same steps as the single welt seam. You must put two rows of sewing machine stitching on the right. For a slot seam, lay the two edges of the cloth together. Turn the seams under. Reinforce them with another strip of cloth as shown in Diagram 20. For smocking, first decide on your design. Then decide how much fullness you want to include.

passages.old: Next mark with small dots, one-half inch apart, the depth of the tucks desired to hold in the fullness. (See Diagram 20.) Then placing the first two tucks together, sew them at the dots. Sew the first dots together taking two or three stitches to form a knot. Then slip the needle under on the wrong side of the cloth and skipping one dot join the tucks together at the third dot. Continue to sew at every other dot until the full length of the design is finished. Then bring up another tuck and sew it to the last tuck only and at the dots that were skipped.
passages.plain: Mark the depth of the tucks you want to use. Place these marks as small dots that are one-half inch apart. Look at Diagram 20. Put the first two tucks together. Sew them at the dots. Sew the first dots together. Use two or three stitches to make a knot. Put the needle under the cloth on the wrong side. Skip one dot. Join the tucks at the third dot. Keep sewing at every other dot. Finish the full length of the design. Bring up another tuck. Sew it to the last tuck only. Also sew it at the dots that you skipped.

passages.old: Place one tuck after another sewing only to the last one and at every other dot until the design is completed. (See DIAGRAM 21 The Home Dressmakers* Guide Arrow Head ARROWHEADS are used considerably for trimming, finishing plaits, darts, ends of pockets and at many other places. They are made in the following way : First outline the size desired with the button hole twist or the embroidery silk you are going to use. This outline in the form of a triangle may be one-half inch wide at the base and one inch long at the bring the needle through from the wrong side of the cloth at the lower right hand corner and bring it up to the point and put it through to the wrong side again just at the left of the point of the triangle.
passages.plain: Sew one tuck after another. Only sew to the last one and at every other dot until you finish the design. See Diagram 21. Arrowheads are used often for trimming. They finish plaits, darts, pocket ends, and many other places. You make them in the following way. First, outline the size you want with the buttonhole twist or the embroidery silk you plan to use. This outline is a triangle. It can be one-half inch wide at the base and one inch long at the point. Bring the needle through from the wrong side of the cloth at the lower right hand corner. Bring it up to the point. Put it through to the wrong side again just at the left of the point of the triangle.

passages.old: Bring the needle through from the wrong side of the cloth just at the right of the point of the triangle and put it through to the wrong side again at the lower left hand corner of the outline. Continue in this manner until the outline is all filled in leaving only Bound Button Hole When a slash is made in a girdle, through which to put the ends, the slash can be finished like a bound button hole. Often a slash is made at the waist of a garment and the sash is brought through these slashes.
passages.plain: Take the needle through the cloth from the wrong side. Start just to the right of the triangle point. Put the needle through to the wrong side again at the lower left corner of the outline. Keep doing this until you fill in the whole outline. Leave only the Bound Button Hole empty. When you make a slash in a girdle to put the ends through, you can finish that slash like a bound button hole. Sometimes a slash is made at the waist of a garment. You can pull a sash through these slashes.

passages.old: They also can be finished in the same manner. At many places slits are made to run ends through, these all may be finished like a bound button hole. The first thing to do is to ascertain the size of the button hole required. This is obtained by placing the button to be used on the cloth and marking the diameter of the button with chalk on the right side and follow this line with small basting stitches, giving the length of the button hole on the under side of the cloth.
passages.plain: You can finish these in the same way. In many places, slits are made to run ends through. You can finish all of these like a bound buttonhole. First, you must find the size of the buttonhole you need. To do this, place the button you want to use on the cloth. Mark the diameter of the button with chalk on the right side. Follow this line with small basting stitches. This gives you the length of the buttonhole on the underside of the cloth.

passages.old: The diameter of the button The Home Dressmakers' Guide Then place the piece of cloth to be used for the binding over the mark made for the diameter of the button. Have the right side of the cloth for the binding next to the right side of the cloth of the garment. Then mark the length of the button hole on the wrong side of the binding by using small basting stitches, taking these stitches through both the cloth and the binding. (See Next, determine the width of the binding that is to show from the right side of the garment when the button hole is finished.
passages.plain: Place the piece of cloth for the binding over the mark you made for the button diameter. Put the right side of the binding cloth next to the right side of the garment cloth. Mark the length of the button hole on the wrong side of the binding. Use small basting stitches to do this. Take these stitches through both the cloth and the binding. See the next step to find the width of the binding that should show on the right side of the garment after the button hole is finished.

passages.old: Then sew with the sewing machine a single row of stitching, one above and one below the mark made for the button hole The distance between the mark for the button hole and the rows of sewing machine stitching is the amount the binding will show. One-fourth of an inch between the two rows of sewing machine stitching will make a good looking binding. Now cut the button hole with the scissors following the marked length, but do not cut the button hole the entire length of the stitching, as that would spoil the button hole.
passages.plain: Use your sewing machine to sew one row of stitches above and one row of stitches below the button hole mark. The space between the mark and these rows of stitching shows how much of the binding will be visible. You should leave one-fourth of an inch between the two rows of machine stitching for a good look. Cut the button hole with scissors along the marked length. Do not cut the button hole the entire length of the stitching because that will ruin the button hole.

passages.old: Cut up to within one-fourth inch of each end and mitre from this line to each of the four corners. The corners are mitred by cutting with the scissors as shown at ''/)'' DIAGRAM 'S.i 14 The Home Dressmakers* Guide The last proceedure is to pull the binding through the button hole to the wrong side of the garment. Turn the binding evenly over the edge of the button hole, being careful not to turn any of the body part of the button hole v^ith the binding. It is just the binding that is pulled through and turned over the edge of the button hole.
passages.plain: Cut the fabric up to one-fourth inch from each end. Cut at an angle from this line to each of the four corners. You should cut the corners like the angle shown in Diagram S. The last step is to pull the binding through the buttonhole to the wrong side of the garment. Turn the binding evenly over the edge of the buttonhole. Be careful not to turn any part of the buttonhole itself with the binding. Only the binding should be pulled through and turned over the edge of the buttonhole.

passages.old: None of the body part of the garment must be pulled through (See ''E" Fasten the binding that has been pulled through down to the cloth of the garment on the wrong side. Do this neatly by hand. Do not put any sewing machine stitching on a bound button hole when it will show on the right side of a garment. Press the binding with a warm flat iron. When using sheer material and a slash is to be made for the sash or for trimming, hemstitching may be used instead of binding. When this is the case have the hemstitching the length desired for the slash and clip it in the centre as for picotting. This will look more dainty than binding. The Home Dressmakers' Guide
passages.plain: Do not pull any part of the garment body through. Fasten the binding that you pulled through to the wrong side of the cloth. Sew this neatly by hand. Do not use a sewing machine to stitch a bound buttonhole if it will show on the right side of the garment. Press the binding with a warm flat iron. You can use hemstitching instead of binding when you make a slash for a sash or trimming on sheer material. If you do this, make the hemstitching the length you want for the slash. Clip it in the center like you do for picotting. This will look more dainty than binding.

chapters.why: Understanding foundational sewing techniques remains essential for anyone wanting to create high-quality garments by hand or machine.

chapters.title: Measurements

passages.old: The proper place at which to start to make a garment for yourself is at your own measurements. First take the necessary measurements correctly and then apply them to your pattern, altering your foundation to fit you, and you have robbed dressmaking of most of its annoyances. It will be readily understood that these measurements must be accurate and judgment used in taking them. If, for instance, you take a measurement too snugly, the garment will doubtless be too tight. It is better, however, to take measurements a little loose rather than too snugly, as it is easier trimming off than piecing on.
passages.plain: You should start making a garment for yourself by taking your own measurements. First, take the necessary measurements correctly. Then, apply them to your pattern. Change your foundation to fit you. This will remove most of the problems in dressmaking. You must understand that these measurements must be accurate. You must use good judgment when taking them. For example, if you take a measurement that is too tight, the garment will be too tight. It is better to take measurements a little loose instead of too snugly. It is easier to trim off extra fabric than it is to add pieces on.

passages.old: It is also necessary to have an accurate tape measure. Test your tape carefully and if Fasten a tape around the natural waist of your model, for a waist line, from which to take measurements. This may of course be dispensed with when you shall have become proficient in gauging with the eye. diagram 1, you will now proceed, writing down each measurement as you take it. ure. Measure around the base of the neck; that is, at the line where it joins the body. Measure just back base of the neck to the DIAGRAM 1 tip of the shoulder. 16 The Home Dressmakers' Guide Place the tape measure around the largest part of the bust, close up under the arm and across the shoulder blades, in a straight line to the center of the back.
passages.plain: You must have an accurate tape measure. Test your tape carefully. Fasten a tape around the natural waist of your model to create a waist line for your measurements. You can skip this step once you are good at judging sizes by looking at them. Follow Diagram 1. Write down every measurement as you take it. Measure around the base of the neck. This is the line where the neck joins the body. Measure from the back base of the neck to the tip of the shoulder. Place the tape measure around the largest part of the bust. Keep the tape close under the arm and across the shoulder blades. Keep the tape in a straight line to the center of the back.

passages.old: Standing directly in the rear of your model, hold the union of the tape measure, that is, as you bring it together, firmly between the forefinger and thumb of the left hand, while with your right, thus freed, you run the forefinger* under the tape from back to front, to ascertain the proper amount of fullness required. This then gives you what is called the Bust Line, w^hich, with the Waist Line already determined, are important in the ascertainment of other measurements. 4., The Front Measurement, Is taken from the base of the neck in front down to the waist line.
passages.plain: Stand directly behind your model. Hold the end of the tape measure firmly between your left thumb and forefinger. Use your right hand to slide your forefinger under the tape from back to front. Do this to find the amount of fullness needed. This gives you the Bust Line. The Bust Line and the Waist Line are both important for finding other measurements. Step 4 is the Front Measurement. Take this measurement from the base of the neck in the front down to the waist line.

chapters.title: How to select a skirt pattern

passages.old: PATTERNS, SKIRT How to Select a Skirt Pattern In selecting a pattern for a skirt the lines of the individual should be studied. Regardless of the prevailing fashion one should select a becoming style, one that will add beauty to the figure -and not accentuate the defects. The large, stout v^^oman should have lines that will detract from her size and give the appearance of length. We talk a great deal about lines, perfect lines, beautiful lines, w^hen lines are nothing more than seams in the proper place on the body.
passages.plain: How to Select a Skirt Pattern. When you choose a pattern for a skirt, you should study your own body lines. You should choose a style that looks good on you regardless of current fashions. Choose a style that adds beauty to your figure and does not highlight your flaws. A large or stout woman should choose lines that make her look smaller and taller. People talk a lot about perfect lines or beautiful lines. However, lines are just seams placed in the correct spots on the body.

passages.old: Seams therefore give lines. Plaits sometimes give lines where they are needed, and trimming in just the right place will add much in securing the desired effect. A well-proportioned panel is always becoming to a stout person as it detracts from the width and increases the appearance of length. A slightly raised waist line is also good in securing this effect. A two or three-piece skirt should seldom be worn by a large woman. A gored skirt is better, as it gives the lines so necessary for the stout figure if the skirt is to be becoming.
passages.plain: Seams create lines. Plaits sometimes create lines where they are needed. Trimming in the right place helps you get the effect you want. A well-proportioned panel looks good on a stout person. It makes the width look smaller and makes the person look longer. A slightly raised waist line also helps you get this effect. A large woman should rarely wear a skirt with two or three pieces. A gored skirt is better. It gives the lines that a stout figure needs to look good.

passages.old: There are many styles that may be worn by stout figures, adding grace and not accentuating defects. A tall woman can wear skirts with yokes and plaits. Drapes are also becoming. A small, slender woman can wear the more simple styles. Gathered skirts look well on small, slender figures. Styles should be selected that will increase the appearance of height and not detract from it. When purchasing a pattern for a skirt select the size from the hip measurement rather than from the waist, as the size at the waist is easier altered than at the hip.
passages.plain: There are many styles for stout figures. These styles add grace and do not highlight flaws. A tall woman can wear skirts with yokes and plaits. Drapes are also becoming popular. A small and slender woman can wear simpler styles. Gathered skirts look good on small and slender figures. You should choose styles that make you look taller. Do not choose styles that make you look shorter. When you buy a pattern for a skirt, choose the size based on your hip measurement. Do not choose the size based on your waist. It is easier to change the size at the waist than at the hip.

The skirt pattern should be measured and altered to fit the individual perfectly before the cloth is cut. If all alterations are made in the pattern there is no wasting of material and very little fitting after the skirt is cut out.
passages.plain: If you cannot find a pattern that matches your exact hip measurement, choose a larger size instead of a smaller size. It is easier to make a pattern smaller than it is to make it larger. You should measure and change the skirt pattern to fit you perfectly before you cut the cloth. If you make all the changes to the pattern first, you will not waste any material. You will also have very little fitting to do after you cut out the skirt.

passages.old: Proportioning of Measurements It is of the utmost importance that the skirt should be proportioned properly for the individual. The seams must come in the right place if the skirt is to look well. To do this it is necessary to divide the waist and hip measurements, getting the half and the quarter of them. An easy way to do this is to take your waist or hip measurement and then fold the tape, getting just the half, then folding the half and getting the quarter. It may be that this division will not bring the side seams exactly at the half of you, owing to the amount of flesh in front.
passages.plain: It is very important to proportion the skirt correctly for your body. The seams must be in the right place for the skirt to look good. You must divide your waist and hip measurements to find the half and the quarter of those numbers. One easy way to do this is to take your waist or hip measurement. Fold the tape to find the half. Fold that half again to find the quarter. These divisions might not put the side seams exactly at your side. This happens because of the amount of flesh in the front.

passages.old: Should this be so, place a pin exactly at the center of the right and left side, where the side seams should come, and measure from pin to pin for the front, and from pin to pin for the back. Divide these measurements by folding the tape and you have proportioned your measurements correctly for a two, three or four-piece skirt. If one side is very much larger than the other you can place a pin at the center front and center back and measure from pin to pin, dividing the measurement in the same way.
passages.plain: If this happens, place a pin exactly at the center of the right side and the left side. These are the spots where the side seams will go. Measure from pin to pin for the front. Then measure from pin to pin for the back. Divide these measurements by folding the tape. You now have the correct proportions for a skirt with two, three, or four pieces. If one side is much larger than the other, place a pin at the center front and a pin at the center back. Measure from pin to pin. Divide that measurement in the same way.

passages.plain: All patterns are cut to the proportions of a model. Very few women have measurements that match the model exactly. You can change a three or four piece pattern in the same way you change a two piece pattern. You can alter any skirt to fit you, whether it has a two, three, or four piece foundation. You can also adjust the yokes, girdles, pockets, or any other design parts to match your new measurements. This allows you to keep every detail created by the designer.

passages.old: DIAGRAM ;$ When One Side Measures More Than the Other It often happens that one side length measurement is longer than the other. This can be taken into consideration when the pattern is being altered. Allow for this extra length above the waist line. (See dotted line marked D on Diagram 3.) You can make allowance when placing the pattern on the material. Cut both sides alike to the longest length and trim off the short side afterward. Altering a Skirt Pattern For a High Abdomen It should be remembered that the hip line is the balance line for a skirt.
passages.plain: Sometimes one side of a measurement is longer than the other. You can account for this when you change the pattern. Add the extra length above the waist line. Look at the dotted line marked D on Diagram 3. You can also handle this when you place the pattern on the fabric. Cut both sides to the longest length. Trim off the short side later. Remember that the hip line is the balance line for a skirt. You can alter a skirt pattern for a high abdomen.

passages.old: If the front-length measurement is longer than the back, as is often the case and always when the abdomen is high, the extra length must be added at the top, above the hip line, never at the bottom. (See X in Diagram U, showing the extra length added at the top and tapering off toward the back.) The Home Dressmakers' Guide When a Skirt "Hikes" In Front When a skirt has a tendency to hike up in front it is because the skirt has been cut too low in front at the waist line.
passages.plain: Check the front length and the back length. If the front length is longer than the back, you must add the extra length at the top. This happens often. It always happens if the abdomen is high. Do not add the extra length at the bottom. Look at X in Diagram U. It shows the extra length added at the top. It shows the length tapering off toward the back. This is from The Home Dressmakers' Guide. A skirt hikes up in the front if it is cut too low at the front waist line.

passages.old: To remedy this fault it is necessary to increase the length of the pattern in the front at the waist line, adding a little to the sides and tapering off to nothing gram 4-J Altering a Six Gored Skirt DIAGRAM 4 If, when making a gored skirt, there is to be a panel in the front or back, this panel must be proportioned for the individual. A panel that is too narrow will not look well upon a large women ; the panel should be proportioned to the width of the gores.
passages.plain: To fix this problem, you must make the front of the pattern longer at the waist line. Add a little bit to the sides and make it smaller until it disappears. This is for Diagram 4, Altering a Six Gored Skirt. If you are making a gored skirt with a panel in the front or back, you must size that panel for the person. A panel that is too narrow will not look good on a large woman. The panel should be the same width as the gores.

passages.old: A narrow panel with wide gores will not look right. Regardless of prevailing style the gores and the panel must be proportioned to give the correct lines on the body. When applying individual measurements to a six-gored The Home Dressmakers' Guide skirt pattern and the waist measures more or less than the waist line of the pattern, do not make any change in the panel or on the side of the gore next to the panel. Always make the alteration for increase or decrease of the waist or hip line at the side seam. (See dotted lines in Diagram 5, "A" for decrease of size and ''B" shoiuing the size increased.) If the length of the pattern from the waist line to the hip line is less than you measure cut the pattern across as you did for the two-piece skirt and set in a piece of paper.
passages.plain: A narrow panel with wide gores will not look correct. The gores and the panel must have the right proportions to create the correct lines on the body. When you use your measurements on a six-gored skirt pattern, your waist measurement might be slightly different from the pattern's waist line. Do not change the panel or the side of the gore next to the panel. Always make changes to the waist or hip lines at the side seam. Look at the dotted lines in Diagram 5. Part A shows how to decrease the size. Part B shows how to increase the size. If the pattern length from the waist line to the hip line is shorter than your measurement, cut the pattern across. Do this the same way you did for the two-piece skirt. Then, set in a piece of paper.

passages.old: If it is too long, fold a tuck in the pattern at the same place. Likewise make the alteration for the finished length of the skirt as you did for the two-piece skirt. (See *'X" Diagram 5.) Allowance must be made below the finished length of the skirt for a hem. diagba:vi 6 In all gored skirts having an uneven number of gores, the odd one is placed in front. Thus, when cutting, mark it out first, making it any width desired, according to the size and style you have selected.
passages.plain: If the piece is too long, fold a tuck in the pattern at that same spot. Make the same change for the finished length of the skirt as you did for the two-piece skirt. Look at Diagram 5. You must leave extra space below the finished length of the skirt for the hem. In all gored skirts with an odd number of gores, place the odd one in the front. Mark it out first when you are cutting. Make it any width you want based on the size and style you chose.

passages.old: For instance, a large or The Home Dressmakers' Guide 29 stout woman should have a wider front gore than a woman possessing a slender figure. On the other hand, the prevailing styles, regardless of size, may dictate a wide or narrow front panel. No fixed rule, therefore, may be laid down in this respect. When a suitable front gore or panel has been marked out and cut, subtract from the waist, hip and bottom measurements the number of inches used for the waist, hip and bottom of the front gore or panel.
passages.plain: A large or stout woman should have a wider front gore than a slender woman. However, the current fashion styles might require a wide or narrow front panel regardless of a person's size. There is no fixed rule for this. Once you have marked and cut a suitable front gore or panel, subtract the inches used for the waist, hip, and bottom of that piece from your own waist, hip, and bottom measurements.

passages.old: Divide the remaining number of inches at the waist and hip by the remaining number of gores to be provided for, which in this instance is six, and you will have the individual size of each. The bottom widths of the remaining number of gores should be proportioned as shown in Diagram 6. A Gathered Skirt Pattern A pattern for a straight gathered skirt can be regulated only in length and that can be done at the bottom of the pattern. A Draped Skirt Pattern A draped skirt pattern can only be altered in length and this may also be done at the bottom of the pattern.
passages.plain: Divide the remaining inches of the waist and hip by the number of gores you have left. In this case, there are six gores left. This gives you the size of each gore. You should make the bottom widths of these gores like the ones in Diagram 6. A Gathered Skirt Pattern can only be changed in length. You can do this at the bottom of the pattern. A Draped Skirt Pattern can also only be changed in length. You can do this at the bottom of the pattern too.

passages.old: If there are to be Cascade drapes sewed into the seams they must also be altered in length in proportion to the alteration made for the length of the skirt. How To Cut a High Waist Line Sometimes a high waist line will be more becoming than the natural waist line given on the pattern. The high waist line may be added in the following way: Measure the number of inches you desire the waist line raised above the natural waist line and draw a line parallel to the natural waist line and extending onehalf inch beyond the natural waist line on each side.
passages.plain: If you sew Cascade drapes into the seams, you must change their length. You must change them by the same amount you changed the length of the skirt. Sometimes a high waist line looks better than the natural waist line on the pattern. You can add a high waist line by following these steps. First, measure how many inches you want to raise the waist line above the natural waist line. Next, draw a line parallel to the natural waist line. This line should go one half inch past the natural waist line on each side.

passages.old: Curve to the natural waist line as shown in Diagram 7. The Home Dressmakers' Guide Altering a Plaited Skirt Pattern First you lay the plaits in the pattern following the perforations and determine how it is going to fit. If it is too small let out each plait sufficiently to give you the required amount. Be careful to have each plait a uniform size. If it is too large lap each plait enough to make the pattern fit and pin the plaits carefully. Measure the pattern for the finished length of the skirt and mark with a pencil the line where the hem is turned and also the hem allowance.
passages.plain: Curve the pattern to the natural waist line as shown in Diagram 7. First, lay the plaits in the pattern. Follow the perforations to see how it fits. If the pattern is too small, let out each plait enough to get the size you need. Make sure every plait is the same size. If the pattern is too large, lap each plait enough to make the pattern fit. Pin the plaits carefully. Measure the pattern for the finished length of the skirt. Use a pencil to mark the line where the hem is turned. Also mark the hem allowance.

passages.old: Then draw a line with the pencil on the pattern along the edge of each plait, and another line on the plait, just at the fold where the plait was turned. (See Diagram shoiving thei dotted lines where the plaits are marked. The dotted line "A" shows the mark on the plait and "B*' shows the line along the edge of the DIAGRAM 8 plait.) Trying On the Pattern After the individual measurements have been applied to the pattern and the alterations have all been made in the pattern, pin the pattern together for a try-on.
passages.plain: Draw a line with a pencil on the pattern along the edge of each plait. Draw another line on the plait at the fold where the plait was turned. Look at Diagram 8. It shows the dotted lines where the plaits are marked. Dotted line A shows the mark on the plait. Dotted line B shows the line along the edge of the plait. Apply the individual measurements to the pattern. Make all the alterations to the pattern. Pin the pattern together to try it on.

passages.old: Always pin the seams on the outside of the pattern as it is easier making alterations, if further alterations are necessary, if the seams are pinned on the outside. It will also help if a tape, the size of the waist measurement, is folded exactly in half and the center front line of the pattern pinned at one fold and the center back line of the pattern pinned at the other fold of the tape. The pattern can then be fastened to the tape at the waist line with a few pins.
passages.plain: Always pin the seams on the outside of the pattern. This makes it easier to make changes if you need to alter the garment again. You can also use a piece of tape. The tape should be the same size as your waist measurement. Fold the tape exactly in half. Pin the center front line of the pattern to one fold of the tape. Pin the center back line of the pattern to the other fold of the tape. You can then fasten the pattern to the tape at the waist line with a few pins.

passages.old: This will help in the fitting, keep the pattern from tearing and be a great help in determining the amount of alteration necessary at the side seams. The Home Dressmakers' Guide Designing Yokes And Girdles There are many pretty girdles and yokes that may be added to the skirt, or changed to suit the individual, without getting another pattern. When the foundation has been fitted to you, lay a piece of tissue paper on the pattern and outline yokes or girdles, copying the picture or creating the design yourself. passages.plain: This helps with the fitting. It keeps the pattern from tearing. It also helps you see how much you need to change at the side seams. You can add many pretty girdles and yokes to the skirt. You can also change them to fit you without getting a new pattern. Once the foundation fits you, put a piece of tissue paper on the pattern. Outline the yokes or girdles on the paper. You can copy a picture or create your own design.
