chapters.title: How to select a waist pattern

passages.old: PATTERNS, WAIST How To Select a Waist Pattern While the lines in a skirt should receive the most consideration when selecting a pattern, because they have more to do with the appearance of being well fitted and becomingly gowned than have the lines of the waist, yet, care and thought should be bestowed upon the selection of the waist pattern. What will be beautiful on one will not become another. Perhaps the gown worn by your friend, and so greatly admired would not look well if worn by you. Study the contour of your face and the size of your shoulders and above all take into consideration the length of your arm.
passages.plain: You should pay the most attention to the lines in a skirt when choosing a pattern. This is because the skirt lines matter more for a good fit and a nice look than the waist lines do. However, you must still think carefully about choosing the waist pattern. What looks beautiful on one person might not look good on another. A dress worn by your friend might look great on her but would not look good on you. You should study the shape of your face. You should also look at the size of your shoulders. Most importantly, you must consider the length of your arm.

passages.old: If your arm is long keep away from an unbroken length in the sleeve pattern and avoid cuffs that flare or give points over the hand. Likewise if your arm is short study to add the appearance of length. Do not break the length lines of the sleeve pattern and add cuffs that taper over the hand. V necks should be worn by one whose face is broad and round and square yokes by the lady with a long thin face. The short stout woman should not wear trimming and yokes that will add to the breadth of her figure and the tall thin lady should avoid lines that contribute to her highth.
passages.plain: If your arm is long, do not use a sleeve pattern with a single unbroken length. Avoid cuffs that flare out or have points over your hand. If your arm is short, try to make it look longer. Do not break the length lines of the sleeve pattern. Add cuffs that taper over your hand. You should wear V necks if your face is broad and round. You should wear square yokes if you have a long thin face. A short stout woman should not wear trimmings or yokes that make her figure look wider. A tall thin lady should avoid lines that make her look taller.

passages.old: When Purchasing a Waist Pattern The pattern must be selected according to the bust measurement. If the correct size is not obtainable, choose the larger size rather than a smaller one ; it is always easier to decrease the size of a pattern than it is to increase it. Applying Measurements to the Pattern The application of individual measurements to the waist pattern is one of the most important features pertaining to home-dressmaking. Without this knowledge the making of a garment is a difficult task and very discouraging to most beginners.
passages.plain: When you buy a waist pattern, you must choose it based on your bust measurement. If you cannot find your exact size, choose a larger size instead of a smaller one. It is always easier to make a pattern smaller than it is to make it larger. You must apply your individual measurements to the waist pattern. This is one of the most important parts of making clothes at home. Without this knowledge, making a garment is a difficult task. It can be very discouraging for most beginners.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide When one has learned to measure the pattern, substituting ones own measurements where they differ from those of the model, and making the alterations on the pattern, there is little or no fitting and seldom an alteration after the garment has been cut out. When the alterations have all been made pin the pattern with the seams on the outside and try it on. The Waist Line DIAGRAM 1 First, identify the wait line upon the pattern; this line is usually marked with perforations. Using a yard stick for a guide, draw a pencil line straight across the pattern, marking the waist line plainly.
passages.plain: You should learn how to measure the pattern. You must replace the model's measurements with your own measurements if they are different. You must make these changes on the pattern. If you do this, you will have little or no fitting. You will rarely need to change the garment after you cut it out. You must pin the pattern with the seams on the outside after you make all the changes. Then you should try it on. You must find the waist line on the pattern. This line is usually marked with small holes. Use a yardstick as a guide. Draw a straight pencil line across the pattern. Mark the waist line clearly.

passages.old: Do this on both the front and the back half of the pattern. (See the line marked Then starting at the center front, one-half inch below the straight line just drawn, draw a line on the front half of the pattern like the dotted line in Diagram 1. Starting at the center back, one-half inch above the straight line, draw a line on the back half of the pattern like the dotted line in Diagram 1. The Home Dressmakers' Guide This dotted line gives one-inch raise from the center front to the center back and is the proper angle for the waist line, giving the correct line for the average figure.
passages.plain: Do this on both the front and back halves of the pattern. Look at the line marked Then. Start at the center front. Go one-half inch below the straight line you just drew. Draw a line on the front half of the pattern like the dotted line in Diagram 1. Start at the center back. Go one-half inch above the straight line. Draw a line on the back half of the pattern like the dotted line in Diagram 1. This dotted line gives a one-inch rise from the center front to the center back. This is the correct angle for the waist line. It gives the correct line for the average figure.

passages.old: It is the line to be used hereafter as the waist line. All length measurements for the waist must be measured from this waist line up. It is very important that the individual length measurements be applied to the pattern from the waist line up. If, when measuring the pattern, from the waist line at the center front up to the base of the neck, the individual measures more than the pattern, it is very necessary that the length be added above the waist line. Especially is this so if the garment extends below the waist line.
passages.plain: Use this line as the waist line from now on. You must measure all waist lengths starting from this waist line upward. It is very important that you apply these individual measurements to the pattern from the waist line up. If you measure from the center front waist line up to the base of the neck and your measurement is longer than the pattern, you must add that extra length above the waist line. This is especially important if the garment goes below the waist line.

passages.old: If the needed length from the waist line to the neck is not added above the waist line the garment will draw up in the front or pull down in the back. This is also true of the back. Measure from the waist line at the center back up to the neck of the pattern; any addition to the length of the pattern must be added above the waist line. The Bust Line DIAGRAM 2 Having found and marked the correct waist line you are now ready to locate the bust line.
passages.plain: If you do not add the correct length from the waistline to the neck above the waistline, the garment will pull up in the front or pull down in the back. This also applies to the back. Measure from the center back waistline up to the neck of the pattern. You must add any extra length above the waistline. You have found and marked the correct waistline. You are now ready to find the bust line.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide For this once measure down from the neck of the patwith pencil where your bust line should come on the pattern. (See line mo.rked "Bust Line" in Diagram.) Draw a line on your pattern like the line marked ''Bust Line" in Diagram 2. This line should be one inch below the armseye at the under-arm seam. Continue this line across the back half of the pattern. You will remember that this line crosses the shoulder blades at the back. The line on your pattern should therefore be drawn to correspond to the bust line in Diagram 2. (Read again the instructions for taking measurement Number 3, in Chapter 2.) You will have no difficulty in locating the correct bust line for you at the center front of the pattern, and following these instructions, with Diagram 2, you will be able to mark a bust line across the front and back half of your pattern that will be accurate enough for all purposes.
passages.plain: Measure from the neck of the pattern to the point where your bust line should be. Look at the line marked Bust Line in Diagram 2. Draw a line on your pattern like the one in Diagram 2. This line must be one inch below the armseye at the under-arm seam. Continue this line across the back half of the pattern. Remember that this line crosses your shoulder blades at the back. Draw the line on your pattern to match the bust line in Diagram 2. Read the instructions for measurement number 3 in Chapter 2 again. You will find the correct bust line at the center front of the pattern easily. Follow these instructions and use Diagram 2. You will be able to mark a bust line across the front and back of your pattern. This line will be accurate enough for all purposes.

passages.old: The designer, when planning the pattern has taken into consideration the fullness needed for the different garments at the bust line, and has made all the allowances accordingly. It is therefore not necessary to apply individual bust and waist measurements to the pattern for a blouse, dress or coat. These measurements are applied for a form fitted garment only. The Under- Arm Alteration The Home Dressmakers' Guide After marking the bust line the next measurement to be applied is the under-arm measurement. Measure up from the waist line on your pattern to the armseye. (See ''A" in If the pattern is too short for you it may be because the armseye has been cut too low.
passages.plain: The designer already planned the amount of extra fabric needed for the bust line of each garment. They made all the necessary adjustments for you. You do not need to add your own bust and waist measurements to the pattern for a blouse, dress, or coat. You only use those measurements for a form-fitted garment. To make the under-arm alteration, find the bust line on your pattern. The next measurement you need is the under-arm measurement. Measure up from the waist line on your pattern to the armseye. If the pattern is too short for you, the armseye might have been cut too low.

passages.old: If this seems to be the case build up the armseye by adding a piece of paper just so shown by the dotted line marked '*B", in Diagram 3. Do this on both the front and the back half of the pattern. If the armseye does not seem too large, and you need to increase or decrease the length from the waist tern across and set in a piece of paper, making it the length required, or fold a tuck across the pattern to de- The Back-Length Alteration When the under-arm measurement of the pattern has been tested, and, if necessary, altered, the next measurement to apply is your back length.
passages.plain: If this is the case, build up the armseye. Add a piece of paper as shown by the dotted line marked *B in Diagram 3. Do this on both the front and back halves of the pattern. If the armseye does not seem too large, you may need to change the length. To increase or decrease the length from the waist, turn the pattern across. Set in a piece of paper to make the required length. You can also fold a tuck across the pattern to decrease the length. This is the Back-Length Alteration. After you test and change the under-arm measurement, the next measurement is your back length.

passages.old: Measure from the waist line up to the back of the neck of the pattern at the center back. (See "Length If the pattern is found to be too short you must fasten a piece of paper to the pattern and add the needed length to the back of the neck and shoulders as shown by the dotted line en that the pattern needs to be altered in this way for round or stooped shouldered persons. Such a figure must have the extra length at the top of the pattern, otherwise the garment will pull down from the neck.
passages.plain: Measure from the waistline up to the center back of the neck on the pattern. Look at the section called Length. If the pattern is too short, you must attach a piece of paper to the pattern. Add the extra length needed to the back of the neck and shoulders. Follow the dotted line. You must change the pattern this way for people with round or stooped shoulders. You must put the extra length at the top of the pattern. If you do not, the garment will pull down from the neck.

passages.old: Raising the back length at the neck necessitates the neck line being raised and the shoulder line raised at the neck and tapering off to the tip of the shoulder. Follow closely The Home Dressmakers' Guide If the length of the back of the pattern from the waist line up to the neck should be too long for you, fold a tuck in the pattern as shown by the line marked ''H" in Diagram 4, making it correspond to your measurements. This is done on the back half of the pattern only.
passages.plain: If you increase the length of the back at the neck, you must also raise the neckline. You must also raise the shoulder line at the neck. This line should then get narrower as it goes toward the tip of the shoulder. Follow The Home Dressmakers' Guide closely. If the back of the pattern is too long from the waistline to the neck, fold a tuck into the pattern. Use the line marked H in Diagram 4 to make it match your measurements. Do this only on the back half of the pattern.

passages.old: When the individual back length measurements is shorter than the pattern, making it necessary to lay a tuck in the back half of the pattern as just described, it is usually found that the front length measurement is long. We therefore do not cany this alteration across the front half of the pattern until after the front length has been measured. Front-Length Alteration After the back length measurement has been applied to the pattern the front length of the pattern should be measured. Measure up from the waist line to the neck as was done for the back length. (See "Length of Front", Dia- If your front length measurement is more than the front length of the pattern, increase the length of the pattern by adding the required amount at the neck as shown by the dotted line marked "D.
passages.plain: If your back length measurement is shorter than the pattern, you must put a tuck in the back half of the pattern. Usually, the front length measurement is also long. Do not change the front half of the pattern until you measure the front length. Front-Length Alteration: After you adjust the back length on the pattern, measure the front length. Measure from the waistline to the neck just like you did for the back length. Look at the section called Length of Front, Dia. If your front length measurement is longer than the pattern length, make the pattern longer. Add the extra amount at the neck. Follow the dotted line marked D.

passages.old: Notice that the shoulder line is raised the same amount as the neck, tapering off to the shoulder tip but the width of the shoulder is not increased. Should it be necessary to decrease the front length of the pattern, do so by folding a tuck in the pattern at the line DIAGRAM The Home Dressmakers' Guide DIAGRAJM 6 When the front length of the pattern has been made to conform to your front length measurement, then measure the shoulder of the pattern. Apply your shoulder measurement, taken from the base of the neck to the tip of the shoulder, to the shoulder of the pattern.
passages.plain: Notice that the shoulder line is raised by the same amount as the neck. It tapers off to the shoulder tip. The width of the shoulder does not increase. If you need to make the front length of the pattern shorter, fold a tuck in the pattern at the line. Once the front length of the pattern matches your front length measurement, measure the shoulder of the pattern. Apply your shoulder measurement to the pattern. This measurement is taken from the base of the neck to the tip of the shoulder.

passages.old: Increase or decrease the shoulder of the pattern, as shown by the dotted decrease of the shoulder width. Do this on both the front and back half of the pattern. Armseye Alteration You are now ready to alter the armseye. If you have had to decrease the front or back length of your pattern by folding a tuck, you have no doubt changed both the size and the shape of the armseye of the pattern. Measure the armseye with your tape measure. If the armseye is too small trim it out to the proper size preserving the original shape.
passages.plain: Change the width of the shoulder on the pattern. Follow the dotted line to show how to make it smaller or larger. Do this on both the front and back parts of the pattern. You can now change the armseye. If you shortened the front or back of the pattern by folding a tuck, you changed the size and shape of the armseye. Use a tape measure to check the armseye. If the armseye is too small, trim it to the correct size. Keep the original shape of the armseye.

passages.old: Be careful about trimming it out too much at this time. When the garment is tried on and the armseye seams too tight it is very easy to trim it out then. If the armseye is found to be too large fill it out by fastening a piece of paper to the pattern and decreasing the The Home Dressmakers' Guide size of the armseye as shown by the dotted lines marked "B" in Diagram 6. If there has been no length alterations made in the pattern the armseye may be too large and the alteration shown by the dotted lines marked "B" will be necessary.
passages.plain: Do not trim the fabric too much at this stage. You can easily trim the armseye seams later when you try on the garment. If the armseye is too large, you must make it smaller. Fasten a piece of paper to the pattern. Decrease the size of the armseye by following the dotted lines marked B in Diagram 6. If you did not change the length of the pattern, the armseye might be too large. In that case, you must make the alteration shown by the dotted lines marked B.

passages.old: This may change the under-arm length again. If this is so, and upon measuring, the length of the pattern under the arm from the waist line to the armseye is found to be too long, shorten it by folding a tuck in the pattern at ''E" in Diagram 3, but not interfering with the back or front length measurements. The Neck Alteration If the alteration for the increase of the front or back length of the pattern has been made, the size of the neck has doubtless been altered. If the length of the pattern was found to need no alteration, the neck may still require some changing.
passages.plain: This might change the under-arm length again. If you measure the pattern and find the length from the waist line to the armseye is too long, you must shorten it. Fold a tuck in the pattern at E in Diagram 3. Do not change the back or front length measurements. You may have already changed the front or back length of the pattern. If you did, the neck size has likely changed. If you did not need to change the length of the pattern, the neck might still need to be changed.

passages.old: Measure the neck of the pattern. The number of inches between points X and X on the front half of the pattern, (See Diagram 7) and the number of inches between X and X on the back half of the pattern, (See Diagram 7) added together, should be half your neck measurement. Apply the individual neck measurement to the pattern. If for example, the pattern is found to measure one-half inch more than one-half of vour neck measure- DIAGRAM The Home Dressmakers' Guide nient, decrease it bj' taking one-fourth of an inch off the front and one-fourth of an inch off the back of the pattern as shown by '*A" in Diagram 7.
passages.plain: Measure the neck of the pattern. Add the number of inches between points X and X on the front half of the pattern to the number of inches between X and X on the back half of the pattern. This total should be half of your neck measurement. Apply your individual neck measurement to the pattern. If the pattern measures one-half inch more than half of your neck measurement, decrease it. Take one-fourth of an inch off the front of the pattern and one-fourth of an inch off the back of the pattern as shown by A in Diagram 7.

passages.old: Likewise if the pattern is too small at the neck increase it the required amount as shown by the dotted line marked *'B", in Diagram 7. Having measured and applied the individual measurements to the pattern, pin it together with the seams on the outside and try it on. Sometimes w^hen the pattern has appeared to be alright, it may when tried on, require some alteration. If the pattern is too long between the bust line and the neck lay a tuck in the pattern, or if it is too short alteration in the same manner between the bust and waist It is rarely, if indeed it ever happens, that a pattern needs all the foregoing alterations.
passages.plain: If the pattern is too small at the neck, increase it by the amount shown by the dotted line marked B in Diagram 7. Measure and apply your individual measurements to the pattern. Pin the pattern together at the seams on the outside and try it on. Sometimes a pattern looks correct but needs changes when you try it on. If the pattern is too long between the bust line and the neck, put a tuck in the pattern. If it is too short, make an alteration in the same way between the bust and the waist. It is rare for a pattern to need all of these changes.

passages.old: Sometimes one alteration suffices, again, two may be needed. Different figures require different alterations, but which ever one is needed to make a pattern fit, it is made in the manner set forth. Diagram No. 8 shows all the alterations and may be followed when making any single alteration. DIAGRAM 8 The Home Dressmakers' Guide The Waist Line The pattern has been purchased according to the bust measure and will therefore need little, if any, alteration at the bust line. It may have been necessary however, to purchase a pattern larger than the size of your bust measurement.
passages.plain: Sometimes you only need one change. Other times you might need two. Different body shapes need different changes. You must follow the steps provided for whichever change you need to make the pattern fit. Diagram No. 8 shows all the changes. You can follow it when you make any single change. Diagram 8 is from The Home Dressmakers' Guide and covers The Waist Line. You bought the pattern based on your bust measurement. Because of this, the bust line will need very little or no change. However, you might have bought a pattern that is larger than your bust measurement.

passages.old: The waist may also be too large, making it necessary to decrease the pattern at the waist line as well as the bust line. First pin the under-arm seam together. The darts in both the front and back of the pattern must also be pinned together. Place the pattern flat on the table. Measure the pattern from the center front to the center back at the waist line. Do not include the seam allowance in this measurement. The number of inches from the center front to the center back of the pattern should be half of your waist measurement.
passages.plain: The waist might be too large. You may need to make the pattern smaller at the waist line and the bust line. First, pin the under-arm seam together. You must also pin the darts in both the front and back of the pattern together. Lay the pattern flat on the table. Measure the pattern from the center front to the center back at the waist line. Do not include the seam allowance in this measurement. The number of inches from the center front to the center back of the pattern should be half of your waist measurement.

passages.old: Subtract half your waist measurement from the number of inches found in the pattern and you have the amount the pattern must be decreased at the waist line. Decrease the waist line of the pattern by making the dart deeper or taking a deeper under-arm seam. (See Diagram 9.) For example we will assume that your waist meassuming the pattern measured 14 inches at the waist line, there is a diiference of two inches to be taken ofl^ the pattern. Take one inch off the front half and one inch off the back half of the pattern.
passages.plain: Subtract half of your waist measurement from the number of inches in the pattern. This result is how much you must decrease the pattern at the waist line. You can decrease the waist line by making the dart deeper or by making the under-arm seam deeper. Look at Diagram 9. For example, if your waist measures 14 inches and the pattern measures 14 inches, there is a difference of two inches to take off the pattern. Take one inch off the front half and one inch off the back half of the pattern.

passages.old: The pattern can be increased at the same place. DIAGRAM 9 The Home Dressmakers' Guide The Bust Line If the pattern is too large at the bust line run the dart up reducing the pattern to j^our bust measurement. You may get into trouble here by having taken your bust measurement too tight. Be sure to take an easy comfortable .bust measure, otherwise your pattern will be too small after it has been altered. Any lining pattern may be pinned together, measured and altered in the same manner. The dart shown in Diagram 9 is the proper place to alter the waist or bust line of any lining pattern.
passages.plain: You can increase the pattern in the same place. Look at Diagram 9. This shows the bust line. If the pattern is too large at the bust line, move the dart up. This will reduce the pattern to your bust measurement. You might have a problem if you took your bust measurement too tightly. Make sure you take a comfortable bust measurement. If you do not, your pattern will be too small after you change it. You can pin any lining pattern together. You can measure and change it in the same way. The dart in Diagram 9 is the correct place to change the waist or bust line of any lining pattern.

passages.old: The Drop Yoke There are many designs that can be worked from a plain foundation pattern. Among the simplest of these, and one that is continually in style, is the drop yoke. Pin the shoulder seams of the plain blouse pattern on the exact seam line, as shown by Diagram 10. Then measure from the inches on the front of the pattern as shown by Diagram 10. Cut the pattern at this point, not forgetting to allow for seams when cutting the cloth. You have taken 2i^ inches from the front of the pattern and have added it to the back thus dropping the shoulder that amount. When cutting the front of the blouse from the cloth, allow for '"fullness" to be The Home Dressmakers' Guide 43
passages.plain: You can make many designs from a plain foundation pattern. One simple and popular design is the drop yoke. Pin the shoulder seams of the plain blouse pattern on the exact seam line. This is shown in Diagram 10. Measure 2 1/2 inches from the front of the pattern as shown in Diagram 10. Cut the pattern at this point. Remember to leave extra space for seams when you cut the cloth. You have taken 2 1/2 inches from the front of the pattern and added it to the back. This drops the shoulder by that amount. When you cut the front of the blouse from the cloth, allow for fullness.

chapters.title: How to select the sleeve

passages.old: PATTERNS, SLEEVE How To Select the Sleeve A garment that is beautiful and satisfying in every detail owes much to the sleeve. Few dressmakers and not many home-sewers enjoy making sleeves and yet they are most important, demanding careful consideration. No part of a garment is more conspicuous. Nothing detracts so completely from a style as does a poorly made sleeve, or add to its beauty as does a well made, properly fitting one. How often an otherwise perfectly becoming gown has been spoiled by an unbecoming sleeve. We cannot always w^ear the sleeve designed for the gown we have selected.
passages.plain: The sleeve is very important to a beautiful garment. Many dressmakers and home sewers do not enjoy making sleeves. However, they require careful thought. No part of a garment is more noticeable than the sleeve. A poorly made sleeve ruins a style. A well made and properly fitting sleeve improves the beauty of a garment. A perfect gown can be ruined by a bad sleeve. You cannot always wear the sleeve that was designed for the gown you chose.

passages.old: It is very necessary that the shape and size of the arm be considered and the sleeve planned to detract from the defects of the arm that is not w^ell proportioned. Study the size and shape of your arm. For instance, the short, thick arm should have long unbroken lines predominating in the sleeve; points that taper over the hand will also help to add length. This arm should never be divided up with straight round cuffs. A becoming cuff, for the short fleshy arm, is one that has the point going up on the front of the arm instead of the back.
passages.plain: You must consider the shape and size of your arm. You should plan the sleeve to hide any flaws in an arm that is not well proportioned. Study the size and shape of your arm. For example, a short and thick arm needs long unbroken lines in the sleeve. Points that taper over the hand will also help add length. You should never divide this arm with straight round cuffs. A good cuff for a short fleshy arm has the point going up on the front of the arm instead of the back.

passages.old: This gives length to the back of the arm. Moreover, it is always best to have a well shaped, closely fitting sleeve curved into the arm at the wrist, with a point either on the back or over the hand. If cuffs are used, they will be found most becoming if pointed or flared over the hand. A tailored blouse may have a mannish cuff, but never much fullness in the sleeve. A row of buttons on the back of a sleeve, when they are worn for trimming, adds to its attractiveness and also gives length.
passages.plain: This gives length to the back of the arm. It is best to have a sleeve that is well shaped and fits closely. The sleeve should curve into the arm at the wrist. The end of the sleeve should be a point on the back or over the hand. If you use cuffs, they look best if they are pointed or flared over the hand. A tailored blouse can have a man style cuff. However, the sleeve should never have much fullness. A row of buttons on the back of a sleeve looks attractive when used for trimming. These buttons also give the sleeve more length.

passages.old: Long, slender arms must have lines broken. I have known arms that were extremely long, having almost an ungainly appearance, made to look well proportioned by choosing a sleeve with length lines broken here and there. The length may be divided by means of a cuff almost to the elbow. All trimmings should follow around the arm, transversely, never up and down. No points should be permitted over The Home Dres»Kikas^ Guide the hands^ :i it possibly c&r be avoiikid, for the Tery ssigp»iiiit to break the length, APPLYING MEASURE^IEyT'S TO TKE ONE -PIE '.""E BISHOP SLEEVE PaTTIPN The Home Dressmakers' Guide is ''held in full" and eased into the armhole.
passages.plain: You must break the lines of long and slender arms. I have seen arms that were very long and looked awkward. You can make them look well proportioned by choosing a sleeve with broken length lines. You can also divide the length by using a cuff that reaches almost to the elbow. All trimmings must go around the arm horizontally. They should never go up and down. You must not let any points go over the hands. This is because the trimmings might break the length. For the one-piece bishop sleeve pattern, hold the pattern in full and ease it into the armhole.

passages.old: If the sleeve pattern measures larger than your armseye measurement, lay a plait lengthwise in the pattern extending from the top of the sleeve to the wrist. See the dotted line marked "B" tern measures less than 2 inches larger than the armseye measurement, cut the pattern in the same place and set in a piece inches larger than the measure taken for the armseye. This alteration may be made when cutting this Place the pattern on the cloth sleeve out of the material, with the fold of the pattern far enough inside the fold of the cloth to make the necessary increase, or far enough outside the fold of the cloth to decrease it the required amount.
passages.plain: Check if the sleeve pattern is larger than your armseye measurement. If it is, place a fold in the pattern lengthwise. This fold should go from the top of the sleeve to the wrist. Look at the dotted line marked B. If the pattern measures less than 2 inches larger than your armseye measurement, cut the pattern at that spot. Then, add a piece that is larger than your armseye measurement. You can make this change when you cut the pattern. Place the pattern on the cloth. Put the fold of the pattern inside the fold of the cloth to make the sleeve larger. Put the fold of the pattern outside the fold of the cloth to make the sleeve smaller.

passages.old: If the pattern measures more than 21/^ inches larger than the armseye it may be because it has been cut too high, as shown by the line marked "Extreme Curve, in Diagram 3." This is often the case with some makes of pattern. The pattern may also measure less than the number of inches required for the armseye, or it may measure just right and still be cut too high. The sleeve pattern for a Bishop sleeve should be shaped at the top as shown by the dotted line marked "C" in Diagram 3.
passages.plain: Check the pattern. If it is more than 1/2 inch larger than the armseye, it might be cut too high. This is shown by the line marked Extreme Curve in Diagram 3. Some patterns are made this way. The pattern might also be smaller than the required number of inches for the armseye. It might also be the correct size but still cut too high. For a Bishop sleeve, you must shape the top of the sleeve pattern. Follow the dotted line marked C in Diagram 3.

passages.old: If the pattern appears to be cut too high as shown by the line marked ''Extreme Curve", pencil a line like the dotted line marked "C" and measure along this line for the size of the sleeve at the top. If the pattern has been cut too high, and many of them are, do not cut this fullness off. Mark the pattern by drawing a line like the dotted line marked "C" in Diagram 3, and run a trace thread in the cloth, following the line on the pattern, and baste the sleeve into the armseye on this line.
passages.plain: Check if the pattern is cut too high. You can tell by the line marked Extreme Curve. If it is too high, draw a line like the dotted line marked C. Measure along this new line to find the size of the sleeve at the top. Do not cut off the extra fullness if the pattern is too high. Many patterns are cut this way. Draw a line like the dotted line marked C in Diagram 3. Run a trace thread in the cloth along this line. Baste the sleeve into the armseye on this line.

passages.old: When the garment is tried on, the exact amount of this fullness needed can be determined. The Home Dressmakers* Guide Very often all the width given in the pattern above the elbow is required, but from the elbow to the wrist a little less width is desired. For this alteration follow the lines Any style of cuff may be worn with the Bishop sleeve. Subtract from the length measurements the number of inches desired for the cuff before cutting the sleeve as the sleeve would have to be cut just that much shorter.
passages.plain: You can find the exact amount of fullness needed when you try on the garment. Often, you need all the width shown in the pattern above the elbow. From the elbow to the wrist, you need a little less width. Follow the lines to make this change. You can wear any style of cuff with a Bishop sleeve. Subtract the number of inches you want for the cuff from the length measurements. Do this before you cut the sleeve. The sleeve must be cut shorter by that exact amount.

passages.old: This is a very comfortable sleeve for a dress and especially good for a short thick arm. The Width Alteration First, measure around the top of the sleeve pattern to determine how many inches it is larger than the armseye of the garment. If it measures larger than the armseye, it must be reduced. This sleeve pattern may also be cut too high at the top as is shown by the line marked **Extreme Curve" in Diagram 3. If this is so, pencil a line like the dotted line marked ure along this line for the width at the top of the sleeve.
passages.plain: This sleeve is very comfortable for a dress. It is especially good for a short and thick arm. To change the width, first measure around the top of the sleeve pattern. Compare this number to the armseye of the garment. If the sleeve is larger than the armseye, you must make it smaller. This sleeve pattern might also be cut too high at the top. You can see this in Diagram 3 at the line marked Extreme Curve. If it is too high, draw a pencil line along the dotted line marked ure. Use this new line for the width at the top of the sleeve.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide This sleeve pattern is increased or decreased in width by folding a plait or setting in a piece where the dotted line *'G" for increase. The width at the elbow may also be measured and this alteration extended at the elbow. If the elbow is alright let the alteration taper to nothing at the elbow. If the width at the elbow is altered the alteration must extend to the wrist, taking off or adding an equal amount on both the upper and under sleeve and preserving the original proportions.
passages.plain: You can change the width of this sleeve pattern. To make it wider, fold a pleat or add a piece at the dotted line marked G. You can also measure the width at the elbow and change it there. If the elbow width is correct, let the change fade away at the elbow. If you change the width at the elbow, the change must go all the way to the wrist. You must add or remove the same amount on both the top and bottom of the sleeve. You must keep the original proportions.

passages.old: The Length Alteration When the width has been altered the sleeve pattern must be measured for the length. Fold the pattern and apply the measurement taken from the shoulder to the elbow to the pattern, measuring along t h ^ dotted line marked ^'X" in Diagram 6. This measurement is number 8 in the Chapter on Measurements. Increase or decrease the length of the pattern to make it conform to your measurement by folding a tuck, or setting in a piece of paper, between the shoulder and the elbow where the dotted line is shown in Dia- In the same manner apply the ''elbow to wrist" measurement, (number 9 in the Chapter on Measurements) and make the alteration where the dotted line is shown between the elbow and the wrist.
passages.plain: You must now change the length of the sleeve pattern. First, fold the pattern. Look at Diagram 6. Find the dotted line marked X. This line is between the shoulder and the elbow. Use the measurement you took from the shoulder to the elbow. This is number 8 in the Chapter on Measurements. Change the pattern length to match your measurement. You can do this by folding a tuck or by putting in a piece of paper between the shoulder and the elbow. Next, do the same for the elbow to wrist measurement. This is number 9 in the Chapter on Measurements. Make this change at the dotted line between the elbow and the wrist.

passages.old: The "Inside Length" measurement could be applied to the pattern, and the pattern altered to correspond to this measurement. It will readily be seen that the dart should come to the elbow, therefore if the inside length measurement is applied to the pattern, the difference between the individual measurement and the pattern must be added or taken off without interfering with the position of the elbow. The dart should come just to the elbow and the separation in the pattern should continue The Home Dressmakers' Guide "Fullness" For the Elbow In a sleeve with a dart to the elbow it is very necessary to have some **fuir ness" in the elbow.
passages.plain: You can apply the Inside Length measurement to the pattern. You can then change the pattern to match this measurement. You will see that the dart should reach the elbow. If you apply the Inside Length measurement to the pattern, you must add or subtract the difference between your measurement and the pattern. You must do this without changing the position of the elbow. The dart should reach exactly to the elbow. The separation in the pattern should continue. The Home Dressmakers' Guide says there must be fullness in the elbow. This is very necessary for a sleeve with a dart to the elbow.

passages.old: If the pattern does not allow for this it must be provided for when the pattern is being measured and altered. This ^'fullness" in the elbow will make the sleeve more comfortable and will also cause it to wear better. Fold the pattern and if the upper part of the sleeve does not extend one inch beyond the under, at the wrist, add this inch just as shown by the dotted line marked "B'* in Diagram 7. This inch of fullness is held in at the elbow and distributed part above and part below the elbow as shown by the Diagram 7.
passages.plain: If your pattern does not include this, you must add it when you measure and change the pattern. This extra space in the elbow makes the sleeve more comfortable. It also helps the sleeve last longer. Fold the pattern. If the top part of the sleeve is not one inch longer than the bottom part at the wrist, add that inch. Do this like the dotted line marked B in Diagram 7. This one inch of extra space stays at the elbow. It spreads out partly above and partly below the elbow as shown in Diagram 7.

passages.old: It has been my privilege to stand before thousands of women in many cities, helping to solve the problems that make dressmaking difficult. One trouble common to all and a subject of universal interest is the sleeve that twists and how to remedy it. By ''sleeve twisting" we mean when the inside seam of the sleeve will twist around to the top of the arm at the wrist. This is not only annoying 'but very uncomfortable. The proper starting point to remedy this trouble is first to determine from the pattern if the sleeve is going to twist.
passages.plain: I have had the privilege of standing before thousands of women in many cities. I helped them solve problems that make dressmaking difficult. One common problem that everyone is interested in is a sleeve that twists. You must know how to fix it. Sleeve twisting happens when the inside seam of the sleeve twists toward the top of the arm at the wrist. This is annoying and very uncomfortable. The first step to fix this problem is to check the pattern. You must determine if the sleeve is going to twist.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide How To Determine From the Pattern If the Sleeve Will Twist (This applies to a Bishop sleeve and a sleeve with a dart Place the pattern on the table bringing the inside seams together at the point side of the sleeve projects two inches beyond the under side of the sleeve at the wrist, the sleeve will not tv/ist. (See plain upper side of the sleeve and the dotted the inside seam meets all the way and is even at the wrist, the sleeve may twist, indeed it is very probable that it will.
passages.plain: This guide shows you how to tell if a sleeve will twist by looking at the pattern. This applies to Bishop sleeves and sleeves with a dart. Place the pattern on the table. Bring the inside seams together. Look at the point side of the sleeve. If it projects two inches beyond the under side of the sleeve at the wrist, the sleeve will not twist. Look at the plain upper side of the sleeve. If the dotted line of the inside seam meets all the way and is even at the wrist, the sleeve may twist. It is very likely that it will twist.

passages.old: When the inside seam has been brought together at the point marked ''X" in Diagram 8 and the pattern has been folded on the line designed for the outside seam, if then, the under side of the sleeve projects beyond the upper, the sleeve will twist in spite of all you can do unless the trouble is remedied before the sleeve is cut. How To Alter the Pattern To Prevent the Sleeve Twisting Diagram 9 shows how the under sleeve part of the pattern must be dropped until the upper projects two inches beyond the under, at the wrist.
passages.plain: Bring the inside seam together at the point marked X in Diagram 8. Fold the pattern on the line for the outside seam. If the bottom of the sleeve sticks out further than the top, the sleeve will twist. You cannot fix this later. You must fix it before you cut the fabric. To fix the pattern, look at Diagram 9. You must lower the bottom part of the sleeve pattern. Do this until the top part sticks out two inches past the bottom part at the wrist.

passages.old: The line marked "X" shows the underside of the pattern. Causing the upper part of the pattern to project two inches beyond the under part of the sleeve at the wrist, brings the inside seam of the sleeve into the correct position on the arm. It seems unnecessary to caution you about trimming this inside seam, making both the upper part of the pattern and the under, the same size again, as that would bring you back to where you started, yet that is what many women do. All you trim off is the amount on the under sleeve that extends below the wrist line of the upper The Home Dressmakers' Guide The line at the wrist marked "X" shows the amount that may be trimmed off.
passages.plain: The line marked X shows the underside of the pattern. You should make the upper part of the pattern stick out two inches past the bottom part of the sleeve at the wrist. This puts the inside seam of the sleeve in the right spot on the arm. You do not need to be warned about trimming this inside seam. If you trim it, the upper part and the bottom part will be the same size again. This would put you back where you started. However, many women do this anyway. You only trim off the amount on the bottom sleeve that goes below the wrist line of the upper part. The line at the wrist marked X shows how much you can trim off.

passages.old: At the top of the sleeve pattern the under sleeve must be built up by adding the amount that was dropped. The space between the original line marked that must be added. Fasten a piece of paper to the top of the under sleeve pattern and build it up to its original size and shape. The dotted line marked *'A" v/as the original line for the top of the under sleeve pattern. It is necessary to do this, otherwise the pattern would be shortened. The Two-Piece Coat Sleeve The sleeve for a tailored suit must of necessity be closer fitting than the fuller sport coat or top coat sleeve.
passages.plain: You must build up the top of the under sleeve pattern. Add the amount that was dropped. Use the space between the original line. Fasten a piece of paper to the top of the under sleeve pattern. Build it up to its original size and shape. Use the dotted line marked A as the original line for the top of the under sleeve pattern. You must do this or the pattern will be too short. A tailored suit sleeve must fit closer than a sport coat or top coat sleeve.

passages.old: There must be room for the action and natural curve of the arm, and yet, unlike the two piece dress sleeve, for instance, which clings to the arm and follows its every movement, the tailored sleeve requires straighter lines, and attention must be given to have the right balance. The individual measurements are applied to the two piece coat sleeve similarly as for the sleeve with a dart to the elbow. The Width Alteration Measure the top of both the upper and under parts of the pattern, using a tape measure, and following the curves of the pattern.
passages.plain: You must leave enough room for your arm to move and curve naturally. A tailored sleeve is different from a two piece dress sleeve. A dress sleeve stays close to the arm and follows every movement. A tailored sleeve needs straighter lines. You must pay attention to the balance of the sleeve. You use the same individual measurements for a two piece coat sleeve as you do for a sleeve with a dart to the elbow. To find the Width Alteration Measure, use a tape measure. Measure the top of both the upper and under parts of the pattern. Follow the curves of the pattern while you measure.

passages.old: Do not include the seam allowances in this measurement, measure from seam line to seam line on both parts of the pattern. The top of the sleeve inches larger than the armseye of the coat, otherwise the sleeve would be spoiled. If the sleeve pattern measures larger than the armseye measurement, the sleeve pattern must be made narrower by laying a plait in the pattern as shown by the dotted line marked "C in Diagram must be taken from both the upper and un» der sleeve pattern., diagram 10 The Home Dressmakers' Guide If the sleeve pattern measures less than the extra 2 inches required, the pattern must be made wider by cutting at the lines marked ''C" and setting in a piece of paper making the pattern the necessary width.
passages.plain: Do not include the seam allowances in this measurement. Measure from seam line to seam line on both parts of the pattern. The top of the sleeve must be larger than the armseye of the coat. If it is not, the sleeve will be ruined. If the sleeve pattern is larger than the armseye measurement, you must make the sleeve pattern narrower. Do this by laying a pleat in the pattern. Follow the dotted line marked C in Diagram 10. You must do this for both the upper and under sleeve patterns. If the sleeve pattern is less than the extra 2 inches required, you must make the pattern wider. Cut at the lines marked C. Then, set in a piece of paper to make the pattern the correct width.

passages.old: This must also be done on both the upper and the under pattern. It may be that the top of the upper sleeve pattern has been cut too high, allowing too much fullness on the top of the sleeve to be worked into the armseye. If this seems to be so, do not cut it off. Mark the pattern with a pencil as shown by the dotted line in Diagram 10, and, when cutting the sleeve, run a trace thread in the cloth following the line on the pattern. Baste the sleeve into the armseye on the line made by the trace threads.
passages.plain: You must do this on both the upper and under patterns. Sometimes the top of the upper sleeve pattern is cut too high. This can cause too much extra fabric at the top of the sleeve to go into the armseye. If you see this, do not cut the fabric off. Mark the pattern with a pencil. Use the dotted line in Diagram 10 as a guide. When you cut the sleeve, sew a trace thread in the cloth along that line. Sew the sleeve into the armseye using the line made by the trace threads.

passages.old: Occasionally the pattern gives just the desired width for the sleeve from the elbow to the wrist, but it is too wide from the elbow to the shoulder. More often the pattern is too narrow from the elbow to the shoulder while it gives just the width required below the elbow. When this is the case the pattern is not reduced or made larger at the dotted lines marked "C" but is altered as shown by the dotted lines marked "A" and "B" in Diagram crease of size and pattern wider.
passages.plain: Sometimes the pattern gives the correct width for the sleeve from the elbow to the wrist. However, it might be too wide from the elbow to the shoulder. More often, the pattern is too narrow from the elbow to the shoulder but gives the correct width below the elbow. When this happens, do not make the pattern smaller or larger at the dotted lines marked C. Instead, change the pattern as shown by the dotted lines marked A and B in the diagram. This makes the crease of size and pattern wider.

passages.old: An equal amount must be added or taKen from both seams on both the upper and under sleeve pattern. The Length Alteration Apply your "shoulder to elbow" measurement to the under part of the pattern. If the pattern is too long lay a plait where the dotted line is shown in Diagram 12. If the pattern is not long enough cut it in the same place and set in a piece of paper making it the required length. The Home Dressmakers' Guide Apply your **elbow to wrist" measurement in the same way.
passages.plain: You must add or take away the same amount from both seams on both the upper and under sleeve patterns. Use your shoulder to elbow measurement on the under part of the pattern. If the pattern is too long, fold it at the dotted line in Diagram 12. If the pattern is too short, cut it at that same place. Then, add a piece of paper to make it the correct length. Use your elbow to wrist measurement in the same way.

passages.old: The length measurements are applied and the alteration made the same, on both the upper and under sleeve Next apply your ''inside length" measurement to the sleeve pattern. This measurement is No. 12 in the Chapter on Measurements. If the pattern measures more or less than 3'our inside length measurement make the alteration, half above and half below the elbow, but not interfering with the back length measurement that has just been altered. When making this two piece coat sleeve it is very necessary to have the inside seam on the under part of the sleeve, 1/2 inch longer than the inside seam of the upper part of the sleeve. (See the dotted line marked "0" in This 1/2 inch mxUst be held in ''fulness" between the the elbow and the top of the sleeve when the sleeve is basted. Therefore when applying the inside length measurement to the pattern this 1/2 inch must be added to the under sleeve pattern if this allowance has not been provided for. DIAGRAM 12 The Home Dressmakers' Guide 53
passages.plain: Apply the length measurements and make the same change to both the upper and under sleeve. Next, apply your inside length measurement to the sleeve pattern. This is measurement number 12 in the Chapter on Measurements. If the pattern is longer or shorter than your inside length measurement, make the change. Make half of the change above the elbow and half below the elbow. Do not change the back length measurement that you just altered. When you make this two piece coat sleeve, the inside seam on the under part of the sleeve must be 1/2 inch longer than the inside seam of the upper part of the sleeve. Look at the dotted line marked 0 in Diagram 12 on page 53. This 1/2 inch must stay in the fullness between the elbow and the top of the sleeve when you baste it. When you apply the inside length measurement to the pattern, you must add this 1/2 inch to the under sleeve pattern if it is not already there.

chapters.why: Understanding how sleeve proportions affect the overall silhouette helps in creating flattering and well-fitted clothing.

This is not so apt to cut or leave holes in the delicate fabric after the threads have been removed. When taking out, cut basting threads. Do Not pull ruthlessly. Many a fine garment has been cut and ruined by the thin, tough thread. The better way is to clip in small sections before removing. Pressing To press Woolens, lay a wet cloth, preferably cotton, on the garment just where you want it pressed.
passages.plain: Use threads for basting. These materials hold the cloth firmly and keep it cotton. It is best to use sewing silk to baste Taffeta or Soft Silk. This type of thread will not cut or leave holes in delicate fabric after you remove it. Cut the basting threads when you take them out. Do not pull them hard. Many fine garments have been cut and ruined by thin, tough thread. The better way is to clip the thread in small sections before removing it. To press woolens, lay a wet cloth on the garment. Use a cotton cloth if possible. Place it just where you want to press the fabric.

passages.old: For seams it is even better to use a squeezed-out sponge. Lay a square of good tailor's canvas on cloth about to be pressed ; indeed, this makes ideal sponging material, and will keep the cloth from becoming shiny or marked. Rub the wet sponge over its surface. It is best to use a hot iron for pressing. The reverse is true in pressing silk. A very hot iron will take the life out of a silken fabric. It is then liable to crack, and is virtually worthless, as many a garment has become, the blame, however, being placed upon the silk, when it rested entirely with the presser.
passages.plain: You should use a squeezed-out sponge for seams. Place a square of good tailor's canvas on the cloth you want to press. This canvas is the best material for sponging. It stops the cloth from getting shiny or marked. Rub the wet sponge over the canvas. You should use a hot iron for pressing most fabrics. This is not true for silk. A very hot iron will ruin silk fabric. The silk may crack and become worthless. Many clothes have been ruined this way. People often blame the silk, but the fault is actually with the person pressing it.

passages.old: Sponging and Shrinking Woolens Take five yards of unbleached muslin, or a sheet, if the other is not obtainable, and wring it out of cold water. Then laying your woolen goods as it came from the store, full length, and folded double, cover the fabric with the wet cloth and roll up the entire material, letting it remain for several hours, or over night. When removing out of the sponge, hang the goods upon a clothes line to dry. DO NOT press with a hot iron, or you will hopelessly mark it and render it liable to shininess under the slightest wear.
passages.plain: Take five yards of unbleached muslin. If you cannot find it, use a sheet instead. Wring the fabric out in cold water. Lay your woolen goods out in their original store shape. Fold the goods in half. Cover the fabric with the wet cloth. Roll up the entire material. Let it stay rolled for several hours or overnight. Take the goods out of the sponge. Hang the goods on a clothes line to dry. Do not press the goods with a hot iron. A hot iron will mark the fabric. It will also make the fabric shiny when you wear it.

passages.old: Slow natural dry, is always best. It is then ready to cut. Shrinking White Wash Goods Lay the material in a pan of cold water and let come to a boil. Then hang up to dry. Such shades as lavender, pink, blue or green, should be dried in the shade, to prevent fading. \Mien tracing seams on silk, do not use a tracing wheel ; it will cut the silk.
passages.plain: Slow natural drying is always best. The fabric is ready to cut once it is dry. To shrink white wash goods, put the material in a pan of cold water. Let the water come to a boil. Hang the material up to dry. When it is only slightly damp, press it with a hot iron. It will look as good as it did before you put it in the water. To set the color, put a little salt in the water. You should dry colors like lavender, pink, blue, or green in the shade. This prevents the colors from fading. When you trace seams on silk, do not use a tracing wheel. It will cut the silk.

passages.old: Tracing with a colored thread will give satisfactory results. ^Tien making a skirt that has plaits or a stitched welt seam, leave one seam unbasted until all the other seams are stitched. The back seam, if there is one, is the best to leave open. ^^Tlen sewing soft silks, crepe, chiffon or any thin material, stitch on paper; this will prevent the seams from puckering. The pattern has been measured and altered to the individual measurement. The length desired for the finished skirt has been determined and, below this line, a 31/0 inch hem allowance has been marked upon the pattern.
passages.plain: You can use colored thread for tracing to get good results. When you make a skirt with plaits or a stitched welt seam, leave one seam unbasted until you stitch all the other seams. If there is a back seam, it is best to leave that one open. When you sew soft silks, crepe, chiffon, or any thin material, stitch on paper. This will stop the seams from puckering. The pattern has been measured and changed to fit the individual measurements. You have decided on the length for the finished skirt. A 3/4 inch hem allowance is marked on the pattern below this line.

passages.old: The width for the bottom of the skirt has been decided upon, taking into consideration the width of the material, and the next procedure is placing the pattern upon the cloth. Placing the Pattern Upon the Cloth One can hardly make a mistake in placing the pattern on the material, the instructions that come with the pattern makes this very plain. It is of the utmost importance that the entire pattern be placed upon the cloth, before any part is cut, and the cutting planned economically. Failure to do this has resulted in a vexing predicament that could have been avoided.
passages.plain: You have decided on the width for the bottom of the skirt based on the width of your fabric. The next step is to place the pattern on the cloth. You can hardly make a mistake during this step because the pattern instructions make it very clear. It is very important that you place the entire pattern on the cloth before you cut any part of it. You must plan your cutting to use the fabric economically. If you do not do this, you will face a frustrating problem that could have been avoided.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide Corners should not be pieced at the bottom of the skirt; this will not be necessary if the entire pattern is placed on the cloth. When it happens that the width of the material will hardly give the width desired for the bottom of the skirt, an inch or two can be added by placing the pattern on the cloth so as to have the full width of the material where the hem is turned, and then piecing the hem allowance. For example, Diagram 1 shows 36-inch material, with the pattern placed to give the full 18 inches in the bottom of the front half of the skirt.
passages.plain: You should not sew pieces together at the bottom of the skirt. You do not need to do this if you place the entire pattern on the cloth. If the fabric is not wide enough for the bottom of the skirt, you can add one or two inches. Do this by placing the pattern on the cloth so that the hem uses the full width of the material. Then you can sew the hem allowance. For example, Diagram 1 shows 36 inch material. The pattern is placed to give the full 18 inches at the bottom of the front half of the skirt.

passages.old: The space marked "0" is where the hem is pieced. This will not show when the hem is turned. If the material should prove to be too narrow for the width of the skirt at the bottom decided upon in the pattern, it is much better to have more seams in the skirt than it is to piece the gores. Then again it is sometimes necessary to make a greater allowance at the back, for gathers at the waist line, if the design selected calls for gathers. Take time and study every detail carefully before cutting and there v/ill be nothing to worry over or get nervous about after the skirt has been cut.
passages.plain: The space marked 0 is where you join the hem pieces. You will not see this part when you turn the hem. If your fabric is too narrow for the width of the skirt bottom in the pattern, it is better to add more seams to the skirt. Do not piece the gores. Sometimes you need to allow for more fabric at the back for gathers at the waist line. This is only if your chosen design uses gathers. Take time to study every detail carefully before you cut the fabric. You will not have to worry or feel nervous after the skirt is cut.

passages.old: The beginner is especially cautioned not to hurry as it is when hurrying mistakes are made. The Grain of the Cloth Be sure the pattern is placed in the right relation to the grain of the cloth. Some weaves have a decided "up and down grain." Especially is this true of Broad-cloth. Great care must be exercised here so that no mistakes are made, as they often prove costly and valuable material is wasted. Broad-cloth, and indeed almost every material with a nap except velvet, should be cut with the nap running down.
passages.plain: You should not hurry when you are starting out. You will make mistakes if you rush. You must make sure the pattern is placed correctly against the grain of the cloth. Some weaves have a clear up and down grain. This is especially true of broad-cloth. You must be very careful here. Mistakes can be expensive and waste valuable material. You should cut broad-cloth and almost every material with a nap running down. This does not include velvet.

passages.old: Rub the hand gently down over the cloth, the smooth feeling will show the map running down, while rubbing against the nap will feel rough. Be absolutely certain, both that the nap is running down, and that every part of the garment has the nap running the same way.
