passages.plain: Rub your hand gently down over the cloth. The smooth feeling shows the nap running down. Rubbing against the nap will feel rough. You must be sure that the nap is running down. You must also be sure that every part of the garment has the nap running the same way. It often happens that you need more fullness for gathers at the back of the skirt than the pattern allows for.

passages.old: This is very easily remedied by placing the pattern on the cloth as shown in Diagram 3. Notice that three inches is allowed at the waist line. This is on the folded cloth giving six inches of fullness to gather. Bias It is not always desirable to have all the bias at the sides of the skirt. In a four piece skirt, where there is a seam in the back, it is much better to have part bias at the side and part at the back. Therefore, when placing the pattern on the cloth arrange for this by placing the pattern as shown in Dia- DIAGRAM 3 The Home Dressmakers' Guide 57 Using a Pattern on Striped Material When making a dress or a skirt out of material that has stripes or plaids it is very necessary that the stripes or plaids be matched perfectly.
passages.plain: You can fix this easily by placing the pattern on the cloth like Diagram 3 shows. You should leave three inches at the waist line. This is on the folded cloth. It gives you six inches of extra fabric to gather. It is not always good to have all the bias at the sides of the skirt. In a four piece skirt with a seam in the back, it is better to have some bias at the side and some at the back. You can do this by placing the pattern like Diagram 3 shows. When you make a dress or a skirt from striped or plaid material, you must match the stripes or plaids perfectly.

passages.old: A very simple way to do this is as follows : Having cut the front or back half of the garment as the case may be, take the other half of the pattern and placing it beside the cloth already cut, mark upon the pattern, with a pencil, a continuation of the stripes or plaids. When this half of the pattern is placed upon the cloth the pencil markings can be made to correspond with the stripes on the cloth. Using a Pattern for a Plaited Skirt In Chapter 3 will be found the instructions for altering a plaited skirt pattern.
passages.plain: Follow these steps to do this. First, cut the front or back half of the garment. Take the other half of the pattern. Place it next to the cloth you already cut. Use a pencil to mark the stripes or plaids on the pattern. Place this half of the pattern on the cloth. Make the pencil marks match the stripes on the cloth. You can find instructions for changing a plaited skirt pattern in Chapter 3.

passages.old: The diagram in Chapter 3, shows how to mark the plaits in the pattern, after the pattern has been altered to fit the individual, and the plaits folded in the pattern. After each plait has been carefully marked with a pencil, both upon the plait and along its edge, the pattern can be smoothed out flat and placed upon the folded cloth. Fasten the pattern securely in place upon the cloth with pins. Cut the cloth and before taking the pattern off, mark the plaits with tailor tacks, by following the pencil lines drawn upon the pattern.
passages.plain: Look at the diagram in Chapter 3. It shows how to mark the plaits in the pattern. You must do this after you change the pattern to fit the person and fold the plaits in the pattern. Mark each plait carefully with a pencil. Put a mark on the plait and along its edge. You can then smooth the pattern flat. Place the pattern on the folded cloth. Pin the pattern securely to the cloth. Cut the cloth. Before you remove the pattern, mark the plaits with tailor tacks. Follow the pencil lines you drew on the pattern.

passages.old: Take the tailor tacks, or trace threads, through the pattern and both thicknesses of cloth. When the threads are clipped and the pattern lifted off, the plaits will be marked evenly on both sides of the cloth. (See instructions for Tailor Tacks on Page U, Diagram 6.) Fold the plaits in the cloth upon the lines marked with the tailor tacks and baste them carefully. By following this method with a plaited skirt pattern the plaits will be even alike on both sides. • It will not be out of place here to remind the home sewer that perfect results follow careful attention to these things, that are too often, considered unimportant.
passages.plain: Take the tailor tacks or trace threads. Pass them through the pattern and both layers of cloth. Cut the threads and lift the pattern off. The pleats will be marked evenly on both sides of the cloth. Look at Page U, Diagram 6 for instructions on tailor tacks. Fold the pleats in the cloth along the lines marked by the tailor tacks. Baste them carefully. If you follow this method with a pleated skirt pattern, the pleats will be even on both sides. Perfect results come from paying attention to these small details.

passages.old: A tailor would never attempt to put a garment together without first marking every plait, seam, hem, waist line, pockets, yokes, etc., with tailor tacks. On the other hand many home sewers would not think of giving the time to anything so superfluous as tailor tacks. It is for this reason the skirt or suit tailored at home The Home Dressmakers' Guide has an unprofessional appearance. It pays to take the time to do a thing right. Tailor tacks are important and necessary. Mark the pattern with a pencil (if it has been altered so the perforations are useless) outlining pockets, yokes, plaits, seams, waist line and hip line, and take the tailor tacks through the pattern and both thicknesses of cloth, following these pencil markings.
passages.plain: A professional tailor always marks every part of a garment before sewing. They mark every pleat, seam, hem, waist line, pocket, and yoke with tailor tacks. Many people sewing at home do not take the time to use tailor tacks. This is why clothes made at home can look unprofessional. You should take the time to do the job correctly. Tailor tacks are important and necessary. If you changed your pattern and the holes are no longer useful, mark the pattern with a pencil. Outline the pockets, yokes, pleats, seams, waist line, and hip line. Then, put the tailor tacks through the pattern and both layers of cloth along these pencil marks.

passages.old: The garment can then be put together more perfectly and with less trouble. The plaited skirt is always worn in some style or other. It may be merely a plait on each gore, or it may be a cluster of them on each side of the panel. But which ever is used, they can be arranged so that they will be becoming to any figure. Sometimes they can be stitched down almost to the knee, and again, only down to the hip line, it is really a matter of choice and good judgment, influenced by prevailing styles.
passages.plain: You can put the garment together more perfectly and with less trouble. The plaited skirt is always worn in some style. You can put a plait on each gore. You can also put a cluster of them on each side of the panel. You can arrange them so they look good on any figure. Sometimes you can stitch them down almost to the knee. Other times you can stitch them down only to the hip line. It is a matter of choice and good judgment. This choice is influenced by current styles.

passages.old: The illustration shows side plaits all around from the front to the back, meeting with an inverted plait on the back. A Plaited Skirt Without a Pattern It is not necessary to have a pattern when making a plaited skirt out of straight lengths of cloth. Take three widths, say of 36-inch material, and cut them to your longest length measurement. Sew the three widths together, leaving one seam open, so the cloth can be spread flat upon the table. Next find the center of the entire width and pin a box plait, making it any width desired.
passages.plain: The picture shows side plaits from the front to the back. These meet an inverted plait on the back. You do not need a pattern to make a plaited skirt from straight pieces of cloth. Take three widths of fabric. For example, use material that is 36 inches wide. Cut these three widths to your longest length measurement. Sew the three widths together. Leave one seam open so you can lay the cloth flat on a table. Find the center of the total width. Pin a box plait there. You can make it any width you want.

passages.old: The center of this box plait is the center front of the skirt. Beginning at this box plait lay each plait at the hip line, plaiting one side of the cloth first into half the hip measurement. Then plait the other half in a like manner. Be sure to plait at the hip line first as it is the balance line for the skirt. The Home Dressmakers' Guide Next fold the plaits from the hip line to the waist line, curving them to get the exact measurement. Always keep the straight grain of the cloth on the top of the plait and all the bias underneath.
passages.plain: The center of this box pleat is the center front of the skirt. Start at this box pleat. Place each pleat at the hip line. Pleat one side of the cloth first. This side should be half of the hip measurement. Then pleat the other half in the same way. You must pleat at the hip line first because it is the balance line for the skirt. Next fold the pleats from the hip line to the waist line. Curve them to get the exact measurement. Always keep the straight grain of the cloth on top of the pleat. Keep all the bias underneath.

passages.old: This is to keep the plaits from swinging out at the bottom when the skirt is finished. When the plaits are carefully basted above the hip line, they may be basted below the hip line so they can be pressed with a warm iron. The back seam can then be sewed, two plaits being brought together to form an inverted plait. This seam may be sewed all the way up and the placket closing can be placed under any one of the plaits at the left side. Plaits may be stitched down with the machine to just below the hip line or they may only be stitched part way.
passages.plain: Do this to stop the plaits from swinging out at the bottom of the finished skirt. You should first carefully baste the plaits above the hip line. Then you can baste them below the hip line so you can press them with a warm iron. You can then sew the back seam. You must bring two plaits together to make an inverted plait. You can sew this seam all the way up. You can place the placket closing under any one of the plaits on the left side. You can use a machine to stitch the plaits down just below the hip line. You can also choose to stitch them only part way.

passages.old: When plaits are not stitched on the outside to the hip line, a piece of cambric, about two inches wide, may be used to hold the plaits. Have the strip of cambric long enough to go around the skirt at the hip line and fasten the underside of each plait to it using the tacking stitch. It is very easy plaiting a striped silk in this manner as the stripe can be followed for the top of the plait. A Skirt With a Drape on the Side This skirt is made wath three widths of 36-inch cloth, cut to the desired length and basted together.
passages.plain: If you do not stitch the plaits to the outside at the hip line, you can use a piece of cambric. This strip should be about two inches wide. Make the strip long enough to go around the skirt at the hip line. Fasten the underside of each plait to this strip using a tacking stitch. It is very easy to plait a striped silk this way because you can follow the stripe for the top of the plait. A Skirt With a Drape on the Side: You make this skirt with three widths of 36-inch cloth. Cut the cloth to the length you want. Sew the pieces together with basting stitches.

passages.old: The center of one width is in front and is the center front of the skirt. One of the seams comes at the center of the back of the skirt and the other two seams come at the sides. The Home Dressmakers' Guide - Cut a belting to the exact waist measurement, and planning to have the skirt closing to the right or left, pin the cloth to this belting at the center front and back. Now gather the cloth nine inches each side of the center front (making a total of 18 inches) gathered into half the waist line and, treating the back in the same manner, baste to the belting, allowing the remainder of the cloth at each side to drop one yard to form the drape.
passages.plain: The center of one width of fabric is the center front of the skirt. One seam goes at the center back of the skirt. The other two seams go at the sides. Cut a belt to your exact waist measurement. Decide if you want the skirt to close to the right or the left. Pin the cloth to this belt at the center front and the center back. Gather the cloth nine inches on each side of the center front. This makes a total of 18 inches. Gather this into half of the waist line. Do the same thing for the back. Baste the fabric to the belt. Let the rest of the cloth on each side drop one yard to make the drape.

passages.old: This drape may be made less if desired by gathering more fullness into the waist line at front and back. Soft satins or any soft material drapes well in this skirt. A very simple skirt to make yet very effective and becoming to slender figures. Cascade Drape This cascade drape can be inserted into the skirt seams in various ways. gestion of how Diagram 6. It may be made of the same cloth and faced, or can be picoted on the edge for finish. The cascade drape will look well on the four-piece skirt.
passages.plain: You can make this drape smaller if you want. Do this by gathering more fabric into the front and back waistline. Soft satins or any soft material will drape well in this skirt. This skirt is very simple to make. It looks very good on slender figures. You can insert this cascade drape into the skirt seams in different ways. See Diagram 6 for how to do this. You can make the drape from the same cloth and add a facing. You can also picot the edge for a finished look. The cascade drape will look good on the four-piece skirt.

passages.old: Basting After the skirt has been cut and marked with tailor tacks and the pattern lifted off, the next thing is to baste it carefully together on the lines marked for the seams. Do not hold a skirt, or any full length garment, in your hands while basting it. If you do the seams will stretch and be far from even when the bottom is reached. The Home Dressmakers' Guide 61 The pieces of a skirt should be handled very carefully after they are cut and before they are basted.
passages.plain: Cut the skirt and mark it with tailor tacks. Remove the pattern. Next, baste the pieces together along the marked seam lines. Do not hold the skirt or any long garment in your hands while you baste it. If you hold it, the seams will stretch. They will not be even by the time you reach the bottom. You must handle the skirt pieces very carefully after you cut them and before you baste them.

passages.old: Especially is this true where there is bias. Just moving the material will sometimes cause it to stretch. Often the home dressmaker will cut out one piece of a skirt, and, picking it up by the edge will throw it over the back of a chair while another piece is cut out. This often results in a gore stretching three or four inches. The proper way to baste the side seams in a skirt, or any full length garment, is to carefully lay the pieces flat upon the table and pin the top of the seam together evenly.
passages.plain: This is especially true when there is bias. Moving the fabric can sometimes cause it to stretch. A home dressmaker might cut one piece of a skirt and then pick it up by the edge to throw it over a chair while cutting another piece. This often causes a gore to stretch three or four inches. The correct way to baste the side seams in a skirt or any full length garment is to lay the pieces flat on the table. You must pin the top of the seam together evenly.

passages.old: Likewise pin the bottom of the seam together evenly. Where there is bias the seam will doubtless have stretched. Work this back into its original length by smoothing the cloth with your hands. Beginning at the ends of the seam press gently toward the center, continuing until the entire amount that was stretched has disappeared. Next take a piece of cambric or any firm material, cut lengthwise and one inch wide. Do not tear the cambric into inch wide lengths, cut it. When the skirt is the garment being basted, these lengths should be cut the exact number of inches desired for the side length of the finished skirt.
passages.plain: Pin the bottom of the seam together evenly. The seam will likely have stretched in areas where the fabric is on the bias. You must return the fabric to its original length by smoothing it with your hands. Start at the ends of the seam and press gently toward the center. Continue until all the stretching is gone. Next, take a piece of cambric or any firm material. Cut it lengthwise to be one inch wide. Do not tear the cambric into strips. You must cut it. When you are basting a skirt, cut these strips to the exact number of inches you want for the side length of the finished skirt.

passages.old: Measure your pattern from the natural waist line to where the hem is to be turned. This pattern, if it was measured and altered as it should have been, will be the exact length desired. These strips of cambric are to be used for staying the side seams. Any seam in a full length garment where there is bias must be stayed. Where bias meets the straight of the cloth the edge stay is not necessary. It is also unnecessary to stay seams where there is no bias. Pin the edge stay in with the seam.
passages.plain: Measure your pattern from your natural waistline to the point where you want the hem turned. If you measured and changed the pattern correctly, it will be the exact length you want. Use these strips of cambric to reinforce the side seams. You must reinforce any seam in a full length garment that has a bias. You do not need an edge stay where the bias meets the straight grain of the cloth. You also do not need to reinforce seams that have no bias. Pin the edge stay into the seam.

passages.old: It does not matter upon which side of the seam allowance the edge stay is placed. Pin it at the waist line first, then at the bottom of the skirt where the line has been traced upon which to turn the hem. The edge stay need not extend below this line. After pinning the edge stay at the top and bottom, pin it here and there along the length of the seam so as to hold the cloth and stay together. Now, beginning at the top, baste carefully down to the bottom, using a small even basting stitch, and basting the edge stay in with the seam.
passages.plain: It does not matter which side of the seam allowance you place the edge stay on. First, pin it at the waist line. Then, pin it at the bottom of the skirt on the line you traced for the hem. The edge stay does not need to go below this line. After you pin the edge stay at the top and bottom, pin it in other spots along the length of the seam. This will hold the cloth and the stay together. Start at the top. Sew a careful basting stitch down to the bottom. Use a small and even stitch. Sew the edge stay into the seam.

passages.old: Do not use a long basting stitch here, because, if you do, the sewing machine will shove the cloth, causing puckers that may be difficult to press out. When sewing this seam with the machine place the cloth side next to the feeder and the The Home Dressmakers' Guide stay on top. Placing the cloth side next to the feeder allows the feeder to take care of the extra length or fullness, that has been held on to the edge stay. After sewing this seam remove the bastings and overcast or bind it.
passages.plain: Do not use a long basting stitch. If you do, the sewing machine will push the cloth. This will cause wrinkles that are hard to iron out. When you sew this seam with the machine, place the cloth side next to the feeder. Place the stay on top. Putting the cloth side next to the feeder lets the feeder handle the extra length or fullness. This extra length is held on the edge stay. After you sew this seam, remove the bastings. Then overcast or bind the seam.

passages.old: The seam is then pressed open and the edge stay is pressed under one side of the seam allowance. When overcasting the seams in a skirt always start at the bottom and work to the top. In doing so the threads are held down smoothly with the left thumb and finger while you overcast from right to left taking one stitch at a time. When binding the seam begin at the bottom and work toward the top. (See Binding and Overcasting in the Chapter on Stitches). The Placket The extension for the facing of the upper lapof the placket and the extension for the under lap of the placket may be cut with the skirt. {See diag- DIAGRAM 7 Pla<'ket with the extension cut in the seam.
passages.plain: Press the seam open. Press the edge stay under one side of the seam allowance. When you overcast the seams in a skirt, always start at the bottom and work toward the top. Hold the threads down smoothly with your left thumb and finger. Overcast from right to left. Take one stitch at a time. When you bind the seam, start at the bottom and work toward the top. See Binding and Overcasting in the Chapter on Stitches. The Placket: You may cut the extension for the facing of the upper lap of the placket and the extension for the under lap of the placket at the same time as the skirt. See Diagram 7 Placket with the extension cut in the seam.

passages.old: Pla<?ket with the facing sewed to the seam. When this extension and the skirt is cut in one piece I would advise cutting it on both the left and the right side, because you are cutting your skirt double and it is better to cut it on both sides, keeping the cloth even, and trim off the useless extension on the right side, than to haggle into your cloth. If, to save material or to fit the gores in more economically when cutting, you do not cut the placket extension The Home Dressmakers' Guide 63 This extension should be 21/2 inches wide and about 2 inches longer than the opening for the placket.
passages.plain: Sew the placket with the facing to the seam. If you cut this extension and the skirt as one piece, you should cut it on both the left and right sides. You are cutting the skirt double. It is better to cut both sides and keep the cloth even. You can then trim off the extra piece on the right side. This is better than trying to squeeze the fabric. If you want to save material or fit the gores better, you can choose not to cut the placket extension. This extension should be 2.5 inches wide. It should be about 2 inches longer than the opening for the placket.

passages.old: The length of the placket depends on the individual. It should be of sufficient length to permit the skirt being slipped over the woman. Whether the extension for the facing of the upper lap of the placket and the extension for the under lap is cut with the gore or sewed on, they both must be stayed. Use a piece of straight material such as cambric, lawn or silk. By "straight" we mean not bias. This stay must also be Fold the facing for the upper side of the placket over the stay and sew the facing and the stay neatly to the body of the skirt, using a hemming stitch.
passages.plain: The length of the placket depends on the person. It must be long enough so you can slip the skirt over the woman. You can cut the extensions for the upper and under laps with the gore or sew them on. You must stay both of them. Use a piece of straight material like cambric, lawn, or silk. Straight means not on the bias. Fold the facing for the upper side of the placket over the stay. Sew the facing and the stay neatly to the body of the skirt using a hemming stitch.

passages.old: The edges of the cloth may be bound, overcast, or the edge folded and hemmed. Before the facing for the upper side of the placket is folded over the stay and stitched, the belting should be put in. (See the instructions in this Chapter teaching how the belting is put on the skirt). The under lap of the placket is faced on the wrong side with a piece of staying material. This strengthens the under lap for the eyes or snap fasteners. The edges of the under lap may be finished by binding, overcasting or any way that seems desirable.
passages.plain: You can finish the edges of the cloth by binding them, overcasting them, or folding and hemming them. You must put in the belting before you fold over and stitch the facing for the top side of the placket. You can find instructions in this chapter on how to put the belting on the skirt. You should face the under lap of the placket on the wrong side with a piece of staying material. This makes the under lap strong enough for eyes or snap fasteners. You can finish the edges of the under lap by binding, overcasting, or any other way you like.

passages.old: This extension was cut two inches longer than the placket proper; this makes a neat strong placket. The seam is sewed up two inches beyond the edge of the facing. A row of snap fasteners with three strong hooks and eyes at the belt will complete this placket. This is the simplest and best way to finish a placket in a tailored skirt. The placket closing may be in a seam, under a plait or in a slash made in the skirt. There are various ways to finish plackets. For a gathered skirt where a slash is made for the placket, or where it comes in a straight seam, it can be finished with a binding.
passages.plain: You should cut this extension two inches longer than the placket itself. This makes a neat and strong placket. Sew the seam two inches past the edge of the facing. You will finish this placket by adding a row of snap fasteners. Use three strong hooks and eyes at the belt. This is the simplest and best way to finish a placket in a tailored skirt. The placket closing can be in a seam. It can also be under a plait or in a slash made in the skirt. There are many ways to finish plackets. You can finish a gathered skirt with a binding. This applies if you make a slash for the placket or if it comes in a straight seam.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide A Bound Placket Take a piece of the material of which the skirt is made and cut on the straight grain of the cloth. This piece of material should be from 21/2 to 3 inches wide and twice as long as the length of the placket. This is sewed on like a binding. Starting at one end of the opening for the placket, place the right side of the binding next to the right side of the cloth and baste the two together, basting from one end of the opening for the placket down to the bottom, continuing around, and up the other side.
passages.plain: Take a piece of the same fabric used for the skirt. Cut it along the straight grain of the cloth. This piece should be between 2.5 and 3 inches wide. It must be twice as long as the length of the placket. You will sew this piece on like a binding. Start at one end of the placket opening. Place the right side of the binding next to the right side of the cloth. Sew them together with basting stitches. Baste from one end of the opening down to the bottom. Continue around the corner and up the other side.

passages.old: Keep the edges of the cloth and binding even. Next sew the binding from the top down, continuing around the bottom and up the other side. Have the seam as narrow as you can. Turn the binding onto the wrong side of the skirt and sew it down with a hemming stitch or it may be sewed on the machine. When the binding is turned at the lower end of the placket it will be necessary to clip the seam to make a perfect turn and to keep the lower edge of the placket from looking puckered.
passages.plain: Keep the edges of the cloth and the binding even. Sew the binding from the top down. Continue sewing around the bottom and up the other side. Make the seam as narrow as possible. Turn the binding onto the wrong side of the skirt. Sew it down with a hemming stitch or use a sewing machine. When you turn the binding at the lower end of the placket, you must clip the seam. This makes a perfect turn. It also keeps the lower edge of the placket from looking puckered.

passages.old: Arrange the placket so it closes properly and stitch on the inside to keep the lower edge of the placket from gaping. Press with a warm iron. The Belting There are many kinds of belting. Just a straight belting about 2 inches wide is best for slender folks. When the skirt is high waisted a belting as wide as the waist line is high should be used. A stout person can use a belting taped in the center and flaring to both edges. This belting will be form fitting. If this belting cannot be obtained the same result can be secured by taking darts in a wide straight belting.
passages.plain: Arrange the placket so it closes correctly. Stitch it on the inside. This stops the lower edge of the placket from opening. Press it with a warm iron. There are many kinds of belting. A straight belting about 2 inches wide is best for slender people. If the skirt has a high waist, use a belting as wide as the waist line. A stout person can use a belting that is narrow in the center and flares out to both edges. This belting will fit the body's shape. If you cannot find this belting, you can get the same result by putting darts into a wide straight belting.

passages.old: A narrow straight belting should be used for a short waist. Tall slender folks can use a belting three inches wide. In dresses, made from light materials and especially silk The Home Dressmakers' Guide or satin, a boned belting can be used giving excellent results. The bodice for a party dress may be built on a feather boned girdle six inches high. Attaching the Skirt to the Belting There are various ways of attaching the skirt to the belting, any one of which may prove satisfactory. In thirty-five years of dressmaking I have finished hundreds and hundreds of skirts and I have found that turning the skirt over the belting and finishing it on the inside with a seam binding or a cross stitch, gives the best looking finish.
passages.plain: Use a narrow straight belting for a short waist. Tall and slender people can use a belting that is three inches wide. You can use a boned belting for dresses made of light materials like silk or satin. This gives excellent results. You can build the bodice of a party dress on a feather boned girdle that is six inches high. There are many ways to attach the skirt to the belting. Any of these ways may work well. The author has finished hundreds of skirts in thirty-five years of dressmaking. She found that turning the skirt over the belting and finishing it on the inside with a seam binding or a cross stitch gives the best looking finish.

passages.old: This leaves no seam between the cloth and the belting to cause a ridge which is not only annoying but is very noticeable, as it leaves a mark when the skirt is pressed. The belting for a separate skirt with a natural waist line should be 21/2 inches longer than the exact waist measurement. When basting the top of the skirt over the belting place the belting under the placket and right up to where Next turn the seam of the skirt over the belting turning The shaded lines at the top of the belting in Diagram 9 shows the cloth turned over the belting.
passages.plain: This method leaves no seam between the cloth and the belting. A seam would create a ridge. This ridge is annoying and very noticeable. It also leaves a mark when you press the skirt. For a separate skirt with a natural waist line, the belting should be 2.5 inches longer than your exact waist measurement. When you baste the top of the skirt over the belting, place the belting under the placket. Place it right up to the edge. Next, turn the seam of the skirt over the belting. The shaded lines at the top of the belting in Diagram 9 show the cloth turned over the belting.

passages.old: DIAGKAM J) Go The Home Dressmakers' Guide The shaded lines at the center front of this three piece skirt shows the cloth turned back for the hem down the front. Have the belting extend to the end of the extension The skirt is turned over the belting and cross stitched, or the edge bound, from the top lap of the placket to the outer edge of the extension for the under lap. By doing this two rows of hooks and eyes are avoided as one row is all that is necessary.
passages.plain: Diagram J shows a three piece skirt. The shaded lines at the center front show the cloth turned back for the front hem. Make the belting reach the end of the extension. Turn the skirt over the belting. Cross stitch the edge or bind the edge. Do this from the top lap of the placket to the outer edge of the extension for the under lap. Doing this means you only need one row of hooks and eyes instead of two rows.

passages.old: This will be found to be a most satisfactory finish for the top and the simplest and best method of attaching the skirt to the belting. The belting is put in any separate skirt, no matter where the placket is, whether in a seam or under a plait, in the same way. Have the belting under the facing for the upper lap of the placket and extending to where the facing turns. Also have the belting continue to the edge of the extension for the under lap. Where the skirt is gathered or plaited it should not be turned over the belting as that would be bunglesome.
passages.plain: This is a very good finish for the top. It is also the easiest and best way to attach the skirt to the belting. You should put the belting in every separate skirt. It does not matter where the placket is. You can put it in a seam or under a plait. Do it in the same way every time. Put the belting under the facing for the upper lap of the placket. It should go as far as the facing turns. Also make the belting continue to the edge of the extension for the under lap. If the skirt is gathered or plaited, do not turn it over the belting. Doing that would be difficult.

passages.old: If the skirt is gathered in the back only, turn the skirt over the belting until you come to the gathers then trim off the gathers until they come not quite to the top of the belting. Put in two or three rows of shirring to hold the gathers and sew them to the belting, finishing the top with a binding. Where the skirt is altogether gathered let the gathers come half way to the top of the belting and finish the raw edges of the cloth with a binding.
passages.plain: If the skirt is gathered only in the back, turn the skirt over the belting. Stop when you reach the gathers. Trim the gathers so they do not reach the very top of the belting. Sew two or three rows of shirring to hold the gathers. Sew these to the belting. Finish the top with a binding. If the skirt is gathered all around, let the gathers reach halfway to the top of the belting. Finish the raw edges of the cloth with a binding.

passages.old: The girdle will cover both the edge of the cloth and the belting. The girdle is tacked on to the belting. Turning the Hem After the skirt has been attached to the belting and the seams have been finished and pressed open, you are ready to turn and finish the hem. In altering the pattern for the skirt you made it the exact length desired for the finished skirt at the center front, side seams and center back. Below this line which you penciled on the pattern you allowed 3 or 31/2 inches for the hem.
passages.plain: The girdle covers both the edge of the cloth and the belting. You tack the girdle onto the belting. You are ready to turn and finish the hem after you attach the skirt to the belting. You must also finish and press the seams open. When you changed the pattern for the skirt, you made it the exact length you wanted at the center front, side seams, and center back. You drew a line on the pattern for this length. Below this line, you added 3 or 3.5 inches for the hem.

passages.old: When the pattern was placed on the material and the skirt cut out, you followed the penciled line where the hem was to be turned with tailor tacks or trace threads. You therefore have the line upon which the hem is to be turned plainly marked on the cloth. Turn the hem upon this line, baste carefully and try the skirt on to determine the length and to be sure you have it even. The Home Dressmakers' Guide Basting the Hem First, baste where the hem is turned. This is shown by the dotted line in Diagram 10.
passages.plain: Place the pattern on the fabric and cut out the skirt. You should follow the pencil line where the hem will be turned. This line is clearly marked on the cloth. Turn the hem along this line. Sew it with basting stitches carefully. Try on the skirt to check the length and make sure it is even. Baste the hem where it is turned. Diagram 10 shows this with a dotted line.

passages.old: Next, measure carefully marking the depth of the hem all around the skirt. This is to make sure you have the hem the same depth. A simple yet effective method, is to cut a piece of card board the exact depth of the hem and use this card board for a guide. Now, fold the edge of the hem under and baste with a small running stitch. Sew with a slip stitch, remove the bastings and press with a warm iron. Finishing the hem this way will be very satisfactory for thin materials.
passages.plain: Next, measure and mark the depth of the hem all around the skirt. This ensures the hem is the same depth everywhere. One simple and effective method is to cut a piece of cardboard to the exact depth of the hem. Use this cardboard as a guide. Fold the edge of the hem under. Baste it with a small running stitch. Sew it with a slip stitch. Remove the basting stitches. Press the hem with a warm iron. Finishing the hem this way works well for thin materials.

passages.old: If the cloth is heavy the edge of the hem may be bound. Use silk binding ribbon or a bias binding made of cambric or any suitable material. This bias binding should be cut in narrow strips about % of an inch wide. Facing a Hem Although I do not advise it unless absolutely necessary yet a skirt that is very circular may have to be faced. This facing is often referred to as a false hem. This facing must be bias or cut the shape of the bottom of the skirt.
passages.plain: If the cloth is heavy, you may bind the edge of the hem. Use a silk binding ribbon or a bias binding made of cambric or another suitable material. You should cut this bias binding into narrow strips about 1/2 inch wide. You may need to face a skirt that is very circular. This is called a false hem. You should only do this if it is absolutely necessary. This facing must be cut on the bias or cut in the shape of the bottom of the skirt.

passages.old: If the skirt is gored cut the facing for each gore separately and have the seams in the facing and the seams in the skirt meet. This is sewed on like any facing and finished like a hem. Fullness in the Edge of the Hem When skirts are straight and narrow around the bottom we experience no difficulty in making the hem lay smooth and flat. When the skirt is gored and wide at the bottom, we will find, after putting in the first bastings that the edge of the hem is wider than it is where it was turned.
passages.plain: If the skirt has gores, cut the facing for each gore separately. Make sure the seams in the facing line up with the seams in the skirt. Sew it on like any other facing. Finish it like a hem. You will not have trouble making the hem lay flat if the skirt is straight and narrow at the bottom. However, if the skirt is gored and wide at the bottom, you will notice a problem. After you put in the first basting stitches, the edge of the hem will be wider than the part where it was turned.

passages.old: This, we call ''fullness" in the edge of the hem. This fullness may be shrunken out if the material is wool. Take a thread, the same color as the cloth, and, using a small running stitch, run the thread all around the edge of 68 The Home Dressmakers' Guide the hem and draw this thread up until it is exactly the same size as the body of the skirt. This brings the hem up to the proper circumference to fit down closely to the body of the skirt. The extra fulness, or puckers, we will shrink out.
passages.plain: We call this extra fabric in the hem 'fullness.' You can shrink this out if the fabric is wool. Take a thread that is the same color as the cloth. Use a small running stitch to sew the thread all around the edge of the hem. Pull this thread until the hem is the exact same size as the body of the skirt. This makes the hem the correct size so it fits closely against the skirt. You will shrink out the extra fullness or puckers.

passages.old: Turn the hem upon the first bastings and take a sponge cloth, wrung out of water, and lay it upon the turned down hem. Press with a hot iron until all the gathers have been shrunken out and the hem is the same size as the thread. This can be done until not a gather will show and the hem will lay evenly and perfectly along the body of the skirt. Bind the edge of the hem neatly and after basting, sew it to the body of the skirt with the sewing machine.
passages.plain: Turn the hem over the first basting stitches. Take a sponge cloth that you have wrung out of water. Lay it on the turned down hem. Press it with a hot iron. Do this until all the gathers are flat. The hem must be the same size as the thread. Keep doing this until no gathers show. The hem must lay evenly and perfectly along the skirt. Bind the edge of the hem neatly. After basting, sew the hem to the body of the skirt with a sewing machine.

passages.old: The binding may be sewed on with the machine and the hem felled down by hand. The binding may also be basted on and both the binding and the hem sewed with the machine in one operation. The more circular the skirt is the greater the amount of fullness in the hem. Sometimes small plaits can be laid in the hem to take care of this fulness. (See Diagram 10.) This will be found to work satisfactorily. Sewing the Hem When the hem is sewed with the machine place the wrong side of the skirt next the feeder.
passages.plain: You can sew the binding with a machine and sew the hem by hand. You can also baste the binding on first. Then you can sew both the binding and the hem with the machine at the same time. A skirt that is more circular will have more fullness in the hem. You can sometimes put small pleats in the hem to handle this fullness. See Diagram 10. This method works well. When you sew the hem with the machine, place the wrong side of the skirt next to the feeder.

passages.old: The feeder will help to carry any fullness through without showing gathers and the tension will often make a better stitch on the right side. Woolen skirts may be hemmed by hand using the regular hemming stitch. Silks, Satins, Crepes, Voiles and any expensive materials being made up into handsome gowns, should always have the hem finished by hand. To sew the hem of such a gown with the machine not only cheapens the appearance of the garment but it is also more or less injurious to the cloth. Prepare the hem in the usual way and use the regular hemming stitch or the slip stitch.
passages.plain: The feeder helps move extra fabric through the machine without showing gathers. The tension often creates a better stitch on the right side of the fabric. You can hem woolen skirts by hand using the regular hemming stitch. You should always finish the hem by hand for silks, satins, crepes, voiles, and any expensive materials used for gowns. Sewing the hem of these gowns with a machine makes the garment look cheaper. It also harms the cloth. Prepare the hem in the usual way. Use either the regular hemming stitch or the slip stitch.

passages.old: If silk or satin skirts are hemmed with the machine they are handled just the same as the woolen skirts. It often happens that one is alone and there is no one available to help in turning a hem evenly at the bottom of the skirt. After the skirt has been fastened to the belting and you are ready to have the hem turned, put the skirt on The Home Dressmakers' Guide and standing erect (be sure not to look down or sway from side to side) before the glass, go all around yourself with the yard stick as shown in the diagram.
passages.plain: You handle silk or satin skirts the same way as woolen skirts when you hem them with a machine. Sometimes you are alone and no one can help you turn the hem evenly at the bottom. After you fasten the skirt to the belting and are ready to turn the hem, put the skirt on. Stand straight in front of the mirror. Do not look down or sway from side to side. Go all around yourself with the yard stick like the diagram shows.

passages.old: Place a pin at the top of the yard stick at frequent intervals. Pay no attention to the distance of these pins from the waist line. Have the yard stick perpendicular and the pins will be 36 inches from the floor. Take the skirt off and lay it on the table. Place the yard stick again on the skirt with the 36-inch end at the pins. You may now place another inches from the floor. This is where the hem will turn. The distance of the finished skirt from the floor will, of course, depend on the prevailing style or upon individual taste.
passages.plain: Put a pin at the top of the yardstick at regular intervals. Do not worry about how far these pins are from the waist line. Hold the yardstick straight up and down. The pins should be 36 inches from the floor. Take the skirt off and lay it on the table. Place the yardstick on the skirt again. Put the 36 inch end at the pins. You can now place another pin at a different distance from the floor. This is where the hem will turn. The distance of the finished skirt from the floor depends on the current style or your personal taste.

passages.old: Continue to measure from the first pins to where the hem will turn, marking at frequent intervals by placing pins. This second row of pins will be an even distance from the floor all around. When the skirt has been marked all around, run a basting thread evenly around the bottom on the line of the pins. Turn the hem on this basting thread line. If the weave of the cloth is firm, this will assure you of an even length all around the bottom of the skirt. If the cloth is inclined to stretch, you can baste the hem and try it on and see where "it has stretched. You can then change the pins and get it to hang perfectly with little trouble. 70 The Home Dressmakers' Guide
passages.plain: Continue measuring from the first pins to where the hem will turn. Mark these spots by placing pins at regular intervals. This second row of pins must be the same distance from the floor all around. Once you have marked the entire skirt, sew a basting thread evenly around the bottom along the line of pins. Turn the hem on this basting thread line. If the fabric is firm, this will make sure the bottom of the skirt is an even length all around. If the fabric stretches easily, sew the basting hem and try on the skirt to see where it stretched. You can then move the pins to make it hang perfectly with little effort.

chapters.why: The techniques for handling delicate fabrics and pressing woolens remain essential for garment care and preservation.

chapters.title: Cutting and making blouses

passages.old: One of the essentials in every woman's wardrobe are her blouses. Styles come and go and come again but the blouse always remains. Any woman with a few good looking blouses and a well-tailored skirt is always in style and is well dressed. There is such a variety of designs from which to choose and such a wonderful assortment of materials from which to select, that no woman need be without beautiful and becoming blouses. Since the hemstitching machines have come into vogue, for finishing seams, and adding much to the trimming, the problem of blouse expense and making, has to a great extent become solved.
passages.plain: Blouses are a must-have in every woman's wardrobe. Styles change, but the blouse is always popular. You will always look stylish and well-dressed if you have a few nice blouses and a well-tailored skirt. There are many designs to choose from and many types of materials to pick from. Because of this, no woman needs to go without beautiful blouses. Hemstitching machines are now popular for finishing seams and adding decoration. These machines have made it much easier and cheaper to make blouses.

passages.old: In the blouse, perhaps more than in any other garment, exquisite workmanship is necessary if the finished blouse is to have the desired appearance. The finishing of the seams on the wrong side has much to do with the eflfect'when the garment is completed. When the blouse is made from sheer material the under-arm seam and the inside seam of the sleeve should be French seamed. If hemstitching is used all of the seams may be hemstitched. In a tailored blouse the seams are felled and stitched with the sewing machine making a neat finish on the inside as well as giving a smart tailored looked to the outside.
passages.plain: A blouse needs excellent workmanship to look good. The way you finish the seams on the inside of the fabric affects how the finished garment looks. You should use a French seam for the under-arm seam and the inside sleeve seam if you use sheer material. You can hemstitch all of the seams if you choose to use hemstitching. In a tailored blouse, you should fell the seams and stitch them with a sewing machine. This makes a neat finish on the inside and gives a smart tailored look to the outside.

passages.old: A silk or wool blouse may have the seams sewed like an ordinary seam and then overcast neatly or bound with a seam binding. These seams may be finished separately and pressed open, or they may be bound double. After the shoulder and under-arm seam has been basted and sewed, hem the bottom and put a one-half inch elastic inside the hem. Another way to finish the bottom of a blouse is to make a band one inch wide and attach it to the back of the blouse, leaving the front loose, to be held in with the band when it is fastened around the waist.
passages.plain: You can sew the seams of a silk or wool blouse like a normal seam. Then you can overcast them neatly or use a seam binding. You can finish these seams separately and press them open. Or you can bind them double. After you baste and sew the shoulder and under-arm seam, hem the bottom. Put a one-half inch elastic inside the hem. You can also finish the bottom of a blouse in another way. Make a band that is one inch wide. Attach it to the back of the blouse. Leave the front loose. You will hold the front in with the band when you fasten it around the waist.

passages.old: Finishing the Front of a Blouse There are numerous ways to finish the f^ont of a blouse. Just a hem down the front, with the right side lapping over the left, and fastened with buttons and buttonholes is a very simple way. Loops of cord or braid, or crocheted loops may also be used with buttons. The Home Dressmakers' Guide 71 Finishing the Front With a Box Plait A box plait in the front is especially good looking for a tailored blouse. This box plait may be made about 2^2 inches in width and should be basted in the cloth before the blouse is cut.
passages.plain: There are many ways to finish the front of a blouse. One simple way is to make a hem down the front. You can overlap the right side over the left side. You can fasten it with buttons and buttonholes. You can also use buttons with loops of cord, braid, or crochet. A box plait in the front looks very good on a tailored blouse. You can make this box plait about 2 1/2 inches wide. You should sew this box plait into the cloth with basting stitches before you cut the blouse.

passages.old: The box plait must be on the right side of the opening and the center of the box plait should be the center front of the blouse. The opening will therefore be a little to the left. On the left side just a hem is allowed for the underlap of the front. Buttons and button holes are always used with this style of blouse. The box plait may be stitched on each side having the stitching as far from the edge as the individual taste suggests. Finishing the Front With a Slot Seam First baste a hem on the left side of the front of the blouse.
passages.plain: Put the box pleat on the right side of the opening. The center of the box pleat must line up with the center front of the blouse. This means the opening will be slightly to the left. Only a hem is allowed for the underlap on the left side. You must always use buttons and buttonholes with this style of blouse. You can stitch the box pleat on each side. You can choose how far from the edge to place the stitching. To finish the front with a slot seam, first baste a hem on the left side of the front of the blouse.

passages.old: Next cut a strip of the material, lengthwise, and about three inches wide for a fly. This fly is doubled and basted onto the left side, and underneath the hem, with half the width extending beyond the hem. Now stitch the hem with the sewing machine and stitching the fly on to the blouse at the same time. Baste and stitch the hem on the right side of the blouse and the right side will lap the fly meeting the hem on the The front of this blouse is fastened with snap fasteners or hooks and eyes.
passages.plain: Next, cut a strip of material about three inches wide. Cut it lengthwise to make a fly. Fold this fly in half. Baste it onto the left side of the blouse underneath the hem. Make sure half of the width of the fly extends past the hem. Stitch the hem with your sewing machine. Stitch the fly onto the blouse at the same time. Baste and stitch the hem on the right side of the blouse. The right side will overlap the fly and meet the hem. You fasten the front of this blouse with snap fasteners or hooks and eyes.

passages.old: Attaching the Collar to the Blouse When a flat or rolling collar is sewed on to the neck of the blouse and the collar is made double, it is necessary that the underside and upperside of the collar be sewed on separately. The underside or lining of the collar is sewed on first. Baste it on carefully having the blouse right side out and the underside of the collar in its final place with the edge of the collar and the edge of the neck of the blouse evenly together.
passages.plain: You are attaching the collar to the blouse. This applies when you sew a flat or rolling collar to the neck of the blouse and make the collar double. You must sew the underside and the upperside of the collar separately. You sew the underside or lining of the collar first. You must baste it on carefully. Put the blouse with the right side facing out. Place the underside of the collar in its final position. Make sure the edge of the collar and the edge of the neck of the blouse are even together.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers* Guide Sew it on using a short basting stitch. Begin at the center back and sew to first one end and then the other. The upper part of the collar is then placed under the half of the collar that has been sewed on and in the same position as though it were going to be the underpart of the collar. It is, however, placed with the wrong side up and the right side next to the body of the garment. The outer edges of the two parts of the collar are then sewed together and the upper part of the collar turned up over the under part of the collar.
passages.plain: Sew it on using a short basting stitch. Start at the center back. Sew to one end and then sew to the other end. Place the upper part of the collar under the half of the collar that you already sewed on. Put it in the same position as if it were the underpart of the collar. Place it with the wrong side facing up. Place the right side next to the body of the garment. Sew the outer edges of the two collar parts together. Turn the upper part of the collar up over the under part of the collar.

passages.old: The upper collar is/ brought up and turned over the seam at the neck and, with the edge turned under like a hem, is felled down by hand to the body of the garment. It may be finished at the neck with a bias facing like the collar that is made of gram 1, showing the bias facing before it is turned.) When the collar is made of one thickness of cloth you first find the center of the back of the neck of the blouse and the center of the back of the neck of the collar.
passages.plain: Bring up the upper collar. Turn it over the seam at the neck. Turn the edge under like a hem. Sew it down by hand to the body of the garment. You can finish the neck with a bias facing. This is like the collar made in gram 1. You show the bias facing before you turn it. When the collar is made of one thickness of cloth, find the center of the back of the blouse neck. Then find the center of the back of the collar neck.

passages.old: Place the wrong side of the collar next to the right side of the blouse having the two edges come together evenly. Baste carefully from the center back to the front on one side and then on the other. Next cut a bias strip of the cloth, three-fourths of an inch wide, and place the right side of this bias strip next to the right side of the collar and baste carefully. Now sew the three thicknesses together with a running stitch. (See ''B," Diagram 1, showing the bias facing before it is turned).
passages.plain: Place the wrong side of the collar next to the right side of the blouse. Make sure the two edges line up evenly. Sew a temporary stitch carefully from the center back to the front on one side. Do the same on the other side. Cut a strip of fabric on the bias. This strip should be three-fourths of an inch wide. Place the right side of this strip next to the right side of the collar. Sew a temporary stitch carefully. Now sew the three layers of fabric together with a running stitch. Look at Diagram 1, part B, to see the bias facing before you turn it.

passages.old: Turn the bias facing on to the wrong side of the neck of the blouse covering the seam and after basting carefully, sew it down by hand using a small hemming stitch. Some- The Home Dressmakers' Guide 73 times this bias facing may be sewed on with the sewing machine. Finishing the Yoke When there is a yoke on a blouse it should always be sewed on in the following way : Turn the edge of the yoke under and baste it flat on to the body of the blouse.
passages.plain: Turn the bias facing to the wrong side of the blouse neck. It should cover the seam. Baste it carefully. Then sew it down by hand with a small hemming stitch. You can also sew this bias facing with a sewing machine. To finish the yoke, follow these steps. If a blouse has a yoke, you must sew it on this way. Turn the edge of the yoke under. Baste it flat onto the body of the blouse.

passages.old: This will always look best. Never French seam a yoke on to the blouse where there are gathers in the blouse. The yoke should be stitched from the right side or hemstitched. If it is sewed with the sewing machine the seam should be finished neatly on the wrong side by overcasting or binding. A Drop Yoke The drop yoke on the front of a blouse has considerable bias, it is therefore necessary when making a drop yoke blouse out of thin stretchy material, to stay the edge of the yoke with a piece of the cloth cut lengthwise.
passages.plain: This method looks the best. Do not use a French seam to attach a yoke to a blouse that has gathers. You should stitch the yoke from the right side or use a hemstitch. If you use a sewing machine, you must finish the seam neatly on the wrong side. You can do this by overcasting or binding. A Drop Yoke. The drop yoke on the front of a blouse has a lot of bias. If you make a drop yoke blouse from thin stretchy material, you must stay the edge of the yoke. Use a piece of cloth cut lengthwise to do this.

passages.old: Cut this strip about one-half inch wide. If there is a selvage edge to the cloth this may be used. Sew this stay in with the seam. This will prevent the yoke from stretching down over the shoulder. Never French seam a drop yoke on the front of a blouse, especially when the front is gathered. It would not look well from the outside. It is best to fold the edge of the yoke under and place it on to the gathered body of the blouse and, after the stitching is done, finish it on the wrong side with a binding.
passages.plain: Cut a strip about one-half inch wide. You can use the selvage edge of the cloth if it has one. Sew this stay into the seam. This stops the yoke from stretching down over the shoulder. Do not use a French seam on a drop yoke on the front of a blouse. This is true especially if the front is gathered. It will not look good from the outside. You should fold the edge of the yoke under. Place it on the gathered body of the blouse. Finish it on the wrong side with a binding after you finish the stitching.

passages.old: It may be hemstitched or finished with a chain stitch. • The Kimona Blouse The kimona blouse is very simple and may be cut from a plain foundation pattern. A lining pattern having French lines or a plain lining pattern with darts may also be used. Diagram 3 shows a French lining pattern placed on the cloth and the kimona blouse outlined. Place your foundation on the cloth as shown in Diagram 3. The front and back of the pattern is set shoulder to shoulder joining however only at the neck.
passages.plain: You can use a hemstitch or a chain stitch to finish the edges. The Kimona blouse is very simple. You can cut it from a plain foundation pattern. You can also use a lining pattern with French lines or a plain lining pattern with darts. Diagram 3 shows a French lining pattern on the cloth and the outline of the Kimona blouse. Place your foundation on the cloth like it shows in Diagram 3. The front and back of the pattern join at the shoulders. They only join at the neck.

passages.old: This is to avoid bias in back or front. On the other hand, should bias be desired, place the shoulder lines together. The Home Dressmakers' Guide DIAGRAM 2 A Kimona Blouse one of the many varieties of cuffs fashion or individual taste may select. Cut the cuff to fit the wrist, or make it the size of the hand measure. Closing may be fashioned at the front, to the left, or may be made in the back. Any material may be used, and for the medium yards of 36-inch cloth will be required.
passages.plain: Do this to avoid bias in the back or front. If you want bias, place the shoulder lines together. Diagram 2 shows a Kimona blouse. You can choose from many varieties of cuffs based on fashion or your own taste. Cut the cuff to fit your wrist. You can also make it the size of your hand measurement. You can put the closing at the front, on the left, or in the back. You can use any material. You will need about one yard of 36-inch wide cloth.

passages.old: It is well to lay a plait upon the cloth in front, where the dotted line is shown. This plait should start at the top like a dart, and be two inches deep at the waist line. This is to give more and needed fullness over the bust. Between the two X*s on the back of the sleeve, as shown in Diagram 3, hold in one inch of fullness. This will be sufficient to give the elbow greater freedom of action. This blouse may also be made with a seam on the shoulder.
passages.plain: Place a fold on the front of the cloth where the dotted line is. This fold should start at the top like a dart. It should be two inches deep at the waist line. This gives the bust the extra fullness it needs. Hold in one inch of fullness between the two X marks on the back of the sleeve. You can see this in Diagram 3. This will let the elbow move more freely. You can also make this blouse with a seam on the shoulder.

passages.old: Any style collar is adaptable; as also any DIAGRAM n The Home Dressmakers' Guide Blouse With Drop Shoulder and Surplus Front Begin by using a plain lining with darts. From this lining as a foundation, draft the blouse as shown in Diagram 5. Draw the line for the shoulder from the base of the neck straight out to three inches beyond the tip of the shoulder. This .i^ives the shoulder a drop of three mches as clearly shown in Diagram 5. This diagram shows the line for the under arm seam to be just below the armseye, two inches beyond the under arm seam of the plain lining.
passages.plain: You can use any style of collar. You can also make a blouse with a drop shoulder and a surplus front. Start by using a plain lining with darts. Use this lining as a base. Draft the blouse as shown in Diagram 5. Draw the shoulder line. Start at the base of the neck and draw it straight out. Go three inches past the tip of the shoulder. This gives the shoulder a drop of three inches. Diagram 5 shows this clearly. The diagram shows the line for the underarm seam. This line is just below the armseye. It is two inches beyond the underarm seam of the plain lining.

passages.old: DIAGRAM 4 A. Drop Shoulder This may be more or less, according to the amount of fullness desired in the blouse. Copy the lines of the diagram, using good judgment, and no difficulty will be experienced. The surplus front is outlined by drawing a line from the base of the neck at the shoulder and crossing the center front line of the plain lining at the bust point, continue down to three inches below the waist line, below the bust point is optional. DIAGRAM 5 The amount of fullness The back of this blouse is outlined in a similar manner as shown by Diagram 5.
passages.plain: Look at Diagram 4 A for the drop shoulder. You can change this size depending on how much fullness you want in the blouse. Copy the lines in the diagram. Use your own judgment and you will not have any problems. To outline the extra front fabric, draw a line from the base of the neck at the shoulder. Cross the center front line of the plain lining at the bust point. Continue this line down to three inches below the waist line. Drawing below the bust point is optional. Look at Diagram 5 for the amount of fullness. The back of this blouse is outlined in a similar way as shown in Diagram 5.

passages.old: Make the usual allowance for seams and cut. Sew the seams of the lining first, then sew the sleeves into the lining. Next sew the seams of the blouse and finish the drop shoulder with a cord. Then mark the center back of the blouse at the neck and the center back of the collar and baste the collar on carefully. When sewing the collar on finish with a one-inch bias facing. The Home Dressmakers' Guide Face the surplus front or make allowance for a hem when cutting. Make a band one inch wide and attach this band to the back of the blouse at the waist line, or when hemming the bottom of the blouse, put in 1/2-inch elastic.
passages.plain: Add the usual amount of extra fabric for seams and cutting. Sew the lining seams first. Then sew the sleeves into the lining. Next sew the seams of the blouse. Finish the drop shoulder with a cord. Mark the center back of the blouse at the neck. Mark the center back of the collar. Baste the collar on carefully. Finish the collar with a one-inch bias facing. Face the extra front fabric or add extra fabric for a hem when you cut. Make a band that is one inch wide. Attach this band to the back of the blouse at the waist line. Alternatively, put in 1/2-inch elastic when you hem the bottom of the blouse.

passages.old: Baste the cuff onto the sleeve and finish with a facing, the same as for the collar. If a thin material, such as Georgette Crepe, is used, employ French seams. Blouse With a Gibson Plait DIAGRAM 6 The Home Dressmakers' Guide This blouse is always worn; is stylish in cut and becoming in its lines. Particularly is it adapted to the large woman. Invariably it makes a good looking tailored blouse, or, is equally suitable for a house dress. May be cut out of any kind of cloth. Diagram 6 shows both the front and back as they will appear when cut out, and ready to baste.
passages.plain: Sew the cuff onto the sleeve. Finish it with a facing like the one you used for the collar. Use French seams if you use a thin fabric like Georgette Crepe. This is a blouse with a Gibson Plait. It is always worn. It has a stylish cut and nice lines. It is especially good for a large woman. It always looks like a good tailored blouse. It is also good for a house dress. You can cut it out of any kind of cloth. Diagram 6 shows the front and back. It shows how they will look when they are cut out and ready to be sewn together.

passages.old: Place your foundation pattern on the cloth 5 inches back from the edge. Having done this, trace for the center front, including the outline of the neck. Then measure down the center front from the base of the neck 4 inches, and from this point draw a line to B, which in turn must be connected Trace the length of the shoulder and follow this by laying a plait 11/2 inches deep, as shown between points X and X at the waist line of Diagram 6. Pin your goods down and proceed to outline at armseye and under the arm.
passages.plain: Place your foundation pattern on the cloth. Put it 5 inches back from the edge. Trace the center front. Include the outline of the neck. Measure down 4 inches from the base of the neck on the center front. Draw a line from this point to B. Connect B to the next point. Trace the length of the shoulder. Lay a plait that is 1.5 inches deep. This goes between points X and X at the waist line of Diagram 6. Pin your fabric down. Outline the armseye and the area under the arm.

passages.old: Allow three inches below the waist for length and fullness. The back of this blouse is outlined and the plait is laid .The collar for this blouse, (see Diagram 6), must be fashioned to the size of the neck and may be done as follows : Cut a piece of muslin the length of the given neck measurement, and as deep as you desire your collar to -be. Follow the dimensions given in the illustration. Conclude by fitting to the neck, getting the correct size before cutting the cloth. A Gibson plait may be stitched all the way down the back, but looks better in front, just stitched above the break at the armseye.
passages.plain: Leave three inches below the waist for length and fullness. The back of this blouse is outlined and the plait is laid. You must make the collar for this blouse to fit the size of the neck. You can make it like this. Cut a piece of muslin. The length should be your neck measurement. The depth should be as deep as you want the collar to be. Follow the measurements in the illustration. You must fit the collar to the neck to get the correct size before you cut the cloth. You can stitch a Gibson plait all the way down the back. However, it looks better in the front. You should stitch it just above the break at the armseye.

The diagram shows a sleeve with the dart to the elbow but with the lower part of the under sleeve cut from a corner of the cloth.
passages.plain: Look at the star on the front plait in Diagram 6. Diagram 7 shows how to cut a blouse from one and one-half yards of thirty-six inch wide material. The diagram shows how to place a pattern on the cloth. You can get the entire blouse out of that amount of fabric. This works for any woman unless she is extra large. You will have to piece the sleeve under the arm. The diagram shows a sleeve with the dart at the elbow. The lower part of the under sleeve is cut from a corner of the cloth.

passages.old: It is joined to the sleeve as the diagram. To get a sleeve with a dart to the elbow out without piecing, 1% yards will be necessary ; 1% yards, however, giving ample material for almost any sized woman. DIAGRAM 8 The Home Dressmakers' Guide How to Cut a Flat Sailor Collar Pin the shoulder seams together as illustrated in Diagram 9. If a V neck is desired, mark 3 inches down from the front of the neck, which makes a very good depth for the average blouse. Then take a piece of paper and placing the edge upon the center gram 9), trace the line of the neck and down the line for the V, and shape it to any desired size or curves.
passages.plain: Join it to the sleeve like the diagram shows. You need 1.5 yards of fabric to make a sleeve with a dart to the elbow without piecing. 1.5 yards provides enough material for almost any sized woman. Look at Diagram 8. To cut a flat sailor collar, pin the shoulder seams together as shown in Diagram 9. If you want a V neck, mark 3 inches down from the front of the neck. This is a good depth for an average blouse. Take a piece of paper and place the edge on the center line of Diagram 9. Trace the line of the neck and the line for the V. Shape it to any size or curve you want.

passages.old: See Diagram 9 for two styles illustrated; one a flat sailor collar, and the other Dointed in front and rounded at the back. How to Cut a Rolling Collar When a blouse has been cut out, pin the shoulder seams together and cut a V down from the neck line, to the desired depth (see will say, for an example, is 3 inches. Whereupon, place a piece of paper over the blouse, with its edge upon the fold of the back, as in the illustration from X to neck line, as you would for a flat collar.
passages.plain: Look at Diagram 9 to see two styles. One is a flat sailor collar. The other is pointed in the front and rounded at the back. To cut a rolling collar, first cut out the blouse. Pin the shoulder seams together. Cut a V shape down from the neckline to your chosen depth. For example, you might choose 3 inches. Next, place a piece of paper over the blouse. Put the edge of the paper on the fold of the back. Place it from X to the neckline just as you would for a flat collar.

passages.old: Determining the Roll From the natural shoulder line, as at A, Diagram 10, mark down to B at the V point in front, which is 3 inches from the front of the neck. For a slight roll, draw a line from the shoulder point at A, to C. An increased roll may 80 The Home Dressmakers' Guide be obtained by merely widening the angle, so from A to C, or D to F. You will notice how straight is the line from the back of the neck to F. The straighter you have this line, the more the collar will roll in the back.
passages.plain: Look at the natural shoulder line at point A in Diagram 10. Mark a point at B. This is the V point in the front. It is 3 inches from the front of the neck. To make a slight roll, draw a line from shoulder point A to C. You can make a larger roll by widening the angle. You can do this from A to C or from D to F. Notice that the line from the back of the neck to F is straight. The straighter this line is, the more the collar will roll in the back.

passages.old: Some rolling collars are just a straight piece of cloth, cut to the length of the size of the neck. The width at the back of the rolling collar, given in this illustration, is 14 inches across; but, when cutting the half, make your point at the front from which you are working. Work out on paper, various sizes with different shaped corners, excellent collar practice, and you will fast become expert at this highly important and fascinating part of blouse making. The Home Dressmakers' Guide 81
passages.plain: Some rolling collars are just a straight piece of cloth. You cut them to the length of the neck size. In this illustration, the width at the back of the rolling collar is 14 inches. When you cut the half, make your point at the front from where you are working. Practice by making various sizes with different shaped corners on paper. This is excellent collar practice. You will quickly become an expert at this important and fascinating part of blouse making.

chapters.why: The chapter provides fundamental sewing techniques and seam finishing methods that remain relevant for creating high-quality garments today.

chapters.title: Cutting and making the one-piece dress

passages.old: When we talk about the "One-Piece Dress'' we mean a garment all cut in one piece from the shoulder to the hem at the bottom. This style of garment may have close fitting lines like the Princess gown, or it may have straight or semi-fitting lines. It is a matter of choosing the lines that will be most becoming to the one who will wear the dress. The one-piece dress is most becoming to large figures as it gives long lines and can be made to detract from the appearance of stoutness.
passages.plain: A one-piece dress is a garment cut in one piece from the shoulder to the bottom hem. This style can have close fitting lines like a princess gown. It can also have straight or semi-fitting lines. You should choose the lines that look best on the person wearing the dress. The one-piece dress looks best on large figures. It creates long lines. It can be made to hide a stout appearance.

passages.old: This dress may be made from heavy cloth for winter wear and from lighter material for summer. Lining the Dress When a one-piece dress is made from wash material it is not necessary to build it on a lining; a lining in a dress that is to be washed will make the ironing more difficult. When this dress is made from Woolens it is much more satisfactory if the waist is lined as it will not only wear better but the lining will keep the garment in position on the body.
passages.plain: You can make this dress from heavy cloth for winter or lighter material for summer. You should consider the lining of the dress. If you make a one-piece dress from washable material, you do not need to use a lining. A lining makes ironing harder for clothes that you plan to wash. If you make this dress from wool, it is better to line the waist. A lining will help the dress wear better. The lining will also help the dress stay in position on your body.

passages.old: It is always necessary to line the waist of the evening gown and sometimes the skirt also. The lining for the waist of a one-piece dress can be made out of strong net. A curtain net will be found to be stronger and wear much better than any of the finer Brussel Nets. China silk or lawn may also be satisfactorily used. A lining lawn can usually be purchased at the lining department of any Dry Goods Store. How to Make the Lining The lining should first be cut from a fitted foundation pattern.
passages.plain: You must always line the waist of an evening gown. Sometimes you should also line the skirt. You can make the lining for the waist of a one-piece dress out of strong net. Curtain net is stronger and lasts longer than fine Brussel Nets. You can also use China silk or lawn. You can usually buy lining lawn at the lining department of any Dry Goods Store. To make the lining, you should first cut it from a fitted foundation pattern.

passages.old: It should then be basted and tried on, as the fit of the finished garment depends altogether on how the lining fits. It is very necessary that this lining be fitted to the body very carefully. Even though the pattern was altered to fit perfectly the net will stretch, making a careful fitting imperative. In making the net lining fit, it may be necessary to fold a plait all the way down the center back. Or perhaps the two darts at the back will have to be pinned deeper. 82 The Home Dressmakers' Guide After the lining has been drawn tightly until it fits the body perfectly and the darts at the back sewed firmly, the under arm seam may be sewed with the sewing machine.
passages.plain: You should baste and try on the garment. The fit of the finished dress depends entirely on how the lining fits. You must fit the lining to the body very carefully. Even if you changed the pattern to fit perfectly, the net will stretch. This makes a careful fitting necessary.
