When you make the net lining fit, you might need to fold a pleat all the way down the center back. Or, you might have to pin the two darts at the back deeper. After you pull the lining tight until it fits the body perfectly and sew the back darts firmly, you may sew the underarm seam with the sewing machine.

passages.old: Next put the hooks and eyes on to the hem in front. How to Sew Hooks and Eyes on a Lining Hooks must always be sewed on to the right side and eyes on the left. Sew the hooks back from the edge of the lining about a quarter of an inch ; with the spacing between each, one and one-half inch. This will give sufficient strength to the lining. Sew the eyes on the wrong side of the edge, with just enough of projections to catch the hooks. Then turn the edge of the lining over the eyes where the threads show.
passages.plain: Next, put the hooks and eyes on the front hem. You must always sew the hooks on the right side and the eyes on the left side. Sew the hooks about a quarter of an inch back from the edge of the lining. Space the hooks one and one-half inches apart. This makes the lining strong enough. Sew the eyes on the wrong side of the edge. Leave just enough of the eyes to catch the hooks. Turn the edge of the lining over the eyes where the threads show.

passages.old: The fullness in front may be gathered instead of being taken out in darts. If darts are used they may be sewed at the same time with the darts at the back. Having the fullness in front gathered will be more comfortable, especially for slender folks. When the seams and darts are thus taken care of the belting must be measured and attached. Measure the belting having it one inch longer than the waist measurement. This inch is to allow for one-half inch hem at both ends of the belting to give strength where the hooks and eyes are sewed on.
passages.plain: You can gather the extra fabric in the front instead of using darts. If you choose to use darts, you can sew them at the same time as the darts in the back. Gathering the fabric in the front is more comfortable, especially for thin people. Once you finish the seams and darts, you must measure and attach the belting. Measure the belting so it is one inch longer than your waist measurement. This extra inch allows for a half inch hem at both ends of the belting. These hems provide strength where you sew on the hooks and eyes.

passages.old: After the hooks and eyes are sewed on find the line for the center back by folding the belting. The lining should open straight down the front. Mark with a pin the center back and folding the belting again find where the side seams should come and mark them with pins. Next put the belting around the waist, then put the lining on, pinning it to the belting. Pin the side seams of the lining to the place marked for them on the belting and also pin the center back of the lining to the center back line of the belting.
passages.plain: Sew on the hooks and eyes. Fold the belting to find the center back line. The lining must open straight down the front. Mark the center back with a pin. Fold the belting again to find where the side seams should be. Mark those spots with pins. Put the belting around your waist. Put the lining on over it. Pin the lining to the belting. Pin the side seams of the lining to the marks on the belting. Pin the center back of the lining to the center back line of the belting.

passages.old: The lining must be stretched down and made to fit snugly before it is pinned. After the center back and the side lines are pinned the lining may be stretched down and pinned here and there distributing the fullness in front evenly. You may now sew the lining on to the belting by hand carefully removing all pins. Having left the shoulder seams basted, remove the bastings and, if it is necessary, stretch the lining by taking a deeper seam on the shoulders. The Home Dressmakers' Guide 83 If the sleeves of the dress are to be attached to the lining it will be necessary to face the lining all around the armseye.
passages.plain: You must stretch the lining down and make it fit snugly before you pin it. Pin the center back and the side lines. Then you can stretch the lining down and pin it in different spots to spread the extra fabric evenly across the front. You can now sew the lining to the belting by hand. Remove all the pins carefully. Leave the shoulder seams basted for now. Remove those bastings. If you need to, stretch the lining by taking a deeper seam on the shoulders. If you want to attach the sleeves of the dress to the lining, you must face the lining all around the armseye.

passages.old: Use a piece of the material about three or four inches deep for the facing. While the shoulder seams are open the lining may be spread flat upon the table and the facing cut to fit the armseye. The facing is sewed in with the shoulder seam and can be sewed on to the lining by hand or with the sewing machine. When the sleeves are to be sewed into the lining it is necessary to have the lining project enough at the shoulder to allow for a seam. The lining is now ready for the dress.
passages.plain: Use a piece of fabric about three or four inches deep for the facing. Keep the shoulder seams open. Spread the lining flat on the table. Cut the facing to fit the armseye. Sew the facing in with the shoulder seam. You can sew the facing to the lining by hand or with a sewing machine. When you sew the sleeves into the lining, the lining must stick out enough at the shoulder to allow for a seam. The lining is now ready for the dress.

passages.old: How to Bone a Seam in the Lining When the style of garment requires a hea\T, strong lining and boning, the soft feather bone may be sewed on with the machine, resulting in a much stronger seam than was procured by the fancy stitches we formerly employed. Always hold the bone slightly looser than the seam, or, to be more explicit, stretch the seam onto the bone. This will insure a nice, smooth waist line. To Finish Seams on the Lining Bind with a seam binding, or stitch flat in a French welt seam.
passages.plain: Follow these steps if the style of your garment needs a heavy, strong lining and boning. You can sew soft feather bone with a sewing machine. This makes a stronger seam than the fancy stitches used in the past. Always hold the bone slightly looser than the seam. To be more specific, stretch the seam onto the bone. This will make sure you have a nice and smooth waist line. To finish the seams on the lining, use a seam binding or stitch them flat in a French welt seam.

passages.old: Then after the seam has been sewed with the machine, trim off one side of it with the shears, and fold in the other edge of the seam, that is, the one not trimmed, over the one that has been trimmed, and baste down flat, completing the stitch with the machine. When fitting a lining or blouse, never cut out the arm hole or neck, more than that allowed by your pattern. Snip the cloth a bit when it feels tight, and later, before attaching the collar or sleeve, trim out what is necessary.
passages.plain: Sew the seam with your machine. Trim one side of the seam with your shears. Fold the other edge of the seam over the trimmed side. Baste it down flat. Finish the stitch with your machine. When you are fitting a lining or a blouse, do not cut the arm hole or the neck more than your pattern allows. Snip the cloth a little when it feels tight. Later, before you attach the collar or the sleeve, trim out what is necessary.

passages.old: Sewing a Shield Protector Into the Armseye Sew in four places; just through the binding, but with care, lest the rubber is punctured. This would permit moisture to penetrate through to the gown. Then sew the part that goes inside of the sleeve to the seam of the sleeve ; the outside to the under arm seam of the blouse, and, the other two ends also to the ^eam of the sleeve, just stitching through the binding and seam of the sleeve. Again a word of caution : Do not get the shield tighter 84 The Home Dressmakers' Guide than the sleeve seam, or you will find you have made the armhole both tight and uncomfortable.
passages.plain: Sew the shield protector into the armseye in four places. Sew through the binding. Be careful not to puncture the rubber. If you puncture the rubber, moisture will get into the gown. Sew the part that goes inside the sleeve to the sleeve seam. Sew the outside part to the under arm seam of the blouse. Sew the other two ends to the sleeve seam. Stitch only through the binding and the sleeve seam. Do not sew the shield tighter than the sleeve seam. If you do, the armhole will be tight and uncomfortable.

passages.old: Sewing the Seams and Attaching the Dress The side seams of the dress may now be sew^ed up and pressed. It may be necessary to clip the seams a few times at the waist line, allowing the seam to "Spring" and causing the dress to fit more perfectly at the waist line. The seams of the skirt may be stayed and finished like any separate skirt. The hem may be turned and the placket finished as explained in the chapter on making skirts. Baste the dress carefully onto the lining and baste the shoulder seam of the dress in with the shoulder seam of the lining, being careful to baste the shoulder seams as you had them after fitting the lining.
passages.plain: You can now sew and press the side seams of the dress. You might need to clip the seams a few times at the waist line. This lets the seam spring out so the dress fits the waist perfectly. You can stay and finish the skirt seams like you would for a separate skirt. You can turn the hem and finish the placket like the instructions in the chapter on making skirts. Carefully baste the dress onto the lining. Baste the shoulder seam of the dress to the shoulder seam of the lining. Make sure you baste the shoulder seams in the same positions they had after you fitted the lining.

passages.old: You will find that the dress, when it is finished, will be more satisfactory and wear better by being anchored to the lining at the shoulder seam and across the back of the neck. WTien the collar is attached to the dress the outside cloth and lining are sewed together. \^nien the dress is attached to the lining in this way the belt at the waist line of the lining will help to hold the garment in position. This will also make the dress very comfortable as it will fit beautifully and the well-fitted lining will hold it perfectly in place.
passages.plain: Your dress will look better and last longer if you anchor it to the lining at the shoulder seam and across the back of the neck. Sew the outside cloth and the lining together when you attach the collar to the dress. When you attach the dress to the lining this way, the belt at the waist line of the lining will help hold the garment in place. This will also make the dress very comfortable. It will fit beautifully because the well-fitted lining will hold it perfectly in place.

passages.old: VvTien the dress has been so far completed the side seams may be finished, after which the correct length at the bottom can be regulated. Putting the Sleeve Into the Armseye There are various ways to determine where the inside seam of the sleeve should be placed when putting the sleeve into the armseye. If the under arm seam of the garment comes as it should, in the center of the side of the body, then, 214 inches in front of the under arm seam will be the correct place for the inside seam of the sleeve.
passages.plain: The dress is mostly finished. You can now finish the side seams. After that, you can adjust the length at the bottom. There are different ways to decide where to put the inside seam of the sleeve into the armseye. If the under arm seam of the garment is in the center of the side of the body, you should place the inside seam of the sleeve 1/4 inch in front of the under arm seam.

passages.old: This is for an armseye of average size. If the armseye is very large it will be necessary to measure more than 214 inches in front of the under arm seam and if the armseye is very small measure less than 2% inches. A very simple and yet very satisfactory method for putting the sleeve in correctly is to find the natural shoulder seam or where the natural shoulder seam should come, and measure one inch back of this seam. Hold the armseye at this point and find the corresponding point at the bottom of the armseye.
passages.plain: This instruction is for an armseye of average size. If the armseye is very large, you must measure more than 2 1/4 inches in front of the underarm seam. If the armseye is very small, measure less than 2 1/2 inches. A simple and good way to put the sleeve in correctly is to find the natural shoulder seam or where it should be. Measure one inch back from this seam. Hold the armseye at this point. Then find the matching point at the bottom of the armseye.

passages.old: This point will be the correct position for the inside seam of the sleeve. The Home Dressmakers' Guide 85 The sleeve should always be from 2 to 21/^ inches larger than the armseye. This amount of "fullness" should be distributed, part at the back and part at the front of the top of the shoulder but never on the top of the shoulder. See A-B, Diagram 3, in the chapter on making a Tailored Coat. Sewing the Sleeves Into the Armseye If the sleeves are sewed into the lining the armseye of the outside dress may be finished with a bias facing.
passages.plain: This point is the correct spot for the inside seam of the sleeve. The sleeve must be 2 to 2.5 inches larger than the armseye. You should spread this extra space between the front and the back of the top of the shoulder. Do not put any of it on the very top of the shoulder. Look at A-B in Diagram 3 of the chapter on making a Tailored Coat. If you sew the sleeves into the lining, you can finish the armseye of the outside dress with a bias facing.

passages.old: The bias facing may be basted on and then stitched and turned so none of it shows. It may be turned leaving a little of it showing to form a piping. If a cord is used to finish the armseye of the dress it is first covered with the bias facing. The facing is then sewed on and turned allowing the covered cord to show, and is sewed on by hand through the cord at the edge of the armseye. This cord cannot be sewed on with the machine. The finishing of the armseye is a matter of choice and also depends on the prevailing style.
passages.plain: You can sew the bias facing on and then turn it so that none of it shows. You can also turn it so that a little bit shows to make a piping. If you use a cord to finish the armseye of the dress, you must cover the cord with the bias facing first. Then you sew the facing on and turn it. This lets the covered cord show. You must sew it by hand through the cord at the edge of the armseye. You cannot sew this cord with a machine. How you finish the armseye is your choice. It also depends on the current style.

passages.old: If the outside dress has a natural armseye and the sleeve is to be sewed into the dress it must be attached to both cloth and lining and the stitches taken through both. Building the Gown A gown not cut in one piece but has the waist and skirt attached, must be proceeded with a little differently than was the case with the dress hanging from the shoulders. A dress form will be of great assistance in building this gown. If one is not obtainable the one for whom the garment is being made must have the gown built upon her.
passages.plain: If the outside dress has a natural armseye and you want to sew the sleeve into the dress, you must attach it to both the cloth and the lining. You must sew through both layers. You must build the gown differently if the waist and skirt are attached instead of the dress hanging from the shoulders. A dress form will help you build this gown. If you cannot get a dress form, the person who will wear the garment must have the gown built on her.

passages.old: First measure the belting and make it the exact size of the waist measurement plus one inch. There must be onehalf of an inch at each end of the belting to turn over making it stronger for the hooks and eyes. Next find and mark the center back on the belting and also the two sides. These marks at the two sides are where the side seams of the garment should come on the belting. Proceed to fit the lining as you did for the one-piece dress. When the lining has been fitted and attached to the belting, the outside of the waist part of the dress is next draped and arranged over the lining.
passages.plain: First, measure the belting. Make it the exact size of the waist measurement plus one inch. You must leave one half of an inch at each end of the belting to turn over. This makes it stronger for the hooks and eyes. Next, find and mark the center back on the belting. Also mark the two sides. These marks at the two sides are where the side seams of the garment should meet the belting. Next, fit the lining just as you did for the one-piece dress. Once you have fitted and attached the lining to the belting, drape and arrange the outside of the waist part of the dress over the lining.

passages.old: Be sure the side seams of the waist are exactly in the center, not toward the front nor toward the back, but where the mark was 86 The Home Dressmakers' Guide made on the belting. Sew the shoulder seams of the dress in with the shoulder seams of the lining and when the collar is put on the dress is sewed to the lining at the back of the neck. Next pin the cloth carefully around the waist line, not stretching it too tight on the lining and baste the cloth and lining together at the armseye.
passages.plain: Make sure the side seams of the waist are exactly in the center. They should not be toward the front or the back. They must be where the mark was made on the belting. Sew the shoulder seams of the dress together with the shoulder seams of the lining. When you put on the collar, the dress is sewn to the lining at the back of the neck. Next, pin the cloth carefully around the waist line. Do not stretch the cloth too tight on the lining. Baste the cloth and the lining together at the armseye.

passages.old: The skirt is put on next and if there are side seams in the skirt, they must meet the side seams of the waist. Pin the skirt so these seams correspond. Pin the center back of the skirt to meet the center back of the waist. If there are gathers in the skirt arrange them and pin them carefully. Two draw threads, half of an inch apart will help hold the gathers in place while the skirt is being sewed onto the waist. Be sure the line for center front is exactly where it should be and pin the skirt securely onto the waist.
passages.plain: Put on the skirt next. If the skirt has side seams, they must line up with the side seams of the waist. Pin the skirt so these seams match. Pin the center back of the skirt to the center back of the waist. If the skirt has gathers, arrange them and pin them carefully. Use two draw threads half of an inch apart to hold the gathers in place while you sew the skirt onto the waist. Make sure the line for the center front is in the exact right spot. Pin the skirt securely onto the waist.

passages.old: The gown is then taken off and the skirt and waist is sewed to the belting, sewing through the four thicknesses, the skirt, the waist, the lining and the belting. The raw edge of the skirt above the waist line may be turned under before the skirt is sewed to the waist, or it may be finished with a piece of seam binding. Lay the binding on flat and sew it on by hand. This will make a neat finish. An outside belt or crushed girdle will complete this gown.
passages.plain: Take off the gown. Sew the skirt and the waist to the belting. You must sew through four layers. These layers are the skirt, the waist, the lining, and the belting. You can turn under the raw edge of the skirt above the waist line before you sew the skirt to the waist. Alternatively, you can finish that edge with a piece of seam binding. Lay the binding flat. Sew it on by hand. This will make a neat finish. An outside belt or a crushed girdle will complete this gown.

passages.old: Whether a belt or a girdle is used will depend on the style of the garment. The placket in the skirt will be finished like the placket in any separate skirt. (See Chapter on Making Skirts.) The lining opens down the center front. If the placket closing comes to the left it will be necessary to have the skirt, from the center front to the closing, separate from the belting. Finish this part of the skirt with a binding and attach it to the belting with snap fasteners or hooks and eyes.
passages.plain: You will choose to use a belt or a girdle based on the style of the garment. Finish the placket in the skirt like you would for a separate skirt. Look at the chapter on Making Skirts for instructions. The lining opens down the center front. If the placket closes to the left, you must separate the skirt from the center front to the closing from the belting. Finish this part of the skirt with a binding. Attach it to the belting using snap fasteners or hooks and eyes.

passages.old: Where the outside part of the bodice will open depends on the style of the garment. After the skirt is attached to the waist the hem at the bottom may be regulated. The sleeves are put in like the sleeves in any dress. (For in-- structions in designing and putting on collars see the Chapter on Blouses). The Home Dressmakers' Guide 87 A Crushed Girdle A crushed girdle is always made from a bias piece of material and may be cut six inches wide, or more, according to the size and shape of the individual.
passages.plain: The opening of the outside part of the bodice depends on the style of the garment. You can adjust the hem at the bottom after you attach the skirt to the waist. You put in the sleeves like you do for any dress. See the chapter on blouses for instructions on designing and putting on collars. A crushed girdle is always made from a piece of material cut on the bias. You may cut it six inches wide or wider depending on the size and shape of the person.

passages.old: A large shortwaisted figure must have a narrow crushed girdle while a tall slender person can wear a wider one. One should be sure the girdle chosen is a becoming one as the girdle can spoil the whole effect of the gown. A girdle can be crushed or draped becomingly to most figures. Finish the closing at the side with sash ends or tabs. This will help to relieve the stiff look that so often spoils the artistic effect. When the girdle is finished it is tacked on to the gown.
passages.plain: A person with a large, short waist should wear a narrow crushed girdle. A tall and slender person can wear a wider girdle. You must make sure the girdle you choose looks good because it can ruin the look of the whole dress. You can crush or drape a girdle to fit most body types. Finish the side closure with sash ends or tabs. This helps remove the stiff look that often ruins the artistic effect. When you finish the girdle, tack it onto the gown.

passages.old: Marking the Finished Length The finished length cannot be regulated until the skirt is attached securely and permanently to the waist part of the gown or to the belting if a separate skirt. When the skirt is finally attached the length at the bottom may be When Bishop sleeves are made out of sheer material such as crepes, voiles, etc., it is necessary to French seam the length seams. (For French seams see Chapter on Stitches) . Preparing the Sleeve for the Cuff When the cuff is to be hemstitched gather the sleeve in the usual way and put in the gathering thread by using a small running stitch.
passages.plain: You cannot set the final length of the skirt until you attach it firmly to the waist part of the dress or to the belt. If the skirt is separate, you attach it to the belt. When the skirt is finished, you can measure the bottom length. When you make Bishop sleeves from sheer fabric like crepe or voile, you must use a French seam on the length seams. You can find instructions for French seams in the chapter on stitches. To prepare the sleeve for the cuff, gather the sleeve in the normal way. Use a small running stitch to put in the gathering thread if the cuff will be hemstitched.

passages.old: Draw the fullness of the sleeve into the size of the cuff. Have more fullness on the top of the arm than on the under part. Sew the cuff on using a small running stitch and the hemstitching will do the rest. When a Cuff Should be Sewed on by Hand If the blouse is made out of a good quality of material and is to be washed, I would advise sewing the cuff on by hand and binding the seam on the wrong side. Sewing the Cuff on a Garment of Wool or Silk The cuff may be made to fit over the hand or if a closer fitting cuff is desired snap fasteners or hooks and eyes may be used.
passages.plain: Draw the extra fabric of the sleeve into the size of the cuff. You should have more fullness at the top of the arm than at the bottom part. Sew the cuff on with a small running stitch. The hemstitching will finish the rest. You should sew the cuff on by hand if the blouse is made of high quality material and will be washed. You should also bind the seam on the wrong side. You can make the cuff to fit over the hand. If you want a closer fitting cuff, you can use snap fasteners or hooks and eyes on a garment made of wool or silk.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide First, prepare the cuff by making it double, facing it or hemming all edges. If buttons are to be used for trimming and the cuff is narrow, buttons may be used in place of snap fasteners or hooks and eyes. Gather the sleeve to fit the cuff and sew a binding on the edge of the gathered sleeve. Use a piece of the cloth, about 11/2 inches wide for the binding. When the gathers are* arranged and before the binding is put on, be sure most of the fullness is on the upper part of the sleeve and not on the under.
passages.plain: First, prepare the cuff. You can make it double, face it, or hem all the edges. If you want to use buttons for decoration and the cuff is narrow, you can use buttons instead of snap fasteners or hooks and eyes. Gather the sleeve to fit the cuff. Sew a binding on the edge of the gathered sleeve. Use a piece of cloth about 1.5 inches wide for the binding. Arrange the gathers before you put on the binding. Make sure most of the extra fabric is on the top part of the sleeve and not on the bottom part.

passages.old: When attaching the cuff find the center and pin the center of the cuff to the binding at the inside seam of the sleeve. Sew the cuff to the binding by using a slip stitch. Follow these instructions when attaching the cuff to the sleeve and you will find it an easy way and when the garment is finished the cuff will look well put on. // you were going to cut the cuff to actual measurement it will be necessary to measure the arm. Measure first where the cuff is going on the arm.
passages.plain: Find the center of the cuff. Pin the center of the cuff to the binding at the inside seam of the sleeve. Sew the cuff to the binding using a slip stitch. Follow these instructions to attach the cuff to the sleeve. This is an easy way to do it. The cuff will look well put on when the garment is finished. If you were going to cut the cuff to the actual measurement, you must measure the arm. Measure the arm first at the spot where the cuff goes on.

passages.old: It may be just below the elbow or it may be half way between the elbow and the waist. Next measure the size of the wrist and also the length of the cuff. Cut the cuff out of paper first, allowing for seams, and try it on the arm. The cuff must have room enough to slip easily up and down on the arm when one is reachirig. Just a suggestion is given in Diagram 1. The dotted line marked "B" shows the under part of the cuff to be narrower than the upper, bringing the seam in the right place on the arm.
passages.plain: The sleeve may end just below the elbow or halfway between the elbow and the waist. Next, measure the size of the wrist and the length of the cuff. Cut the cuff out of paper first. Make sure to include extra space for the seams. Try the paper cuff on your arm. The cuff must be loose enough to slide easily up and down your arm when you reach. Diagram 1 gives a suggestion. The dotted line marked B shows that the bottom part of the cuff should be narrower than the top part. This puts the seam in the correct place on your arm.

passages.old: DIAGRAM 1 The Home Dressmakers' Guide 89 Finishing a Close Fitting Dress Sleeve This sleeve may have a dart to the- elbow or it may be a two-piece sleeve. If it is made of sheer material the seams will have to be French seamed. Baste up the inside seam first, starting at the top and basting to the wrist. Then baste the elbow seams from the bottom up. In the instructions on altering the pattern for a sleeve with a dart to the elbow, the necessity of having the upper sleeve one-half inch longer at the wrist than the under part of the sleeve was explained. (See Diagram 7 in the Chapter on ''Altering a Sleeve Pattern").
passages.plain: This is Diagram 1 from The Home Dressmakers' Guide. You are finishing a close fitting dress sleeve. This sleeve might have a dart at the elbow or it might be a two piece sleeve. You must use French seams if the material is sheer. First, baste the inside seam. Start at the top and baste down to the wrist. Next, baste the elbow seams from the bottom up. The instructions for changing a pattern for a sleeve with an elbow dart explained a rule. The upper half of the sleeve must be one half inch longer at the wrist than the lower part of the sleeve. You can see this in Diagram 7 in the chapter called Altering a Sleeve Pattern.

passages.old: This half of an inch is for "fullness" at the elbow, half When basting the elbow seam it is necessary to begin at the bottom and distribute this fullness at the elbow. This one-half inch of cloth must not be allowed to pucker or form gathers at the elbow, but is held full onto the under part of the sleeve giving room for the elbow and making a comfortable sleeve. Try the sleeve on after it is basted. Sew the inside seam on the machine. It is often necessary to clip the inside seam to cause it to fit well and give an easy graceful look to the sleeve from the right' side.
passages.plain: Use this half inch of fabric to create fullness at the elbow. When you baste the elbow seam, start at the bottom. Spread this fullness out at the elbow. Do not let this half inch of cloth pucker or form gathers. Instead, hold it full against the under part of the sleeve. This gives room for the elbow and makes the sleeve comfortable. Try on the sleeve after you baste it. Sew the inside seam using a sewing machine. You may need to clip the inside seam so it fits well. This makes the sleeve look easy and graceful from the right side.

passages.old: The seam is not clipped straight but the slash is made bias and is clipped from the edge to near the stitching. Be careful not to clip the stitching. Overcast or bind this seam. Sew and overcast or bind the elbow seam. A piece of bias binding at the wrist will prepare the sleeve for the cuff. This style of sleeve may be finished with a small turned back cuff or it may have a flared cuff projecting over the hand. A cuff that tapers over the hand, having long points at the back will look especially well on the short thick arm. The Home Dressmakers' Guide
passages.plain: Do not cut the seam in a straight line. Make a slash on the bias. Clip from the edge toward the stitching. Be careful not to cut the stitching. Overcast or bind this seam. Sew the elbow seam and then overcast or bind it. Put a piece of bias binding at the wrist. This prepares the sleeve for the cuff. You can finish this sleeve style with a small turned back cuff. You can also use a flared cuff that sticks out over the hand. A cuff that narrows over the hand with long points at the back looks very good on a short thick arm.

chapters.why: The principles of choosing garment silhouettes to flatter different body types remain relevant in modern fashion design.

chapters.title: Cutting and making the tailored suit

passages.old: We are to consider first the regulation tailored suit coat and the instructions given will apply to the coat illustrated in Diagram 1. First, the measurements of the one for whom the suit is being made should be taken carefully. (See Chapter on Measurements.) The measurements should then be applied to the pattern and the pattern altered to fit the individual. All measurements are applied to the pattern as for any garment except the bust and waist measurements. Measure and alter the pattern to your own length , measurements; length under the arm; length of back; length of front; length of shoulder and around the armseye.
passages.plain: You will first look at the regular tailored suit coat. The instructions apply to the coat in Diagram 1. First, you must take the measurements of the person who will wear the suit carefully. You can find these instructions in the chapter on Measurements. Next, you will put these measurements onto the pattern. You must change the pattern to fit that person. You apply all measurements to the pattern like you do for any other garment. However, you must treat the bust and waist measurements differently. You must measure and change the pattern to fit your own length. You must also include the length under the arm. You must include the length of the back. You must include the length of the front. You must include the length of the shoulder. You must also include the measurement around the armseye.

passages.old: The armseye of a coat must be at least one inch larger than the measurement taken as the armseye for a suit coat must be larger than the armseye of a dress. When the alterations have been made pin the pattern together with all seams on the outside and the seams pinned to allow all the seam allowance given on the pattern and shown by the perforated lines. Try the pattern on. It is hardly possible to alter a suit coat pattern to fit perfectly without making alterations after the pattern has been tried on.
passages.plain: The armseye of a coat must be at least one inch larger than the measurement for a suit coat. A suit coat armseye must also be larger than a dress armseye. Pin the pattern together after you make the changes. Pin all seams on the outside. Pin the seams to allow for all the seam allowance shown by the perforated lines. Try the pattern on. It is very hard to make a suit coat pattern fit perfectly without making changes after you try it on.

passages.old: The coat must be balanced perfectly. It is also very necessary that the pattern fits without a bulge over the DIAGRAM 1 The Home Dressmakers' Guide 91 shoulder blades at the armseye. See that it fits smoothly and perfectly across the chest at the armseye. It may be necessary to fold plaits in the pattern at either the back or the front, or both, between the shoulder and the bust line. Make any necessary alterations in the pattern while it is on the individual and be sure it is plainly marked before unpinning it.
passages.plain: The coat must be perfectly balanced. The pattern must fit without a bulge over the shoulder blades at the armseye. Make sure it fits smoothly and perfectly across the chest at the armseye. You may need to fold pleats in the pattern at the back, the front, or both. These pleats go between the shoulder and the bust line. Make any necessary changes to the pattern while it is on the person. Mark these changes clearly before you take the pattern off.

passages.old: Mark all seams and alterations with pencil. Do not be afraid to pencil mark the pattern and let me assure you that it is better to spoil several patterns than to spoil the cloth. It is not difficult to make a beautiful tailored suit provided you cut it right and this can only be accomplished by working with the pattern. Decide on the length you want the coat and also make the pattern confirm to the desired width at the bottom. Before the coat is cut from the cloth be sure the material is sponged and shrunk.
passages.plain: Mark all seams and changes with a pencil. Do not worry about marking the pattern with a pencil. It is better to ruin several patterns than to ruin the cloth. You can make a beautiful tailored suit if you cut it correctly. You can only do this by using the pattern. Decide on the length you want for the coat. Make the pattern match the width you want at the bottom. Before you cut the coat from the cloth, make sure you have sponged and shrunk the material.

passages.old: Special attention must also be given to the wrong side and the right side of the cloth ; be sure which is which. The inside of the folded cloth as it comes from the store is usually the right side. Also be certain of the up and down or the grain of the cloth. I have known experienced home dressmakers to make a mistake and cut the garment with part having the nap running up and part with the nap running down. This, of course, was with cloth that was hard to distinguish.
passages.plain: You must pay special attention to the right side and the wrong side of the cloth. Make sure you know which side is which. The inside of the cloth as you buy it from the store is usually the right side. You must also be sure of the up and down direction of the grain. I have known experienced home dressmakers make a mistake. They cut a garment with some parts having the nap running up and other parts with the nap running down. This happened with cloth that was hard to tell apart.

passages.old: Smooth the hand over the right side of the material. The nap running up will feel rough while the smooth feeling will show the nap running down as it should. Placing the Pattern on the Cloth The front section of the pattern is placed on the straight edge of the cloth and pinned carefully. The back section of the pattern is also placed on the straight line of the material. If there is a panel back the center back of the pattern is placed on a fold of the cloth.
passages.plain: Run your hand over the right side of the fabric. The nap running up will feel rough. The smooth feeling shows the nap running down correctly. Place the front part of the pattern on the straight edge of the cloth and pin it carefully. Place the back part of the pattern on the straight line of the fabric. If there is a back panel, place the center back of the pattern on a fold of the cloth.

passages.old: The side front section of the pattern and the side back section of the pattern must be placed on the cloth carefully as the grain of the cloth must run on a perfect line. (See 92 The Home Dressmakers' Guide Diagram 4, and notice the line marked "Straight Line" on the side front and side back sections.) Also place the waist line of the pattern on the "across grain" of the cloth. By "across grain" we mean the woof. The lengthwise threads of the cloth are the warp and the threads crossing the warp are the woof.
passages.plain: Place the side front and side back sections of the pattern on the cloth carefully. The grain of the cloth must run in a perfect line. Look at Diagram 4 on page 92 of The Home Dressmakers' Guide. Notice the line marked Straight Line on the side front and side back sections. Also place the waist line of the pattern on the across grain of the cloth. Across grain means the woof. The lengthwise threads of the cloth are the warp. The threads crossing the warp are the woof.

passages.old: The waist line is therefore placed on the threads called the woof. Pin all of the pattern on the cloth before cutting any part of the garment. The under collar is placed on a true bias while the upper collar is placed on the across grain of the goods. The sleeves are placed so the center back of the sleeve, from the shoulder to the elbow, comes on the lengthwise grain of the cloth. When cutting out the garment it is best to cut the skirt first as the sections of the skirt are the largest and often, where there is no "up or down" to the cloth, the coat sections can be fitted in, making the cutting more economical.
passages.plain: Place the waist line on the threads called the woof. Pin all of the pattern onto the cloth before you cut any part of the garment. Place the under collar on a true bias. Place the upper collar on the across grain of the fabric. Place the sleeves so the center back of the sleeve from the shoulder to the elbow sits on the lengthwise grain of the cloth. It is best to cut the skirt first because the skirt sections are the largest. If there is no up or down to the cloth, you can fit the coat sections in later. This makes the cutting more economical.

passages.old: Cutting the Cloth Having pinned all the sections of the pattern onto the cloth, proceed to cut the garment out carefully leaving all the pattern pinned to the cloth until all seams, waist line, bust line, hem, yokes, pockets, etc., are all marked with tailor tacks, (for tailor tacks see Chapter on Stitches). Marking With Tailor Tacks The tailor tacks are put in through the paper pattern and the two thicknesses of cloth. Take the stitches following the outline marked on the pattern and when the threads are clipped the pattern can be removed and both sides of the cloth will have been marked alike and are ready for basting.
passages.plain: Pin all parts of the pattern onto the cloth. Cut out the garment carefully. Keep all the patterns pinned to the cloth. You must do this until you mark every seam, waist line, bust line, hem, yoke, and pocket with tailor tacks. You can find instructions for tailor tacks in the chapter on stitches. Put the tailor tacks through the paper pattern and the two layers of cloth. Sew the stitches along the outline on the pattern. Clip the threads when you are finished. You can then remove the pattern. Both sides of the cloth will have the same marks. The cloth is now ready for basting.

passages.old: There is no other way to get the garment perfectly together. Putting in Canvas When the cloth for the coat has been carefully cut as outlined, proceed to cut the canvas. It is always best to select a good quality of tailors linen canvas. Whether the coat will hold its shape or not depends on the quality of canvas. This canvas is to support the neck, shape the lapel, hold the front of the coat in shape and strengthen the armseye. The Home Dressmakers' Guide The canvas must be shrunken before it is cut.
passages.plain: There is no other way to make the garment fit together perfectly. After you cut the coat cloth as described, you must cut the canvas. You should always choose a high quality tailors linen canvas. The quality of the canvas determines if the coat will hold its shape. This canvas supports the neck. It shapes the lapel. It holds the front of the coat in shape. It also strengthens the armseye. You must shrink the canvas before you cut it.

passages.old: Lay it, folded just at it comes from the store, in a pan of cold water and leave it for two hours. Take it out and lay it over the clothes line until nearly dry. It can then be pressed with a warm iron. The canvas is always cut on the same grain as the cloth which is lengthwise. The Front Section Cut the canvas the full size of the front section. See Diagram 2, showing the canvas covering the front section. Side Front Section The canvas for the side front section is cut as shown by Diagram 2.
passages.plain: Lay the fabric in a pan of cold water. Keep it folded the way it came from the store. Leave it in the water for two hours. Take it out and put it on the clothes line. Let it dry until it is almost dry. You can then press it with a warm iron. Always cut the canvas on the same grain as the cloth. The grain runs lengthwise. For the front section, cut the canvas to the full size of the front section. Look at Diagram 2 to see the canvas covering the front section. For the side front section, cut the canvas as shown in Diagram 2.

passages.old: The canvas should be 21/2 inches deep under the armseye, and be 2 inches wide at the bottom. Back Sections The canvas is cut for the back of the coat as shown by Diagram 3. When the back of the coat is in two sections the seam is basted temporarily and the canvas is put in for The Home Dressmakers' Guide a try on. Afterward the seam may be sewed and pressed open and the canvas put in finally in the same way. The canvas across the back is three inches in depth at the center The canvas around the armseye is 21/^ inches deep under the arm to meet the canvas on the side front. (See A, Dia- The canvas around the armseye is not attached to the canvas at the back of the neck.
passages.plain: The canvas should be 2.5 inches deep under the armseye. It should be 2 inches wide at the bottom. Cut the canvas for the back of the coat as shown in Diagram 3. If the back of the coat has two sections, sew the seam with basting stitches first. Put the canvas in for a try on. After that, you can sew the seam and press it open. Put the canvas in finally in the same way. The canvas across the back is 3 inches deep at the center. The canvas around the armseye is 2.25 inches deep under the arm. It meets the canvas on the side front. The canvas around the armseye is not attached to the canvas at the back of the neck.

passages.old: They are both separate, the canvas around the armseye lapping the canvas of the back The canvas is sewed in with the shoulder seams. (See also Diagram Uy showing the canvas by dotted lines on all four sections). DIAGRAM 4 The Home Dressmakers' Guide Qf/A CLOTH DIAGRAM 5 When the Front is in One Piece The canvas for a coat that is not a regulation coat, but having the front in one piece, is cut as shown by Diagram 5. The canvas for the back of any coat it cut as shown by Dia- When the garment is a full length coat, the canvas extends to the bottom and is also four inches wide.
passages.plain: The canvas pieces are separate. The canvas around the armseye overlaps the canvas of the back. You sew the canvas in with the shoulder seams. Look at Diagram Uy to see the canvas shown by dotted lines on all four sections. Look at Diagram 4 in The Home Dressmakers' Guide. Look at Diagram 5. If you are making a coat that is not a regulation coat but has the front in one piece, cut the canvas as shown in Diagram 5. You cut the canvas for the back of any coat as shown in Diagram 4. If the garment is a full length coat, the canvas goes to the bottom. It is also four inches wide.

passages.old: When a coat has a peplum, the canvas does not extend below the waist line. Basting the Cloth onto the Canvas When the canvas has been prepared and cut as described in the foregoing instruction, the next thing is to baste the cloth onto it. Do not make the mistake of basting the canvas onto the cloth. If you do, the cloth will be puckered and full in places and stretched in others. Lay the canvas on the table with the cloth on top, and beginning at the top, baste down, smoothing the cloth with the left hand, and using the diagonal basting stitch.
passages.plain: If a coat has a peplum, the canvas does not go below the waist line. After you prepare and cut the canvas as described in the previous instructions, you must baste the cloth onto the canvas. Do not baste the canvas onto the cloth. If you do this, the cloth will look wrinkled and full in some spots and stretched in others. Place the canvas on the table with the cloth on top. Start at the top and baste the pieces together. Use your left hand to smooth the cloth as you work. Use a diagonal basting stitch.

passages.old: The cloth must be basted to the canvas securely, especially across the back and around the armseye. The First Try-on It is advisable to try the coat on now, before the seams are sewed with the sewing machine, and after the canvas is in. Even though the paper pattern fitted perfectly the cloth will often take a different position on the body because the cloth will stretch and the paper pattern will not. Therefore, it should be tried on in the baste and with the canvas in. If alterations are necessary they must be made at this time. iH) The Home Dressmakers' Guide Be sure the coat balances perfectly.
passages.plain: You must sew the cloth to the canvas securely. Pay extra attention to the back and the area around the armseye. You should try on the coat now. Do this before you sew the seams with a sewing machine. You should do it after the canvas is inside. The paper pattern might have fit perfectly. However, the cloth will often sit differently on your body. This happens because the cloth stretches but the paper pattern does not. You must try it on while it is basted and with the canvas inside. You must make any necessary changes at this time. Make sure the coat balances perfectly.

passages.old: It may be necessary to drop the front of the coat or lift the back. This was done in the pattern but sometimes the coat will need to be balanced as well. Open the shoulder seams and cause the garment to hang properly. It is always best to have a good shoulder seam. If the coat has been lifted it may be necessary to trim out the armseye. The coat may be made more from fitting or it may be attached permanently. There are two ways of putting the canvas in the front of a lady's coat.
passages.plain: You may need to lower the front of the coat or raise the back. The pattern included this, but you might still need to balance the coat. Open the shoulder seams so the garment hangs correctly. You should always have a good shoulder seam. If you lifted the coat, you might need to trim the armseye. You can make the coat removable or you can attach it permanently. There are two ways to put the canvas in the front of a lady's coat.

passages.old: The easiest way for the home dressmaker is to first baste the cloth onto the canvas and when sewing the seams, sew the canvas in with the seam ; that is, sew the four thicknesses, the two of canvas and the two of cloth in the one seam. Remember, this is just for the front of the coat; the back is operated differently. Another way used by many tailors, is to sew the seams in the cloth, for the front of the coat, and press them open or baste them down flat and stitch a welt seam, stitching on the right side.
passages.plain: The easiest way for you to do this is to first baste the cloth onto the canvas. When you sew the seams, sew the canvas in with the seam. This means you sew four layers at once. These layers are two of canvas and two of cloth. Remember that this is only for the front of the coat. The back of the coat is made differently. Many tailors use another way. They sew the seams in the cloth for the front of the coat. Then they press the seams open or baste them down flat. Finally, they stitch a welt seam on the right side.

passages.old: Sew the seams in the canvas and press them open and attach the seam of the canvas to the seam of the cloth, using a tacking stitch. Hair Cloth If hair cloth is used in the front of the coat, it must be cut as outlined in Diagram 4. See the dotted lines marked *'hair cloth" in Diagram 4. The hair cloth must be cut crosswise to get the benefit of the stiff hair in the weave. For a large full bust it will be necessary to cut a dart in the hair cloth at the seam of the canvas to make it fit smoothly on the canvas.
passages.plain: Sew the seams in the canvas. Press the seams open. Attach the canvas seam to the cloth seam using a tacking stitch. If you use hair cloth for the front of the coat, you must cut it like Diagram 4 shows. Look at the dotted lines labeled hair cloth in Diagram 4. You must cut the hair cloth crosswise. This lets you use the stiff hair in the weave. If you have a large full bust, you must cut a dart in the hair cloth at the canvas seam. This helps it fit smoothly on the canvas.

passages.old: Cut the dart and just lap the edges of the hair cloth. The hair cloth is sewed onto the canvas, sometimes with the sewing machine, but more often by hand, using the diagonal basting stitch. The hair cloth is padded to the canvas before the canvas is attached finally to the coat. If the hair cloth is put on with the sewing machine it is stitched around and around, beginning at the center and stitching in circles to the outer edge. Binding the Hair Cloth All the edges of the hair cloth must be covered with a strip of lining cut one inch wide.
passages.plain: Cut the dart. Fold the edges of the hair cloth. You sew the hair cloth onto the canvas. You can use a sewing machine, but you usually sew it by hand. Use a diagonal basting stitch for this step. You pad the hair cloth to the canvas before you attach the canvas to the coat. If you use a sewing machine, you stitch in circles. Start at the center and stitch toward the outer edge. You must cover all edges of the hair cloth. Use a strip of lining that is one inch wide.

passages.old: This is to keep the hair The Home Dressmakers' Guide from working through the lining. Binding the edges of the hair cloth will serve the same purpose. The Back of the Coat The canvas for the back of the coat is not sewed in with the length seams. Sew the two back sections together and press the seam open. It may be necessary to clip the seam at the waist line if the garment is form fitting. Clip the seam here and there making the slash bias. If the garment is finished with welt seams, these seams will then be finished in the same way.
passages.plain: Do this to keep the hair from moving through the lining. You can also bind the edges of the hair cloth to do the same thing. For the back of the coat, do not sew the canvas in with the length seams. Sew the two back sections together. Press the seam open. You might need to clip the seam at the waist line if the coat fits closely to the body. Clip the seam in different places along the bias. If the garment has welt seams, finish those seams in the same way.

passages.old: The canvas across the back of the neck is sewed in with the shoulder seam only and is not attached to the length seam. The canvas around the armseye laps the canvas for the back of the neck at the shoulder and is also sewed in with the shoulder seam, and with the under arm seam. The Roll of the Lapel After the canvas is in, try the coat on to determine where the lapel should roll on the neck. Always be very careful where you turn the roll of the lapel.
passages.plain: Sew the canvas across the back of the neck using only the shoulder seam. Do not attach it to the length seam. The canvas around the armseye overlaps the back neck canvas at the shoulder. Sew this piece in with the shoulder seam and the underarm seam. Put on the coat after the canvas is in. Check where the lapel should roll on the neck. Be very careful when you turn the roll of the lapel.

passages.old: If it is turned on a gram 6, there will be no room for the stand of the collar and the coat will continually pull away from the neck. The line upon which the lapel must roll one inch in front of the neck line. This is very necessary if there is to be a good-looking line on the collar and lapel. After the line for the lapel is found, and both lapels turned exactly the same, dampen and press the lapels in place with a hot iron. Press hard and the lapels will always stay in place.
passages.plain: Do not turn the fabric on a gram 6. If you do, there will be no room for the collar stand. The coat will constantly pull away from the neck. You must find the line where the lapel rolls one inch in front of the neck line. This step is necessary to make the collar and lapel look good. After you find the line for the lapel, turn both lapels exactly the same. Dampen the lapels and press them into place with a hot iron. Press hard so the lapels will always stay in place.

passages.old: Padding the Lapel This padding is performed with a succession of small stitches, through both canvas and cloth, to hold them together and keep the lapel in shape, as well as to prevent the canvas from slipping. For this purpose we use the small slanting stitch, similar to the diagonal basting stitch. DIAGRAM « The Home Dressmakers* Guide The large stitch is on the canvas, while the small one is put through just far enough to catch the cloth and hold the two together, as already stated. This is done from the canvas side. stitches are put in rows about a quarter of an inch apart.
passages.plain: You will pad the lapel by using a series of small stitches. These stitches go through both the canvas and the cloth. They hold the pieces together and keep the lapel in shape. They also stop the canvas from slipping. You will use a small slanting stitch. This stitch is like a diagonal basting stitch. The large stitch goes on the canvas. The small stitch goes through just far enough to catch the cloth and hold the two pieces together. You do this from the canvas side. You put the stitches in rows about a quarter of an inch apart.

passages.old: After first outlining the desired size and shape of the lapel with a lead pencil, and before padding, cut aw^ay the canvas, leaving the cloth to extend for a seam upon which to sew the facing. (See lapel, Dia- Then take a flat linen baste it upon the edge of the canvas, and on the under side of the times it is necessary to hold the lapel full and the tape taut. This will be necessary sometimes to shape the front of the coat over the bust. First baste the tape on and This diagram shows the inside of the coat with the tape cross-stitched on the under side of the lapel and on the edge where the lapel is turned.
passages.plain: First, use a lead pencil to outline the size and shape you want for the lapel. Before you add padding, cut away the canvas. Leave enough cloth to make a seam for sewing the facing. Look at the lapel diagram. Next, take a flat linen tape. Baste it onto the edge of the canvas. On the underside of the tape, you must hold the lapel full and keep the tape tight. You will need to do this sometimes to shape the front of the coat over the chest. First, baste the tape on. The diagram shows the inside of the coat. It shows the tape cross-stitched on the underside of the lapel and on the edge where the lapel is turned.

passages.old: The tape, as shown by Diagram 8, extends part way on the neck. This holds the bias at that place. Notice how the tape is turned at the top of the lapel and made to fit around the neck. The tape also is shown extending to the bottom of the coat. DIAGRAM The Home Dressmakers* Guide 99 This holds the coat in place, prevents the cloth from stretching and causes the coat to hang perfectly in front. "A" shows the tape cross-stitched at the edge of the canvas and "B" shows the seam of the cloth, from which the canvas has been trimmed away.
passages.plain: The tape goes part way on the neck as shown in Diagram 8. This holds the bias in that spot. Look at how the tape turns at the top of the lapel and fits around the neck. The tape also goes to the bottom of the coat. This holds the coat in place. It stops the cloth from stretching. It makes the coat hang perfectly in the front. A shows the tape cross-stitched at the edge of the canvas. B shows the seam of the cloth where the canvas was trimmed away.

passages.old: It is to this seam of cloth that the facing is sewed. The tape will hold the front of the coat firm and keep it from sagging. Before putting on the facing, however, press carefully. Place the right side of the facing upon the right side of the coat, and baste it on carefully. Then sew with the machine, after which you will turn and baste on the edge of the facing ; the same on the back edge. Sew to the canvas with a large hemming stitch, and complete by sewing all the other seams in the coat, after which press the garment carefully.
passages.plain: Sew the facing to this seam of cloth. The tape will hold the front of the coat firm and stop it from sagging. Press the fabric carefully before you put on the facing. Place the right side of the facing on the right side of the coat. Baste it on carefully. Sew it with the machine. Turn the facing and baste on the edge. Do the same on the back edge. Sew to the canvas with a large hemming stitch. Sew all the other seams in the coat. Press the garment carefully.

passages.old: After the lapel is padded and the tape cross-stitched, you are ready for the under collar. How to Cut an Under-Collar Lay a piece of tissue paper over the neck of the coat the size of the collar, and commence by marking front **A'' lapel ; this amount is allowed for the step and can be more or less, according to the prevailing style. Next place a mark at the junction of the neck line and the straight line marked for the lapel ; this is shown by ''E" gram.
passages.plain: You are ready for the under collar once you have padded the lapel and cross-stitched the tape. To cut an under collar, place a piece of tissue paper over the neck of the coat. The paper should be the size of the collar. Start by marking the front A lapel. This amount is for the step. You can make it more or less depending on the style. Next, place a mark at the junction of the neck line and the straight line marked for the lapel. This is shown in diagram E.

passages.old: Now draw the neck line from ''A," following the tance from "A" to **B," is determined by measuring the neck of the coat from the step "A'* to the center back of the neck. *'B" is readily seen to be the center back of the collar. less or more, and is governed by the desired stand of the collar. From the stand line measure out 2 inches to *'X." This is for the depth of the roll at the center back. slight curve (See Diagram U-) This will give you a collar that will fit the neck of the coat for which it is cut, perfectly. 100 The Home Dressmakers* Guide A little practice will make this very easy.
passages.plain: Draw the neck line from point A. You find the distance from A to B by measuring the coat neck from point A to the center back of the neck. Point B is the center back of the collar. You can make this distance longer or shorter depending on how high you want the collar to stand. From the stand line, measure out 2 inches to point X. This is for the depth of the roll at the center back. Make a slight curve. This will give you a collar that fits the neck of the coat perfectly. A little practice will make this very easy.

passages.old: Allow for seams when cutting. Any shaped lapel or collar may be substituted for this one. Both canvas and cloth are cut decidedly bias. This, obviously, is to allow the stretching at the edges to shape to the neck of the coat. The stand at the back is stitched with the sewing machine, whereas the remainder is padded similar to the lapel ; stitched in rows one-fourth of an inch apart, beginning at the machine stitching and going out to the edge of the canvas. This canvas is to be cut off to the depth of the seam, upon which is sewed the upper cloth of the collar.
passages.plain: Include extra fabric for the seams when you cut the pieces. You can use any shaped lapel or collar instead of this one. Cut both the canvas and the cloth on a clear bias. This allows the edges to stretch and shape to the coat neck. Sew the back stand with a sewing machine. Pad the rest of the piece like you did the lapel. Sew the padding in rows that are one-fourth of an inch apart. Start at the machine stitching and work out to the edge of the canvas. Cut this canvas to the depth of the seam. Sew the upper cloth of the collar onto this seam.

passages.old: The under collar is fastened to the body of the coat with a small cross-stitch. If the cloth is firm and does not ravel, the collar may be sewed on raw edged, which will result in a smooth, flat finish. It is necessary that the back of the under collar have a slight curve, therefore cut the collar having a seam in the center of the back and cut it, not straight, but slightly curving in. The canvas for the under collar is cut on the same grain as the goods, bias, and must be cut the same size and shape, also having a seam at the back.
passages.plain: You fasten the under collar to the body of the coat with a small cross-stitch. If the cloth is firm and does not unravel, you can sew the collar on with raw edges. This will make a smooth and flat finish. The back of the under collar must have a slight curve. You should cut the collar with a seam in the center of the back. Do not cut it straight. Instead, cut it curving slightly inward. You must cut the canvas for the under collar on the bias. It must be the same size and shape as the collar. It must also have a seam at the back.

passages.old: Sew the seam in the cloth and the canvas separately and lay the canvas on the wrong side of the cloth with the seams on the inside and fasten the seams together securely. The seams are therefore not apparent. The cloth for the under collar must be padded onto the canvas, partly with sewing machine stitching, and partly with the small diagonal stitch with which the lapel was padded. See ''X," Diagram 9, showing the machine stitching, and "0," showing the diagonal stitching. The machine stitching as shown by "X," Diagram 9, is the "stand'* of the collar and is the part that is attached to the neck of the coat.
passages.plain: Sew the seam in the cloth and the seam in the canvas separately. Place the canvas on the wrong side of the cloth. Put the seams on the inside and fasten them together securely. This makes the seams invisible. You must pad the cloth for the under collar onto the canvas. Use sewing machine stitching for some parts. Use the small diagonal stitch for other parts. This is the same diagonal stitch used for the lapel. Look at Diagram 9. Letter X shows the machine stitching. Letter O shows the diagonal stitching. The machine stitching in X is the stand of the collar. This is the part that attaches to the neck of the coat.

passages.old: The diagonal stitching shown by "0" is that part of the collar called the ''roll" and is turned back over the stand. The machine stitching is put in first, beginning, not at the edge and working toward the center, but beginning at the longest row of machine stitching and sewing back and forth, each succeeding row of stitching getting shorter, until the edge of the collar is reached. Likewise the diagonal stitching is put in, beginning at the machine stitching and working toward the other edge The Home Dressmakers' Guide of the under collar.
passages.plain: The diagonal stitching shown by 0 is the part of the collar called the roll. This part is turned back over the stand. You must do the machine stitching first. Do not start at the edge and work toward the center. Instead, start at the longest row of machine stitching. Sew back and forth. Each new row of stitching should get shorter. Stop when you reach the edge of the collar. You must also do the diagonal stitching. Start at the machine stitching and work toward the other edge of the under collar.

passages.old: The machine stitching does not occupy half of the collar, but a little less than half, as the stand must be not quite as high as the roll that covers it, otherwise the stand of the collar would show on the finished coat. The machine stitching is therefore as deep as the collar is DIAGRA3I 9 The Length of the Under-Collar The under collar should not be cut until the neck of the coat fits perfectly. Then measure from the center back of the neck of the coat to where the lapel rolls.
passages.plain: The machine stitching does not cover half of the collar. It covers a little less than half. The stand must be slightly lower than the roll that covers it. If it is too high, the collar stand will show on the finished coat. The machine stitching is as deep as the collar is. Diagram 3. The Length of the Under-Collar. Do not cut the under collar until the neck of the coat fits perfectly. Measure from the center back of the neck of the coat to the point where the lapel rolls.

passages.old: This is half the length of the longest row of sewing machine stitching. The top row of sewing machine stitching should be on the line where the lapel turns. (See Dia- Measuring from the center back on the neck of the coat to where the "step" comes on the lapel will give the length of the under collar, cut double. When the under collar is thus prepared it must be shaped to fit more perfectly the neck of the individual. Shaping the Under-Collar Diagram 9 shows the under collar with the machine stitching and the padding ready to be shaped with a hot iron.
passages.plain: This measurement is half the length of the longest row of sewing machine stitching. Place the top row of sewing machine stitching on the line where the lapel turns. Look at Diagram 9. Measure from the center back of the coat neck to where the step starts on the lapel. This measurement gives you the length of the under collar. Cut the fabric into two pieces. Once the under collar is ready, you must shape it to fit the person's neck perfectly. Diagram 9 shows the under collar with the machine stitching and the padding. It is ready to be shaped with a hot iron.

passages.old: Place the collar flat on the pressing board with the canvas side up and the stand of the collar away from you. Moisten the whole surface of the collar with a wet sponge. Take the hot iron and press the stand side of the collar, stretching the edge both ways from the center as you proceed with the pressing. When the stand side of the collar is dry, turn the other edge of the collar away from you and press and stretch the edge of this side of the collar in the same way until the collar is all dry.
passages.plain: Place the collar flat on the pressing board. Put the canvas side up. Put the stand of the collar away from you. Wet the whole surface of the collar with a wet sponge. Take the hot iron. Press the stand side of the collar. Stretch the edge both ways from the center as you press. When the stand side of the collar is dry, turn the other edge of the collar away from you. Press and stretch the edge of this side of the collar in the same way. Do this until the collar is all dry.

passages.old: When the collar is thus shaped fold it on the line of the longest inside machine stitching and the under collar will have the proper shape as shown by Diagram 7. 102 The Home Dressmakers' Guide Attaching the Under-Collar Before this collar was thus shaped, the canvas was cut off the depth of a seam as shown by the shaded lines in Diagram 9. The under collar is now placed on the body of the coat. Turn the edge of the collar back like a hem and lay it flat onto the body of the coat.
passages.plain: Fold the collar on the line of the longest inside machine stitch. This gives the under collar the correct shape shown in Diagram 7. Before you shaped the collar, you cut the canvas off by the depth of a seam. You can see this in the shaded lines of Diagram 9. Place the under collar on the body of the coat. Turn the edge of the collar back like a hem. Lay it flat onto the body of the coat.

passages.old: Baste it on carefully, beginning at the center back and working toward the lapel; first one side, then the other. Sew the under collar to the coat, using a small cross-stitch. This will be made very plain if a welltailored coat is examined. Cross-stitch the canvas of the lapel to the canvas of the collar and press it down and the coat is ready for the upper collar and facing. Try the coat on to ascertain if the collar is shaped be« comingly and is the proper width where it joins the lapel.
passages.plain: Carefully baste the piece on. Start at the center back and work toward the lapel. Do one side first and then the other. Sew the under collar to the coat using a small cross-stitch. This part will look very plain if you look at a well-tailored coat. Cross-stitch the lapel canvas to the collar canvas. Press it down. The coat is now ready for the upper collar and facing. Try on the coat. Check if the collar has a nice shape. Check if it is the right width where it joins the lapel.

passages.old: Mark the canvas with a pencil while it is on the neck, mak^ ing it the desired size and shape. The collar can then be trimmed, following the penciled lines. Putting on the Facing Before the tape for the lapel and the front of the coat was cross-stitched to the edge of the canvas, the canvas was cut away the depth of a seam. Beginning at the step, the canvas was trimmed off all the way down the front and across the bottom as far as the facing extends. The facing is laid onto the body of the coat with the right side of the facing next to the right side of the coat and the facing stitched to the coat, not through the canvas, but following the edge of the canvas.
passages.plain: Mark the canvas with a pencil while it is on the neck. Make it the size and shape you want. You can then trim the collar by following the pencil lines. Before you cross-stitch the tape for the lapel and the front of the coat to the edge of the canvas, cut away the canvas by the depth of a seam. Start at the step. Trim off the canvas all the way down the front. Trim it across the bottom as far as the facing goes. Lay the facing onto the body of the coat. Place the right side of the facing next to the right side of the coat. Stitch the facing to the coat. Do not stitch through the canvas. Stitch along the edge of the canvas instead.

passages.old: Stitch from the top to the bottom and continue th« stitching across the bottom to the edge of the facing. Turn the facing back to the inside of the coat, and, after turning the back edge of the facing in like a hem, sew to the canvas with a large hemming stitch. When the canvas is trimmed off, the corners at the lapel and at the bottom of the coat must be rounded. I do not mean to cut it decidedly round, but just clip the sharp corners off and when the facing is turned back you will have neat square corners.
passages.plain: Stitch from the top to the bottom. Continue stitching across the bottom to the edge of the facing. Turn the facing to the inside of the coat. Turn the back edge of the facing in like a hem. Sew it to the canvas with a large hemming stitch. Trim off the canvas. You must round the corners at the lapel and at the bottom of the coat. Do not cut them perfectly round. Just clip the sharp corners off. When you turn the facing back, you will have neat square corners.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide 103 The Upper Collar The upper collar must always be cut crosswise on the cloth, or, in other words, following the same grain as that of the coat. The cloth for the upper collar must be cut generously and a little larger than the under collar ; it must never have a seam, but be cut in one piece. Place the upper collar onto the lower collar with the right side of each laid together. Baste the two together carefully and sew with the machine, following the line of the canvas, but not sewing through the canvas.
passages.plain: You must always cut the upper collar across the cloth. This means it must follow the same grain as the coat. You must cut the cloth for the upper collar generously. It should be a little larger than the under collar. The upper collar must be one piece. It must never have a seam. Place the upper collar on top of the lower collar. Put the right sides of both pieces together. Sew them together carefully with basting stitches. Then sew them with a machine. Follow the line of the canvas. Do not sew through the canvas.

passages.old: The upper collar is then turned over the under collar like any facing. Where the upper collar and facing join, the edge of each is folded under and these folds are brought together evenly and basted. When they are finally joined together they are sewed by hand, taking a stitch first in the facing, then in the collar, and drawing the stitches tight, thus bringing the two edges together perfectly. Where the facing ends at the shoulder seam, the cloth of the upper collar is trimmed off and left raw-edged and hemmed down to the body of the coat.
passages.plain: Turn the upper collar over the under collar like a facing. Fold the edges of the upper collar and the facing under. Bring these folds together evenly and sew them with temporary stitches. When you are ready to join them permanently, sew them by hand. Take one stitch in the facing and then one stitch in the collar. Pull the stitches tight to bring the two edges together perfectly. At the shoulder seam, trim the cloth of the upper collar. Leave the edge raw. Hem this edge down to the body of the coat.

passages.old: The lining covers this raw edge. Finishing the Hem The canvas is not turned up with the hem, but is cut off where the hem turns. Where the canvas is covered with the facing it extends to the bottom of the coat minus the seam, as has been explained. When the hem is turned, baste a stay on the inside of the hem. This stay may be made from a piece of cambric, cut crosswise, and just as wide as the hem. Attach this stay to the edge of the hem with a running stitch and tack the hem to each seam of the coat. This will help to hold the hem in place when the lining is attached to it. The hem must be pressed before the lining is put into the coat. The Home Dressmakers' Guide
passages.plain: The lining covers this raw edge. You must finish the hem now. Do not turn up the canvas with the hem. Instead, cut the canvas off where the hem turns. In places where the facing covers the canvas, the canvas should reach the bottom of the coat minus the seam. This was explained before. When you turn the hem, sew a stay on the inside of the hem. You can make this stay from a piece of cambric. Cut the cambric crosswise and make it as wide as the hem. Attach this stay to the edge of the hem with a running stitch. Tack the hem to each seam of the coat. This helps hold the hem in place when you attach the lining. You must press the hem before you put the lining into the coat.

chapters.why: The principles of taking precise measurements and adjusting patterns for a custom fit remain fundamental to modern bespoke tailoring.

chapters.title: The suit coat sleeve

passages.old: The sleeve for a Tailored suit must of necessity be closer fitting than the fuller Sport Coat or Top Coat Sleeve. There must be room for the action and natural curve of the arm, and yet, unlike the two-piece dress sleeve, for instance, which clings to the arm and follows its every movement, the tailored sleeve requires straighter lines, and attention must be given to have the right balance. It must also be remembered that the under sleeve must be one-half inch longer than the upper sleeve (See Altering the Sleeve Pattern, Chapter V).
passages.plain: The sleeve for a tailored suit must fit closer than the sleeves on a sport coat or a top coat. You must leave enough room for the arm to move and curve naturally. However, a tailored sleeve is different from a two-piece dress sleeve. A dress sleeve clings to the arm and follows every movement. A tailored sleeve needs straighter lines. You must pay attention to the balance. You must also remember that the under sleeve must be one-half inch longer than the upper sleeve. See Altering the Sleeve Pattern in Chapter V.

passages.old: How to Baste and Make This Sleeve Proceed to baste the inside seam in the same manner as for the dress sleeve previously considered. Pin the under and upper sleeve parts together. Commencing at the top, hold the half inch of fullness in the under part onto the upper part, between top and elbow, as clearly illustrated between X and X in Diagram 1. This fullness is necessary to shape the sleeve and make it hang properly. Moreover, this is only done in a coat sleeve.
