This completed, sew the seam, and, after dampening slightly with a wet sponge, press the seam open with showing the seam pressed open and clipped.) When sewing the front seam, and especially if you are using a sewing machine, stitch the seam so that no gathers will appear.
passages.plain: Now you will baste the inside seam. Do this the same way you did for the dress sleeve. Pin the bottom and top parts of the sleeve together. Start at the top. Hold the half inch of extra fabric in the bottom part against the top part. Do this between the top and the elbow. Look at Diagram 1 between X and X to see how to do this. You need this extra fabric to shape the sleeve so it hangs correctly. You only do this for a coat sleeve. When you finish, sew the seam. Dampen the seam slightly with a wet sponge. Press the seam open. Show the seam pressed open and clipped. When you sew the front seam, make sure there are no gathers. This is very important if you use a sewing machine.

passages.old: This may be done by stretching the seam when stitching so that the upper part will be stretched to the full length of the under part. Now cut a piece of tailor's canvas, about 5 inches deep, and lay the sleeve flat upon the table, pinning the canvas DIAGRAM The Home Dressmakers' Guide across the wrist. (See Diagram 2.) Diagram 2 shows a coat sleeve with the inside seam pressed open and clipped. (See "B.") The canvas is shown with the arrows marked "C" pointing to where the canvas is tacked to the inside seam to prevent it from working down after the sleeve is finished.
passages.plain: You can do this by stretching the seam while you stitch it. This makes the top part reach the full length of the bottom part. Next, cut a piece of tailor's canvas that is about 5 inches deep. Lay the sleeve flat on the table. Pin the canvas across the wrist. Look at Diagram 2. Diagram 2 shows a coat sleeve with the inside seam pressed open and clipped. The canvas is shown with arrows marked C. These arrows point to where you tack the canvas to the inside seam. This prevents the canvas from moving down after you finish the sleeve.

passages.old: The letter **A" points to the upper lap on the top of the sleeve which is turned back. These laps are finished like a placket in a tailored skirt. (See Plackets, Chapter VI.) Pin the outside seam from the wrist to within 1% inches of the elbow, and likewise from the top down to II/2 inches of the elbow. This will give the 3 inches necessary to hold 106 The Home Dressmakers' Guide in the fullness which must be provided at the elbow. Baste There must be no puckers or gathers in the outside seam at the elbow; work the gathers out when stitching.
passages.plain: The letter A shows the upper lap on the top of the sleeve. This lap is turned back. You should finish these laps like a placket in a tailored skirt. You can see how to do this in Chapter VI under Plackets. Pin the outside seam from the wrist to 1 inch before the elbow. Also pin the seam from the top down to 1/2 inch before the elbow. This creates the 3 inches of extra fabric needed for the fullness at the elbow. Baste the seam. You must not have any puckers or gathers in the outside seam at the elbow. You must work out the gathers while you are stitching.

passages.old: This may be done by using a large pin to keep the presser foot on the machine from shoving the gathers, for this would not look well in a tailored sleeve. Press this seam open. Turn and baste the wrist hem on the marked line, fastening down the edge of the hem to the canvas with a hemming stitch. The sleeve is then ready for the lining. The Lining The sleeve lining is always cut the same size as the sleeve ; but, when sewing the seam, just stitch inside of the basting, as it is necessary to have the lining a trifle smaller than the outside.
passages.plain: You can use a large pin to keep the presser foot from pushing the gathers. This is important because gathers do not look good in a tailored sleeve. Press this seam open. Turn the fabric. Sew a basting stitch on the marked line for the wrist hem. Fasten the edge of the hem to the canvas with a hemming stitch. The sleeve is now ready for the lining. You must cut the sleeve lining the same size as the sleeve. When you sew the seam, stitch just inside of the basting. The lining needs to be slightly smaller than the outside.

passages.old: Baste the inside seam of the lining first, and then the back seam. Do not press the seam open, but lay the lining upon the press board with the upper side of the lining next to the board and with the seams up. Press the seams flat. How to put the Sleeve Lining Into the Sleeve The sleeve lining should always be put into the sleeves before the sleeve itself is sewed into the coat. Lay the sleeve inside out upon the table and the lining also inside out upon the sleeves.
passages.plain: First, baste the inside seam of the lining. Then, baste the back seam. Do not press the seam open. Place the lining on the press board. Put the upper side of the lining next to the board. Keep the seams facing up. Press the seams flat. You must put the sleeve lining into the sleeves before you sew the sleeve into the coat. Lay the sleeve on the table inside out. Lay the lining on the sleeve inside out.

passages.old: Note: The sleeve is not inside the lining, but is separate, the lining on top. Pin the front seam of the sleeve and the front seam of the lining together. Be cautioned against holding the lining tightly. If it is tighter than the outside you will find yourself in a dilemma when the sleeve is turned right side out. Now pin the back seams together and sew both with a running stitch. By inserting the hand inside of the lining, draw the sleeve inside of the lining, turning the sleeve so that the right side of the lining will be on the outside.
passages.plain: The sleeve is not inside the lining. They are separate pieces with the lining on top. Pin the front seam of the sleeve to the front seam of the lining. Do not hold the lining too tightly. If the lining is tighter than the outside fabric, you will have a problem when you turn the sleeve right side out. Pin the back seams together. Sew both seams with a running stitch. Put your hand inside the lining. Pull the sleeve inside the lining. Turn the sleeve so the right side of the lining is on the outside.

passages.old: Turn in the lining at the wrist and baste to the hem of the sleeve. Conclude the operation by re-inserting the hand inside of the sleeve and turning it right side out, after which you may run a basting thread around the sleeve about 5 inches from the top. This holds the lining in place while you are sewing the sleeve into the coat. The Home Dressmakers' Guide Where to Place the Front Seam of a Sleeve in an Armseye ' The front seam of the sleeve is placed about 2% inches in front of the under arm seam; that is, for the average woman.
passages.plain: Turn the lining inward at the wrist. Baste it to the hem of the sleeve. Put your hand inside the sleeve and turn it to the right side out. Sew a basting thread around the sleeve about 5 inches from the top. This keeps the lining in place while you sew the sleeve into the coat. Place the front seam of the sleeve about 2 inches in front of the under arm seam. This is for the average woman.

passages.old: This should be more or less, as the armseye is larger or smaller. Indeed, a reliable method often used is that of holding the armseye from an inch back of the shoulder seam on a perfect bias. The point reached on the front of the coat is then the guide for the front of the sleeve. Sleeves for sport coats, long coats, and, in fact, all top coats, must be cut larger than the suit coat sleeves. That is, all circumference measurements must be increased according to the size desired.
passages.plain: This measurement will change depending on the size of the armseye. One reliable method is to hold the armseye from one inch back of the shoulder seam on a perfect bias. The point you reach on the front of the coat serves as the guide for the front of the sleeve. You must cut sleeves for sport coats, long coats, and all top coats larger than suit coat sleeves. You must increase all circumference measurements based on the size you want.

passages.old: DIAGRAM 4 DIAGRAM 3 The sleeve for the coat must than the armseye, and this fullness carefully distributed as There must not be even the suggestion of a pucker or gathers at the top of a coat sleeve. The coat is turned inside out and the sleeve sewed into the armseye from the inside. (See Diagram Uy showing the sleeve being basted from the inside.) 108 The Home Dressmakers' Guide Having sewed the sleeve into the armseye of the coat and the seam pressed open, you are ready to insert the ''roll" for the top of the sleeve.
passages.plain: Look at Diagram 3 and Diagram 4. The sleeve for the coat must be larger than the armseye. You must distribute this extra fullness carefully. There should not be any puckers or gathers at the top of the coat sleeve. Turn the coat inside out. Sew the sleeve into the armseye from the inside. See Diagram Uy to see how to baste the sleeve from the inside. After you sew the sleeve into the armseye of the coat, press the seam open. You are now ready to insert the roll for the top of the sleeve.

passages.old: This roll is made from two or three thicknesses of sheet wadding and is cut oblong and folded lengthwise, making one edge straight while the other edge is curved. This roll should be about six inches long. It is attached to the sleeve part of the armseye seam of the coat. Baste the top of the sleeve lining to the armseye seam and sew it down by hand using a long running stitch. When the lining of the coat is put in, it is sewed onto the sleeve lining at the armseye.
passages.plain: This roll is made from two or three layers of sheet wadding. You cut it into an oblong shape and fold it lengthwise. This makes one edge straight and the other edge curved. The roll should be about six inches long. You attach it to the sleeve part of the armseye seam of the coat. Baste the top of the sleeve lining to the armseye seam. Sew it down by hand using a long running stitch. When you put the coat lining in, you sew it onto the sleeve lining at the armseye.

passages.old: This gives a neat looking finish and also wears well. When the coat is put on the arm will not rub the sleeve lining seam but will pass over a smooth surface causing the lining to wear longer. Pressing One of the greatest difficulties the Home-dressmaker experiences in pressing is in keeping the cloth from looking shiney and becoming marked. This is owing to the sponge cloth being pressed until it becomes dry. The iron should always be lifted from the sponge cloth while there is steam in the cloth of the garment being pressed.
passages.plain: This method gives a neat finish and lasts a long time. When you wear the coat, the arm will not rub against the sleeve lining seam. It will move over a smooth surface. This helps the lining last longer. Pressing is a hard task for the home dressmaker. It is difficult to keep the cloth from looking shiny or getting marks. This happens when you press the sponge cloth until it is dry. You must always lift the iron from the sponge cloth while there is still steam in the garment cloth.

passages.old: It is this steam and the fact that the press cloth is not dry, that keeps the cloth from being shiney and marked and the seams from showing through. If there are shiney spots or marks from pressing on the cloth, place a wet sponge cloth over the places and put a hot iron on the sponge cloth and take it off quickly. This is called ''steaming." The shine, thread marks, or creases from former pressing, can all be removed by steaming. A piece of unbleached muslin or a piece of tailors canvas makes a good sponge cloth.
passages.plain: Steam and a damp press cloth keep the fabric from getting shiny or marked. These things also stop the seams from showing through. If you see shiny spots or marks from pressing, place a wet sponge cloth over those spots. Put a hot iron on the sponge cloth and remove it quickly. This method is called steaming. You can remove shine, thread marks, or creases from previous pressing by steaming. You can use a piece of unbleached muslin or a piece of tailor's canvas as a sponge cloth.

passages.old: When pressing the seam of a woolen garment always press the seam on the wrong side. Dampen the seam first with a wet sponge and use an iron hot enough to sizzle. When the hem of a dress or skirt is being pressed, place the garment on the table inside out and place the sponge cloth on the wrong side of the hem. Dampen the sponge cloth with a wet sponge and press with a warm iron until the sponge cloth is nearly dry. Lift the sponge cloth off while there is steam in the garment and this will prevent the hem from looking shiney and marked.
passages.plain: Always press the seam of a woolen garment on the wrong side. First, dampen the seam with a wet sponge. Use an iron that is hot enough to sizzle. When you press the hem of a dress or skirt, place the garment on the table inside out. Place the sponge cloth on the wrong side of the hem. Dampen the sponge cloth with a wet sponge. Press it with a warm iron until the sponge cloth is almost dry. Lift the sponge cloth off while there is still steam in the garment. This will stop the hem from looking shiny or marked.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide 109 Any part of a garment where there is canvas should be pressed on the canvas side. It is almost necessary to have a hot iron handy at all times when making a tailored suit. Each part should be pressed as it is made. For instance, when the roll of the lapel is determined it should be pressed. This is also an instance where the garment is pressed on the canvas side. Each seam should be pressed as it is finished. The sleeve should be well pressed before it is finally sewed into the armseye.
passages.plain: Press any part of a garment that has canvas on the canvas side. You almost need to have a hot iron ready at all times when you make a tailored suit. You should press each part as you make it. For example, you should press the lapel once you decide on its roll. This is another time to press on the canvas side. You should press each seam as you finish it. You must press the sleeve well before you sew it into the armseye.

passages.old: When the canvas of the under collar is attached to the canvas of the lapel it must be pressed. When pressing on the canvas rub the canvas with a wet sponge and press until the canvas is dry. Always use a thick sponge cloth on the right side of a garment, as a thick cloth holds the steam, and take the sponge cloth off while the steam is still in the garment. A piece of tailors canvas is decidedly the best to use, for a sponge cloth, for the right side of a garment.
passages.plain: Press the under collar canvas when you attach it to the lapel canvas. Rub the canvas with a wet sponge while you press it. Press until the canvas is dry. Always use a thick sponge cloth on the right side of a garment. A thick cloth holds the steam. Remove the sponge cloth while the steam is still in the garment. A piece of tailor's canvas is the best thing to use as a sponge cloth for the right side of a garment.

passages.old: Dampen the canvas with a sponge and press with a warm iron. The armseye seam can be pressed by putting the end of the pressboard, or sleeveboard, into the armseye from the right side. If you have no sleeve board and you are pressing seams in the sleeves, or any seam where it is not best to touch the cloth with the hot iron, a broom handle will be found to work very satisfactorily. Making the Button Holes First, decide on the number of buttons for the front of the coat.
passages.plain: Moisten the canvas with a sponge. Press it with a warm iron. You can press the armseye seam by putting the end of a pressboard or sleeveboard into the armseye from the right side. If you do not have a sleeve board, you can use a broom handle. This works well for pressing seams in sleeves or any seam where you should not touch the cloth with a hot iron. Make the buttonholes first. Decide how many buttons you want for the front of the coat.

passages.old: If individual taste or prevailing style selects three as the number they must be placed properly. It is not sufficient that the buttons be evenly spaced, the proper position for each button is equally important. With the regulation lapel one of the three buttons must be placed on the waist line, one below the bust line and one above the bust line. Never place one of the buttons right on the bust line, especially if the bust is prominent. Always have one on the waist line so there will be an unbroken line around the waist.
passages.plain: If you choose to use three buttons, you must place them correctly. It is not enough for the buttons to be spaced evenly. The specific position of each button matters. For a regular lapel, you must place one button on the waist line. You must place one button below the bust line. You must place one button above the bust line. Never put a button directly on the bust line. This is especially true if the bust is prominent. You must always have one button on the waist line. This creates a straight line around the waist.

passages.old: The Home Dressmakers' Guide After the position of the buttons the next in importance are the spaces between each button ; they must be the same. (See Having determined the position of the buttons and the space between them, the next in order is the size of the button hole. Place the button on the place marked for it on the cloth and mark the diameter of the button. Now, mark each button hole exactly the same size. It is important that the round hole in the outside edge of the button hole be, at or 1/2 inch back from the stitching if there is stitching showing at the edge of the Cutting the Button Hole The round hole at the outside edge of a tailored buttonhole is made with a button-hole punch.
passages.plain: After you decide where the buttons go, the next important step is the space between each button. These spaces must be the same. Once you have decided on the button positions and the spaces between them, you must decide on the size of the buttonhole. Place the button on the marked spot on the cloth. Mark the diameter of the button. Now mark every buttonhole the exact same size. It is important that the round hole on the outside edge of the buttonhole is at the stitching or 1/2 inch back from the stitching. This applies if there is stitching showing at the edge. You make the round hole at the outside edge of a tailored buttonhole with a buttonhole punch.

passages.old: This button-hole punch is similar to an eyelet embroidery punch and can be obtained at any hardware store. Before punching the hole or cutting the button-hole if the cloth is a loose weave, put in one row of sewing machine stitching each side of the mark for the diameter of the button. Make this stitching the length of the button-hole and cut in between this stitching. This will hold the cloth, canvas and facing together and will also keep the buttonhole from ravelling. Make the hole with the punch first, at the outer edge, and then cut the button-hole.
passages.plain: You can buy a button-hole punch at any hardware store. It is similar to an eyelet embroidery punch. If your cloth has a loose weave, you must sew a row of stitches on each side of the mark before you punch the hole or cut the button-hole. The stitches should be the same length as the button-hole. You will cut between these stitches. This keeps the cloth, canvas, and facing together. It also stops the button-hole from unraveling. Use the punch to make the hole at the outer edge first. Then you can cut the button-hole.

passages.old: Sometimes overcasting the edges of the button-hole will be all that is necessary. This tailored button-hole is finished with a cord called **guimp." The guimp is used on the edge of the buttonbetween the two thicknesses of cloth at the inside end of the button-hole. Hold the cord evenly on the edge of the button-hole and take the button-hole stitches over the cord. The cord will make a strong button-hole. This is called the The Home Dressmakers' Guide 111 Begin to stitch at the inside end of the button-hole (See button-hole next to your left hand.
passages.plain: Sometimes you only need to overcast the edges of the buttonhole. This tailored buttonhole is finished with a cord called guimp. You use the guimp on the edge of the buttonhole between the two thicknesses of cloth at the inside end. Hold the cord evenly on the edge of the buttonhole. Take the buttonhole stitches over the cord. The cord will make a strong buttonhole. Begin to stitch at the inside end of the buttonhole. See the buttonhole next to your left hand.

passages.old: Work out to the edge and continue around the punched hole and back to the inside end again. To secure this end of the cord and make a neat finish at the inside end of the button-hole, a bar can be made. Take about two stitches across the end and wind the thread around these stitches doing so with the needle. This is not a button-hole stitch but just working the thread around the first two stitches and making it look like a cord. Sewing on the Buttons Buttons must not be stitched flat to the body of, a tailored coat.
passages.plain: Sew out to the edge. Continue sewing around the punched hole and back to the inside end. You can make a bar to secure this end of the cord. This makes a neat finish at the inside end of the buttonhole. Take about two stitches across the end. Wind the thread around these stitches using the needle. This is not a buttonhole stitch. You are just wrapping the thread around the first two stitches to make it look like a cord. You must not sew buttons flat to the body of a tailored coat.

passages.old: The buttons must be sewed on leaving a shank between the button and the cloth. To do this leave the thread long when sewing on the buttons; that is, do not pull the thread tight. When the button has been sewed on loosely, wrap the thread around and around the thread between the button and the cloth, thus forming the shank. Never allow the stitches to show on the facing. Never, never sew the button on through the cloth and the facing. Sew through cloth and canvas but stop this side of the facing.
passages.plain: You must sew the buttons so there is a space between the button and the cloth. To do this, leave the thread long while you sew. Do not pull the thread tight. Once the button is sewn on loosely, wrap the thread around the thread between the button and the cloth. This creates the shank. You must never let the stitches show on the facing. You must never sew the button through both the cloth and the facing. Sew through the cloth and the canvas. Stop before you reach the facing.

passages.old: POCKETS The first operation in the making of a pocket is exactly like the procedure for a bound button-hole. (See Bound Button-holes, Chapter L) The first thing to be done is to locate the position the pocket will occupy upon the garment; determine its size and shape and mark the outline on the right side of the cloth. This pocket may be straight across, it may be made lengthwise, or it may be half-moon shape. (See Diagram 6.) The pocket may be shaped according to fancy. Whatever the shape they are all operated in the same way.
passages.plain: The first step in making a pocket is the same as making a bound buttonhole. You can see this in Chapter L. First, find where the pocket will go on the garment. Decide on its size and shape. Mark the outline on the right side of the cloth. The pocket can be straight across. It can be made lengthwise. It can also be a half-moon shape. You can see Diagram 6. You can shape the pocket however you like. All shapes are made in the same way.

passages.old: First, place the binding over the mark for the pocket DIAGRAM 6 binding next to the right side of the garment. 112 The Home Dressmakers' Guide The material is usually called a facing when used in connection with pockets. It is called a binding when used in connection with the bound button-hole. Mark the size and shape of the pocket on the facing and put in two rows of sewing machine stitching, one on each side of the mark for the pocket and about % of an inch apart, just as was done for the bound button-hole.
passages.plain: First, place the binding over the mark for the pocket. This is shown in Diagram 6. The binding goes next to the right side of the garment. People usually call this material a facing when it is used for pockets. They call it a binding when it is used for a bound button-hole. Mark the size and shape of the pocket on the facing. Sew two rows of stitching with your sewing machine. Put one row on each side of the pocket mark. Keep the rows about 1/8 of an inch apart. Do this just like you did for the bound button-hole.

passages.old: Next, cut the pocket following the mark and cutting through both facing and cloth. Do not cut to the ends of the mark, stop before the end is reached so as not to cut the stitching and make the corner just as was done for the bound button-hole. Turn the facing to the wrong side and baste the edges carefully. The facing for the pocket, unlike the bound button-hole is not allowed to show from the right side. Pull the facing until it hardly shows but do not turn any of the body of the cloth with the facing.
passages.plain: Next, cut the pocket along the mark. Cut through both the facing and the cloth. Do not cut all the way to the ends of the mark. Stop before you reach the end so you do not cut the stitching. Make the corner the same way you made the bound button-hole. Turn the facing to the wrong side. Sew the edges with basting stitches carefully. The facing for the pocket must not show on the right side. This is different from the bound button-hole. Pull the facing until it barely shows. Do not turn any of the main cloth with the facing.

passages.old: The inside part of the pocket, or to be correct, the pocket itself, is in two pieces. The pocket may be any depth desired. Sew the front half of the pocket to the lower part of the facing. By the front half of the pocket is meant that half of the inside that is toward the front. It is the lower half. Sew this half of the pocket to the lower edge of the facing from the inside. Next stitch across the lower edge of the opening and pull the threads through and tie them on the inside at the ends of the pocket.
passages.plain: The pocket is made of two pieces. You can make the pocket any depth you want. Sew the front half of the pocket to the lower part of the facing. The front half is the lower half of the inside that faces the front. Sew this half of the pocket to the lower edge of the facing from the inside. Next, stitch across the lower edge of the opening. Pull the threads through. Tie the threads on the inside at the ends of the pocket.

passages.old: The other half of the inside of the pocket is next sewed on. This part of the pocket must have a piece of the material of the coat sewed across the top to keep the lining, (or w^hatever the material of which the pocket is made) from showing through the opening. When this part of the pocket is thus prepared, baste it on to the wrong side of the coat with the piece of the material that has been sewed on next to the opening. This part of the pocket is basted to the facing above the opening.
passages.plain: Sew on the other half of the inside of the pocket. You must sew a piece of coat material across the top of this part of the pocket. This prevents the lining or pocket material from showing through the opening. Once you have prepared this part of the pocket, baste it onto the wrong side of the coat. Place the piece of material that you sewed next to the opening against the coat. Baste this part of the pocket to the facing above the opening.

passages.old: Stitch the last part on, stitching from the right side of the coat. This stitching also makes the finish across the top of the pocket.
